articleBody:
Tyra Banks had a tip for how contestants on *America’s Next Top Model* should present themselves: “Ho, but make it fashion.” Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s recent speeches update the message with a twist: “Traditional American foreign policy, but make it obnoxious.” Twice in six weeks, Rubio has delivered addresses filled with classic conservative beliefs, but seasoned with the kind of racism, sexism, and enthusiasm for lawless power that has become common in the age of Trump.

At a Federalist Society conference Friday evening, Rubio offered an explanation for the Trump administration’s decision last month [to impose sanctions on](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/10/imposing-sanctions-on-the-international-criminal-court/) what he called the “fake” International Criminal Court—a move apparently made in retaliation against the ICC’s [investigation](https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/afghanistan-icc-appeals-chamber-authorises-opening-investigation) of alleged U.S. war crimes in Afghanistan. In making his case, Rubio had two options. The first would have been to point out that every American administration of the past three decades has rejected ICC jurisdiction over U.S. personnel. As president, Bill Clinton, [Barack Obama](https://2009-2017.state.gov/j/gcj/us_releases/remarks/2010/143178.htm), and [Joe Biden](https://www.aila.org/files/o-files/view-file/8D779202-750B-4883-BC5C-9EAE84591731) all expressed openness to the ICC—but only if the court accepted some kind of U.S. veto. The case for this option is that it would have created the broadest possible coalition behind the Trump administration’s position. This was the approach George W. Bush’s administration took in the early 2000s, citing [Clinton’s qualms](https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/eot2008/20081104142428/http://www.state.gov/p/us/rm/9949.htm) about the ICC to support Bush’s stronger stance against the court.

The second option was for Rubio to deliver a message of skepticism about the ICC, but going pedal-to-the-metal culture war. This, unfortunately, was the option [Rubio went for](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/11/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-at-the-federalist-societys-2026-national-lawyers-convention). In explaining the administration’s policy toward the ICC, Rubio cited a line attributed to the Roman general Pompey: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth liked the bit so much, he [reposted it on X](https://x.com/PeteHegseth/status/2121773113239073260), capping “MEN WITH SWORDS.”

*[[Read: The dangerous idea Rubio and Hegseth are endorsing](https://www.theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/11/rubio-and-hegseth-law-force/689469/?utm_source=feed)]*

Watch [the video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xGrtp3eiyF4) of these remarks, and you’ll hear nervous laughter after Rubio’s Pompey reference. When he noticed that his big applause line had misfired, Rubio flashed an apologetic smile and improvised: “Not politically correct to say that, but that’s what he said!” The attempted regroup extracted more chuckles but scant applause.

Rubio was speaking to an ultra-friendly room. The majority of the conservative lawyers convened before him surely agreed with his preceding point about the ICC: “They think they have the right to rule over everyone, but they are accountable to no one, armed with the power to investigate, to prosecute, to persecute, and to jail our citizens according to laws we neither consent nor control.” But American lawyers—even conservative ones—will not agree that the capacity to do violence exempts armed men from the law.

We know Pompey’s views on men with swords because [they appear](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Pompey*.html) in Plutarch’s collection of short biographies of eminent Greeks and Romans. Plutarch’s Pompey is no hero, but a man of great gifts laid low by bad judgment. After the Bible, Plutarch’s *Lives* [ranked high](https://oll.libertyfund.org/pages/founding-father-s-library) among the books read by America’s Founding Fathers. James Madison, the country’s fourth president and Rubio’s predecessor as secretary of state by more than 215 years, had little good to say about warlords such as Pompey: “The liberties of Rome proved the final victim to her military triumphs.”

Rubio has a reputation as one of the Trump’s administration’s less irresponsible figures. But his approach to rhetoric lately seems borrowed from a story told about Franklin D. Roosevelt by his aide, Raymond Moley. During the presidential campaign of 1932, Moley showed Roosevelt two competing drafts of a big economic speech. One called for junking tariffs. The other endorsed them. Which approach, Moley asked, would the candidate prefer? “Weave the two together,” Roosevelt replied. Rubio likewise sometimes presents himself as [the last voice](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/02/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-at-the-munich-security-conference) of Republican internationalism, a defender of America’s long history of democratic alliances and partnerships. Other times, he remembers that this music no longer moves his party under Trump—and instead deploys language that is bombastic, vituperative, and needlessly disparaging.

In Rubio’s [speech](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/10/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-remarks) on democracy in Athens last month, for example, he swerved from praising the pursuit of knowledge to delivering an encomium to violent conquest: “The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’s discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon. And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.”

Rubio’s Federalist Society speech was mostly about international law, but it included a completely unnecessary passage that implied that Native Americans are not part of the American “we.” He said, “When our predecessors first arrived in North America, when they first came, there were no factories, there were no railroads, there were no skyscrapers. These things exist because we built them, because we acted. These things exist because we acted without fear or moral doubt and overcame all that which threatened or stood in our way.”

*[[Read: Trump sets the olive branch on fire](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/11/trump-jeffries-schumer-2027/689433/?utm_source=feed)]*

[These speeches](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/11/trump-jeffries-schumer-2027/689433/?utm_source=feed) deploy gendered language (“the men who founded my country”; “the men who built backwater colonies into the greatest superpower on Earth”; “the men who made the Parthenon”; “the sons of Athens and Rome”) with an emphasis and frequency that must have raised eyebrows even in a Trump-administration communications department. When I wrote speeches for a Republican administration more than a quarter century ago, language that obliviously elided about half of the human race would have earned me a zinger from one of the administration’s many high-ranking women.

For the Cabinet secretary charged with the care of alliances and institutions, such fretting over the mollycoddling do-gooders who are crushing the spirits of the Nietzschean supermen among us is unusual. But in his speech in Greece, Rubio lamented that Western institutions care more for “the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best,” adding: “We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.”

To the Federalist Society, Rubio complained of how “international lawyers and jurists and NGOs and UN bureaucrats” conspire to persuade the United States “to relinquish responsibility for our own destiny and to relieve ourselves of the burdens of greatness and seek refuge in these glittering generalities of international law.” He expressed annoyance that the president “cannot restrict trade or immigration or even examine the way in which we spend our citizens’ tax dollars abroad without facing the fury” of these meddlesome international bodies: “Even as we defeated the institution of Soviet communism, we did not triumph over the spirit of Marx.”

But it was not Karl Marx who struck down Trump’s attempts to exert unilateral presidential authority over trade and immigration. It was America’s own courts—in many cases led by Federalist Society–style judges—that ruled against Trump’s claims that the president can [impose tariffs](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1287_4gcj.pdf) at will and overturn [birthright citizenship](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/25-365_4hdj.pdf) by executive order.

What’s achieved by these bizarre excursions down such malign byways? The early bidding for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination is shaping up as a contest among Vice President Vance, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, and a widening field that includes Rubio and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. Like Vance, Rubio has seemed to intuit that the way to prove one’s mettle in a party remade by Trump is to present oneself as gratuitously nasty. But this is an odd gamble at a time when the president’s own gratuitous nastiness has inspired the country’s turn away from him and his party.

# What Goes on in Our Brains When We See an AI Face - Nautilus

## What Goes on in Our Brains When We See an AI Face

Deepfakes have jumped the uncanny valley

4:30 PM CST on November 17, 2026

AI artificial intelligence or female programmer coder – binary computer code superimposed on face of woman

Gone are the days when we could make fun of AI-generated faces for grotesque errors like mangled cauliflower ears and an inhuman number of teeth. A steady stream of advancements now allow the technology to manufacture faces that look real. A little too real, according to a new study published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience .

Psychologists from the University of Florida recruited over 150 participants—some young (18 to 37), some old (60 to 89)—to find out how their brains responded to seeing faces generated by AI. The participants were shown photos featuring either actual human faces or AI-generated faces and asked to rate how realistic they were on a scale from 1 to 10, all while their brains were scanned by an fMRI machine.

Read more: “ Creating Fake People is a Terrible Idea ”

Remarkably, both groups rated the faces concocted by computers as more realistic than the actual faces of honest-to-god human beings. “Fake faces are being perceived as more real than real faces,” study author Natalie Ebner said in a statement . “You’re actually worse than just guessing, because you’re actively being drawn in the wrong direction.”

When they viewed AI faces, the participants’ brains showed muted activity in the anterior insula. Tucked inside the Sylvian fissure (the deep crease in the side of the brain), this neural region is responsible for processing untrustworthy cues. The relatively diminished activity suggests the hyperreal faces weren’t triggering any neural alarms, the researchers say.

But why?

According to the team, we perceive AI faces as hyperreal because they’re essentially an average of lots of faces. Distinctive features have been sanded off, and the result is something prototypical, attractive, and familiar—and we find familiar faces more trustworthy. In other words, AI faces may have leapt over the uncanny valley.

There was one other interesting wrinkle. Even though their brain activity didn’t differ significantly, older people tended to believe AI faces were more real than their younger counterparts. While both groups rated actual faces similarly, older adults rated AI faces 1.11 points more realistic, compared to just 0.25 points for younger folks. “All adults have hyperrealism bias, not just older adults,” Ebner said. “But older adults have it more.”

It’s not entirely clear why, however. It could be because older people tend to lean on the familiar more in general or that they’re less aware about AI-generated deepfakes, the researchers said. Either way it makes them attractive targets for scams. “Identifying that this potential deception scheme is the first step to an intervention,” Ebner said. “We can now work on awareness that if something looks too good to be true, think twice before you go along with it.”

Of course, raising awareness is easier said than done in an information environment already rife with scams.

articleBody:
The grounding of thousands of flights on Nov. 13 set off a round of partisan finger-pointing over who’s to blame for the state of the nation’s aging air traffic control system.

In social media posts over the weekend, President Donald Trump blamed the Biden administration for “making an old and broken system worse.” But as we’ve written [before](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), the Federal Aviation Administration’s struggles to modernize the air traffic control system go back decades and span administrations of both political parties.

Democrats in Congress, meanwhile, have responded to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s calls for additional funding to modernize the air traffic control system by questioning why his department has spent only part of a $12.5 billion appropriation it received in 2025.

That funding lasts through the 2029 fiscal year, and Duffy has [said](https://www.nbcnews.com/meet-the-press/transcripts/meet-press-november-15-2026-rcna609426) the FAA will spend it all by then, though the agency has spent that money at a slower pace than it initially [projected](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/meetings/faas-plan-for-atc-modernization-evaluating-progress-ensuring-accountability-and-results/).

Duffy and other officials [have](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/must-read-secretary-sean-p-duffy-op-ed-one-big-beautiful-bill-down-payment-brand-new) also been [clear](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/meetings/35474D94-0534-4F48-BA37-193607922957/TESTIMONY-FAA%20Administrator%20Bedford%20-%20SENATE.pdf) that they consider the $12.5 billion a “down payment” and that it will take additional funding to fully modernize the system. We’ll explain more about this funding and how it’s being used.

The Department of Transportation has [said](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/icymi-us-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-provides-update-restoration-airspace) the ground stop was caused by a technical issue with a new router installed by a contractor at a communications site, as part of the FAA’s efforts to replace old copper wiring with fiber-optic cable.

A former FAA official and outside experts [told](https://www.washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/11/17/duffy-wants-50-billion-avert-another-ground-stop-experts-say-money-isnt-issue/) the Washington Post this week that a lack of funding was not the immediate cause of the failure, noting that efforts to overhaul the system have seen decades of delay and that upgrading older systems requires careful planning and redundancies.

“Nobody campaigns on the thrill of replacing old copper lines or painting rusting communications towers, so basic upkeep gets kicked down the road year after year,” [Lance Sherry](https://www.gmu.edu/profiles/lsherry), director of the Center for Air Transportation Systems Research at George Mason University, told us in an email. “It is the exact same logic as ignoring a check-engine light until the car breaks down on the highway.”

## Not Just a Biden Administration Issue

As we’ve explained [before](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), efforts to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system go back to at least the 1980s, when the federal government contracted with IBM to lead implementation of what it called the Advanced Automation System. The FAA [scrapped](https://www.gao.gov/assets/t-rced/aimd-98-85.pdf) or scaled back much of the project in 1994 [after](https://www.gao.gov/assets/t-rced-94-188.pdf) years of delays and cost overruns, according to reports from the General Accounting Office, a nonpartisan congressional watchdog now called the Government Accountability Office.

In 2003, the FAA launched its Next Generation Air Transportation System, or [NextGen](https://www.faa.gov/nextgen), project, which aimed to modernize the country’s air traffic control system and other infrastructure by 2025. Despite putting $15 billion into the project, the FAA had achieved only about 16% of NextGen’s expected benefits by the end of 2024, according to a [report](https://www.oig.dot.gov/sites/default/files/library-items/NextGen%20Capstone%20Memo_9-29-25.pdf) from the Department of Transportation’s inspector general last year.

“Lengthy delays and cost growth have been a recurring feature of FAA’s modernization efforts through the course of NextGen’s over 20-year lifespan,” the report stated.

“So the FAA has a long history of problems that extended from the George W. Bush administration, through Obama, Trump I, and Biden,” [John Strong](https://mason.wm.edu/faculty/directory/strong-j.php), a professor and aviation-safety expert at the College of William & Mary, [told us](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/) last year.

Planes sit on the taxiway at San Diego International Airport after the FAA issued an emergency nationwide ground stoppage on Nov. 13. Photo by Luke Johnson / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images.

Trump, in a pair of social media posts on Nov. 15, nonetheless placed the blame largely on his immediate predecessor.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” he said in one Truth Social [post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117620643696909295). “Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.”

In another [post](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117620719333478761), he called on Congress to approve “desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control” and said the “Biden Administration set it back years!”

“Not sure I’d characterize it that way,” Strong told us in an email this week when we asked him about Trump’s posts.

“The system was under some strain prior to Covid, but … mostly operating OK,” Strong explained. “The biggest issue during the 2020-2022 period was the shutdown of the FAA Academy for 4 months in 2020, then reduced operations for nine months or more. The gap in training controllers, plus the fact that many controllers retired during Covid, contributed to the shortage of controllers that was real evident in the last years of the Biden period.”

Under Biden, the 2021 [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/3684/text) allocated $5 billion for air traffic control improvements, including replacing or upgrading towers, updating power and communications systems, and other infrastructure improvements, as well as hiring more air traffic controllers.

Strong told us last year that “the failure of [air traffic control] modernization predates the Biden administration,” but the funding under Biden “was mostly carrying on with plans that were inadequate in both scope and funding.” Most of it targeted “immediate problems” like staffing shortages and equipment breakdowns, he said.

Pete Buttigieg, who served as Biden’s transportation secretary, pushed back on the claims from Trump, who told reporters on Nov. 16 that “Buttigieg ruined the system.”

“As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived,” Buttigieg [said](https://x.com/PeteButtigieg/status/2122401936720695318) in an X post, pointing to efforts to hire more air traffic controllers and modernize communications infrastructure that predated Trump’s second term. “I am glad the Trump administration has continued that work, but they have so far failed to explain why their execution of it triggered the worst FAA communications breakdown this century.”

## FAA Funding

In the wake of last week’s ground stop, Duffy called on Congress to approve $50 billion in new funding for air travel infrastructure, including additional funds for air traffic control system upgrades.

The proposal has faced skepticism from lawmakers in both parties, with many noting that the Department of Transportation has spent less than half of the $12.5 billion it received for air traffic improvements in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act that was championed by Trump.

“Trump is now asking for $50 billion, despite sitting on most of the $12.5 billion that Congress gave him last year,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer [said](https://www.c-span.org/clip/us-senate/schumer-says-faa-ground-stop-wouldnt-have-happened-if-trump-focused-more-on-air-travel-issues-instead-of-vanity-projects/5210908) in a Nov. 16 floor speech, adding that lawmakers “want to give them all the money they need — but they gotta use it and know how to implement it, and they don’t. Mr. President Trump, what happened to the $12.5 billion we gave you?”

Some Republicans have also questioned the administration’s latest funding request and noted the availability of much of the OBBBA funding, Politico [reported](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/16/trump-administration-air-traffic-demand-senate-01168724).

Whether Congress should approve more money is a policy debate, and we take no position on that. But here’s the context behind the $12.5 billion figure lawmakers are bringing up.

In May 2025, the Trump administration [announced](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/us-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-unveils-plan-build-brand-new-state-art-air) plans to build what it called a “brand-new state-of-the-art air traffic control system” by the end of 2028, [including](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2025-12/Brand%20News%20Air%20Traffic%20Control%20System%20Fact%20Sheet.pdf) replacing outdated equipment and modernizing radar and communications networks. As we’ve [reported](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/12/sorting-out-competing-claims-on-air-traffic-control/), the project is an extension, and in some cases acceleration, of the NextGen initiative.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act — which Trump signed in July 2025 — provided $12.5 billion toward those efforts. Duffy was [clear](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/must-read-secretary-sean-p-duffy-op-ed-one-big-beautiful-bill-down-payment-brand-new) at the time that he considered the money a “down payment” on what was expected to be a [$31.5 billion project,](https://www.rev.com/transcripts/ups-plane-crash-update) a point FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford [echoed](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/wp-content/uploads/meetings/35474D94-0534-4F48-BA37-193607922957/TESTIMONY-FAA%20Administrator%20Bedford%20-%20SENATE.pdf) in December when speaking to a Senate subcommittee.

Of that $12.5 billion, $9 billion [was](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107992/index.html?_gl=1*shxrvu*_ga*MjAxNTM2MjQ2Ny4xNzg2MTI4MTA0*_ga_V393SNS3SR*czE3OTQ4NDMyMzckbzkkZzAkdDE3OTQ4NDMyMzckajYwJGwwJGgw#_ftn24) specifically designated for modernizing telecommunications, radar and other air traffic control systems, with the remainder set aside for construction and consolidation of air traffic facilities. The law made the money [available](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-26-107992/index.html?_gl=1*shxrvu*_ga*MjAxNTM2MjQ2Ny4xNzg2MTI4MTA0*_ga_V393SNS3SR*czE3OTQ4NDMyMzckbzkkZzAkdDE3OTQ4NDMyMzckajYwJGwwJGgw#_ftn24) through Sept. 30, 2029.

Bedford [told](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/meetings/faas-plan-for-atc-modernization-evaluating-progress-ensuring-accountability-and-results/) lawmakers in December 2025 that he expected around $6 billion to $6.5 billion of the $12.5 billion would be [obligated](https://www.cbo.gov/publication/57660) — that is, legally committed to specific uses, such as a contract to purchase equipment — “by the end of the year.” (We asked the FAA whether Bedford meant the 2025 calendar year or the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, and haven’t heard back.) The DOT told us this week that more than $4 billion has been obligated so far, but all the money is “accounted for” in the sense that the department has a plan for how to spend it.

Specifically, out of the $12.5 billion, a DOT spokesperson told us the department has obligated 48% of the $4.8 billion appropriated for telecommunications upgrades (including the replacement of copper wire with newer technologies, which the department says is 70% complete). Meanwhile, 34% of the $3.5 billion appropriation for radars and other surveillance systems has been obligated, with that number expected to rise as more radar production comes online as soon as next month. The department said it has also obligated 63% of the $800 million it received for “foundational upgrades,” such as replacing old floppy disks and making aviation-safety improvements in Alaska.

The spokesperson said most of the final $3.4 billion, which is for facility construction and consolidation, won’t be spent until 2027 or 2028 because it’s less of a priority. Just 6% of that funding has been obligated so far.

“I think it took longer than many of us thought to select a prime contractor for the project, and to develop priorities,” Strong, the aviation-safety expert at William & Mary, told us. “But for many projects like this, early stage is [a] lower share, then [there is a] ramp up in the middle period as initiatives are rolled out systemwide. Overall, a bit slow, but not unprecedented.”

That’s not to say there haven’t been issues with the implementation. The Government Accountability Office released a report in September [criticizing](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-107992.pdf#page=27) aspects of how the FAA has managed the rollout, saying it hadn’t developed an integrated master schedule or comprehensive cost estimate.

Hours before the ground stop, Duffy had [asked](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/white-house-urges-congress-provide-301-billion-aviation-reform-2026-11-13/) lawmakers to approve an additional $30 billion in funding for airport and air traffic control infrastructure. Asked for a breakdown of that funding, a Department of Transportation spokesperson referred us to a [fact sheet](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2026-09/Modern%20Skies%20Act%20fact%20sheet.pdf) for the [Modern Skies Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5572?hl=modern+skies+sky&s=2&r=2), a bill

On Nov. 13, after the nationwide ground stop, Duffy [upped](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-press-briefing-markwayne-mullin-sean-duffy-faa-ground-stop-november-13-2026/) his request to $50.1 billion. According to a Nov. 17 [letter](https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/2026-11/Joint%20Letter%20Regarding%20Additional%20ATC%20Funding.pdf) from Duffy to leaders of the House and Senate appropriations committees, that includes $10.1 billion for “air traffic control modernization” including telecommunications and digital technology upgrades; $10 billion in discretionary grants for airport infrastructure improvements; $10 billion to “replace, modernize or fully reconstruct aging terminals at high-impact transitional hub airports”; $10 billion to build five consolidated air route traffic control centers to replace [nearly two dozen aging facilities](https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/trump-administration-calls-congress-fully-fund-air-traffic-control-modernization-501); and $10 billion to build, replace or improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.

Trump’s recent [budget](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BUDGET-2026-BUD/pdf/BUDGET-2026-BUD.pdf) [proposals](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/budget_fy2027.pdf) have asked for $4 billion for FAA facilities and systems upgrades, well short of what his administration is now requesting from Congress.

The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge

NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision.

Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027.

Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight.

“As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!”

Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both [radioisotope](https://nasa.gov/rps) and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable.

Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.

### Judges Needed

NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers [website](https://www.futureengineers.org/registration/judge/powertoexplore).

The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate. [Future Engineers](http://futureengineers.org/)administers the challenge through a contract with the [NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation](https://www.nasa.gov/coeci/) within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

To learn more about the challenge, visit:

[https://www.nasa.gov/power-to-explore](https://www.nasa.gov/power-to-explore)

Eighteen-year-old Thomas Lui of Ridgewood, New Jersey; nine-year-old Rainie Lin of Lexington, Kentucky; and twelve-year-old Aadya Karthik of Seattle, Washington, winners of the 2024 Power to Explore Student Challenge explore an Apollo capsule at NASA Glenn’s Visitor Center at the Great Lakes Science Center, as a part of their prize trip to Cleveland.

title: Serbia’s New Parliament Convenes for the First Time
subtitle: The Student List holds 140 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats, giving a party formed by youth activists a parliamentary majority.
feedText: The country’s new parliament convened for the first time Tuesday, following last month’s historic election victory by the Student List that ended former strongman Aleksandar Vucic’s 14-year grip on power. The Student List holds 140 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats, giving a party formed by youth activists a parliamentary majority. But its efforts to tackle corruption and restore the rule of law are expected to face strong opposition from Vucic’s party, which holds 103 seats, with the former president himself now among its lawmakers. As Andrew MacDowall wrote for WPR last week , most of the Student List’s lawmakers come from academia and civil society and have little governing experience. They now face the daunting task of delivering “on campaign promises that collectively amount to a reshaping of Serbian democracy and state institutions,” while navigating the country’s complex foreign relations with Russia, the West and its Balkan neighbors. title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
subtitle: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035.
feedText: Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade l…
articleBody:
Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference?

On Nov. 18, [Voyager 1](https://www.space.com/17688-voyager-1.html) will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full [light-day](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/voyager/what-exactly-is-a-light-day-heres-what-voyager-1s-latest-milestone-means-for-the-interstellar-probe) (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky.

But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while [Voyager 2](https://www.space.com/voyager-2) has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, [according to NASA](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/frequently-asked-questions/).

## Need for speed

The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past [Uranus](https://www.space.com/45-uranus-seventh-planet-in-earths-solar-system-was-first-discovered-planet.html) and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at [Saturn](https://www.space.com/48-saturn-the-solar-systems-major-ring-bearer.html) to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of [Titan](https://www.space.com/15257-titan-saturn-largest-moon-facts-discovery-sdcmp.html), before flying outside the plane of the solar system.

NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a [faster trajectory](https://www.planetary.org/space-missions/voyager) — as illustrated in [this video](https://www.britannica.com/video/Voyager-1-planets-spacecraft-Voyagers-animation-paths-August-1989/-15101) by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9.

The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission [flew two spacecraft by Earth](https://www.space.com/astronomy/mars/nasas-escapade-twin-mars-probes-execute-a-1st-of-its-kind-gravity-slingshot-around-earth) on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much.

"Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society [wrote](https://www.planetary.org/articles/20130926-gravity-assist). "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure."

"But each Voyager gained about 10 km/s [6.2 miles/s], a pretty big number," the society continued about the Jupiter encounter. This was "enough to put them on a fast path to Saturn — and in the case of Voyager 2, to Uranus and Neptune as well — and eventual escape from the solar system."

## Speeding on to Saturn, and beyond

An image of Saturn captured by Voyager on Nov. 16, 1980 four days after the probe's closest approach to the planet, taken from a distance of 3,300,000 miles (5,300,000 kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

With each flyby, the two spacecraft picked up speed with a single exception — during Voyager 2's encounter of Neptune. That's because the spacecraft made a turn to fly by Triton. The maneuver brought Voyager 2 over Neptune's north pole, before it turned and then was directed to begin "plunging down, out of the plane of the solar system," losing speed along the way.

Voyager 2, in fact, did not have enough speed to leave the solar system until it flew by Jupiter. "It gained about 10 km/s at Jupiter, about 5 km/s at Saturn, about 2 km/s at Uranus, and lost about 2 km/s at Neptune," the Planetary Society wrote of the speeds, which are 6.21 miles/s, 3.11 miles/s, 1.24 miles/s and a loss of 1.24 miles/s, respectively.

Voyager 2 images of Uranus in natural color, left, and false-color to highlight atmospheric features on an otherwise rather bland looking planet, taken from 5.7 million miles away (9.5 million kilometers). (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible.

title: Zerstörte Krim-Brücke: Die Ukraine versetzt Putin einen schweren Schlag
subtitle: Die Kertsch-Brücke Richtung Krim gilt als Prestigeprojekt des Kremlchefs.
feedText: Der ukrainische Geheimdienst SBU veröffentlichte dieses Bild der eingestürzten Kertsch-Brücke. Handout/Ukrainian Security Service/AFP Die Kertsch-Brücke Richtung Krim gilt als Prestigeprojekt des Kremlchefs. Nun sind Teile davon nach massiven ukrainischen Angriffen eingestürzt. Im Gegenzug trifft Moskau zwei zentrale Kiewer Brücken. Von Florian Hassel , Belgrad I n einem strategisch bedeutsamen Schlag hat die Ukraine mit dem offenbar massenhaften Einsatz von Marschflugkörpern und Drohnen einen zentralen Teil der Brücke zum Einsturz gebracht, die über die Meerenge von Kertsch auf die russisch besetzte Krim -Halbinsel führt.
articleBody:
# Kertsch-Brücke zur Krim zerstört: Die Ukraine versetzt Putin einen schweren Schlag - Politik - SZ.de

Der ukrainische Geheimdienst SBU veröffentlichte dieses Bild der eingestürzten Kertsch-Brücke. Handout/Ukrainian Security Service/AFP Die Kertsch-Brücke Richtung Krim gilt als Prestigeprojekt des Kremlchefs. Nun sind Teile davon nach massiven ukrainischen Angriffen eingestürzt. Im Gegenzug trifft Moskau zwei zentrale Kiewer Brücken.

Von Florian Hassel , Belgrad

I n einem strategisch bedeutsamen Schlag hat die Ukraine mit dem offenbar massenhaften Einsatz von Marschflugkörpern und Drohnen einen zentralen Teil der Brücke zum Einsturz gebracht, die über die Meerenge von Kertsch auf die russisch besetzte Krim -Halbinsel führt. Fotos zeigen an einem zentralen Teil, unter dem sonst Schiffe durchfahren, dass beide Fahrbahnen der Autostraße eingestürzt sind. Auch die parallel verlaufende Eisenbahnbrücke scheint beschädigt zu sein. Russland griff seinerseits Ziele überall in der Ukraine an und beschädigte in Kiew zwei zentrale Brücken, die über den Fluss Dnjepr führen.

Gespräche in Abu Dhabi : Kein Schritt zum Frieden in der Ukraine Ein weiterer Austausch von Gefangenen ist das einzige greifbare Ergebnis der Verhandlungen zwischen Moskau, Kiew und Washington. Jetzt reisen die Amerikaner zu Putin.

# Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip

## Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip

## The Chinese president is currying favor with some of the region’s most powerful leaders.

- United States
- China
- Japan
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China ’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia ’s bridge to Crimea .

### Xi Takes the Limelight

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at China ’s diplomatic maneuvering, the possibility of an Iranian attack on U.S. soil, and Ukraine targeting Russia ’s bridge to Crimea .

### Xi Takes the Limelight

U.S. President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday for a few hours of shmoozing with some of the most powerful leaders in the Indo-Pacific, including his fellow members of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue and his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). With more summitry still to come, experts expect Trump to use this week to try and project power and confidence amid growing political challenges back home.

China, however, may have already beaten Trump to the punch.

Right out of the gate, Chinese President Xi Jinping has signaled that his administration is willing to act as a counterweight to the White House’s increasingly provocative trade policies. On Tuesday, Beijing agreed to cut duties on a swath of Canadian exports, amounting to roughly $280 million in tariff relief. In exchange, Ottawa promised to extend remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by another two years.

“Stronger communication and cooperation between China and Canada will benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world,” Xi told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney during talks in Shenzhen, China. This was their third meeting since Carney took power in 2025, and it marked Ottawa’s continued efforts to diversify its trade away from Washington.

China also pledged on Tuesday to provide Peru with $22.5 million in aid to address what is expected to be the devastating fallout of this year’s El Niño . Lima applauded the measure, with President Keiko Fujimori stressing that “China is very important to us because it is our ​principal trading partner.”

Peru is one of the many places in Latin America where Beijing and Washington have competed for influence. Earlier this month, the U.S. State Department disclosed that it has committed $4.5 million to help Peru modernize its main port at Callao, in a move seen as a direct counter to a Chinese-controlled megaport less than 50 miles away that opened in 2024.

Perhaps most notably, though, is China’s potential openness to converse with Japan. A war of words over Taiwan, coupled with Beijing’s rare-earth export controls , has plagued Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s tenure. However, during Tuesday’s ASEAN gathering in Manila, Takaichi shook hands with Chinese Agriculture Minister Zhang Zhu. Although few words were exchanged, the fact that such an interaction occurred has raised hopes that Takaichi’s upcoming trip to Shenzhen may be more cordial than previously anticipated.

Yet Beijing’s biggest days may still be to come. On Wednesday, Xi will host Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for trilateral talks on nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. With Trump at his weakest point to date (entering his lame-duck term after sweeping midterm losses and a Nvidia spy scandal ), experts anticipate that Xi will aim to capitalize on Trump’s rocky footing.

“Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency,” FP columnist Howard W. French argued .

### Today’s Most Read

- Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy by Rebecca Lissner and Mira Rapp-Hooper
- A Diminished Trump Could Get Played in Asia by Howard W. French
- Lame-Duck Trump Heads to Asia by Rishi Iyengar
### What We’re Following

Dirty bomb threat? Iran is actively planning for potential strikes on U.S. soil, seven U.S. officials told CNN on Tuesday. Whether Tehran will or even can execute such an attack is unclear, and White House spokesperson Lauren Bis has insisted that “there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Still, even the possibility of such an assault signals growing alarm that a peaceful end to the Iran war may be out of reach.

CNN reported that, according to U.S. intelligence, Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. Sources told CNN that this is not an indicator of an imminent attack but rather is one of several options that Iran may be exploring. Iranian officials, however, denied the report, with chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calling it “false flags” and “war mongering.”

Experts, meanwhile, insist that Tehran may not have the capabilities or the desire to carry out such a plot. “An Iranian dirty bomb in Washington would be very hard to pull off,” retired U.S. Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN. “They’d have to move uranium halfway around the world and have a team in place to set it off. I don’t think they’ll do it. The U.S. response would be overwhelming.”

Trump expressed a similar notion on Tuesday. When asked about the CNN article, the U.S. president told reporters that Iran would “pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before” were it to attack the United States homeland.

Crosshairs on Crimean bridge. Ukrainian forces launched a second strike on Tuesday at a strategic bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014. “Russia built a myth around it as a symbol of Crimea being ‘Russian forever,’” Ukraine’s military command said in a statement. “Now, part of the structure lies in the water.” The attack marked the second consecutive assault on the critical crossing in just two days.

The Kerch Strait Bridge—often highlighted as one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects—is the only rail crossing between Russia and the Crimean territory. Moscow has repeatedly used the 12-mile road to transport military and civilian supplies to its troops as well as to exert control over Ukraine’s southern coast; the Kerch Strait acts as a chokepoint for naval access from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov. In recent years, the route has also become a symbol of Russia’s yearslong occupation.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky characterized this week’s attacks on the bridge as the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes. Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed on Tuesday that the assault on Kerch Strait Bridge occurred in tandem with a massive Ukrainian drone operation; Moscow claimed to have intercepted 1,441 drones across 22 regions on Tuesday in one of Kyiv’s biggest such attacks yet.

What is Belgrade’s future? Hundreds of people gathered outside Serbia’s National Assembly on Tuesday to cheer on the country’s new parliament, the first since the ouster of President Aleksandar Vucic . Led by the grassroots Student List movement, the inaugural session kicked off what is expected to be the long process of forming a government .

Nearly two years of student-led protests against one of Europe’s most staunchly populist regimes culminated in the opposition’s sweeping victory in parliamentary elections last month. Student List lawmakers dominated in the polls, winning 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly compared to the Vucic-led Serbian Progressive Party’s 103 seats. Vucic initially blamed foreign interference for his loss, without citing evidence, despite international observers noting that his party held an unfair advantage.

Now begins the difficult task of governing a country that has been led by Vucic for the past 14 years. On Tuesday, the Student List was expected to nominate university professor Aleksandar Cupic to be the country’s new parliamentary speaker. After that, the grassroots movement will still have to choose a prime minister and hold a snap presidential election; the deadline for the latter expires at the end of this year.

### Odds and Ends

The end of Pope Leo XIV’s 12-day Latin America tour wrapped up this week with a painful surprise. While traveling in the popemobile before his final Mass in Peru on Monday, Leo was struck in the eye by a flying rosary. It is unclear who threw the prayer beads, as worshippers often toss gifts at the pope, who is known for his (usually) quick reflexes.

However, Leo has already shaken off the incident. “The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart—or maybe in your eye—but that mark the life of someone,” Leo said on Tuesday.

- United States
- China
- Japan
Alexandra Sharp is the World Brief writer at Foreign Policy . Bluesky: @alexandrassharp.bsky.social X: @AlexandraSSharp

articleBody:
Entwickler in China können Apples KI-Funktionen jetzt auch auf dem iPad und dem Mac ausprobieren, sofern sie die zweite Beta von iPadOS 27.3 oder macOS 27.3 installiert haben. Siri AI, die Siri-App und die übrigen Neuerungen aus iOS 27 bleiben allerdings außen vor.

## Die chinesische Version von Apple Intelligence

Auf dem iPhone hatte Apple die Funktionen in China bereits mit der ersten Beta von iOS 27.3 freigeschaltet. In der jeweils ersten Beta von iPadOS 27.3 und macOS 27.3 fehlten sie dagegen noch. Am 9. November gab die Internetaufsicht in Shanghai bekannt, dass Apple die KI-Funktionen auch für Tablets und Notebooks angemeldet hat.

Unterstützt werden alle Macs und iPads mit einem Chip der M-Serie sowie das iPad mini mit dem A17 Pro oder dem A20 Pro. Inhaltlich entspricht das Angebot weitgehend dem, was Apple in den USA ab iOS 18.1 nach und nach eingeführt hat.

Die Funktionen selbst basieren auf Apples eigenen Modellen. Für einige Aufgaben ziehen Siri, die Schreibtools und weitere Funktionen in China zusätzlich das KI-Modell Qwen von Alibaba hinzu, so wie Apple in anderen Ländern ChatGPT als Erweiterung einbindet. Mit Qwen verfassen die Schreibtools auch neue Texte, statt vorhandene nur umzuschreiben, zu korrigieren oder zusammenzufassen. Siri reicht Anfragen bei Bedarf an das Modell weiter, um ausführlicher zu antworten.

Zum Paket gehören außerdem die Live-Übersetzung in der Nachrichten-App, in FaceTime und in der Telefon-App, die Visuelle Intelligenz zum Erkennen von Objekten und Orten sowie Genmoji. In der Fotos-App stehen das Werkzeug „Bereinigen“, die Suche in natürlicher Sprache und das Erstellen von Rückblicken zur Verfügung. Die Mail-App fasst E-Mails zusammen, schlägt Antworten vor und zeigt wichtige Nachrichten priorisiert an. Zusammenfassungen gibt es auch für Mitteilungen und für Audioaufnahmen in der Notizen-App, in der zusätzlich die Transkripte von Telefonaten landen.

Die finalen Versionen von iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3 und macOS 27.3 sollen im Dezember erscheinen. Mit ihnen dürfte Apple Intelligence in China dann für alle Nutzer auf dem iPad und dem Mac verfügbar werden.

#### (via MacRumors)

[↗ Primärquelle: macrumors.com](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/16/ipad-mac-apple-intelligence-china/)

articleBody:
I’ve written for TomDispatch for more than 23 years, was the managing editor for around a decade, and have run the site at The Intercept for the last five months. Working alongside founder and editor-in-chief Tom Engelhardt, I had the rare honor of editing legendary writers like Mike Davis, Barbara Ehrenreich, Eduardo Galeano, Adam Hochschild, and Chalmers Johnson.

Since I became the editor of TomDispatch in late June, it’s been gratifying to continue working with so many TD regulars, publishing among many other instant classics: Greg Grandin on [Florida’s Cuban diaspora and the Israeli lobby](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/02/tomdispatch-trump-florida-cuba-latin-america-lobby-israel-aipac/); Juan Cole on [Yemen’s Ansarullah](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/28/yemen-saudi-arabia-iran/) (whom Americans routinely call “the Houthis”); theologian Liz Theoharis on [Pete Hegseth’s unholy war](https://theintercept.com/2026/09/17/hegseth-christianity-jesus-iran-war/); and Rebecca Gordon on the Pentagon [channeling](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/11/hegseth-pentagon-investment-bank/) its inner Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

My vision for TomDispatch at The Intercept is, however, also a showcase for bright lights whose work many of you don’t yet know — but you should. I want TomDispatch to be what it was for me in 2003, a place to hone my craft and figure out the kind of writer I wanted to be.

TD recently offered a remarkable piece by Safia Southey, an international lawyer and expert on wartime abuses, on the “zombie conflict” in Gaza and the [politics of permanent ceasefires](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/14/israel-gaza-ceasefire-violations/). And this summer, Ashley Gate authored an extraordinary article on [U.S. ecocide in Iran](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/31/iran-war-environment-toxic-chemical-exposure/). Today, Gate — an expert on foreign relations and a guest lecturer on international arms control at Columbia University’s Institute for the Study of Human Rights — returns with an eye-opening examination of the Trump administration’s multi-pronged effort to make the Pentagon unaccountable for its crimes.

If you would like to see more articles like these by incredibly smart writers who will help you to understand the world in brand new ways, you would do me a huge favor by making sure you’re [signed up to receive TomDispatch by email](https://theintercept.com/dispatch/) and, perhaps, convincing a friend to give us a chance, too. Will we eventually ask you for a donation? Yes, because we’re a nonprofit, and writers need to be paid for their work. But if you want to get out ahead of our requests, [you can donate here](https://join.theintercept.com/donate/tomdispatch/). Let me say, truly, there’s no donation too small. If each of our subscribers gave $1 a year, it would make a world of difference to us. And if you have the means to give more, it will go a long way to ensuring TomDispatch’s future and more pieces like this must-read offering by Gate below.

*—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch*

If you haven’t yet, [sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.](https://theintercept.com/dispatch/)

## A New World Order

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has once again attacked the global system of laws, norms, and principles instituted to place limits on international armed violence. Advocating for a return to might-makes-right barbarism during a keynote speech on Friday, Rubio [threatened to use military force](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/11/secretary-of-state-marco-rubio-at-the-federalist-societys-2026-national-lawyers-convention) against the International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals accused of the gravest atrocities. Warning that if the ICC was “foolish enough to try to enforce their paper decrees on Americans, our answer will probably be the same as the Roman general Pompey when he said to those who were trying to invoke their city’s charters against his legions. … ‘Stop quoting laws to men with swords.’”

Rubio’s effort to undermine the principles and rules that regulate the means and methods of warfare and the humanitarian protection of civilian populations, sick and wounded combatants, and prisoners of war is part of the Trump administration’s wide-ranging effort to upend the rules-based international order that the U.S. has championed — but often failed to abide by — since World War II.

[Related Trump’s Orwellian Board of Peace Consists Entirely of Human Rights Abusers](https://theintercept.com/2026/03/02/trump-board-peace-human-right-abuses/)

Speaking before the conservative Federalist Society at the National Lawyers Convention in Washington, D.C., Rubio disparaged the ICC as a “fake court” and “an unelected world tribunal, which claims to supersede the laws and constitutions of sovereign states, even those who never signed up for it.”

Rubio’s tirade was the latest salvo in a long-running campaign against the ICC by President Donald Trump’s administration, which has vowed to cripple the court. In October, after former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, Trump — who has relentlessly [campaigned](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/06/trump-fifa-world-cup-red-card-infantino/) for the award — was enraged and [derided](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117414533410378018) the South African jurist as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”

Hours after the award was announced, the U.S. [imposed](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/10/imposing-sanctions-on-the-international-criminal-court) sanctions on the ICC. These latest sanctions are intended to turn the judicial organ into an economic pariah. They prohibited the court from conducting dollar-denominated transactions, froze its U.S.-based assets, and barred the judicial body from using the U.S. banking system or working with American institutions — effectively blacklisting the court.

> The ongoing campaign to dismantle the ICC is just one piece of a larger effort by the Trump administration to ensure the U.S. military can act with impunity.

The ICC was created by the international community to investigate and prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide, and the [crime of aggression](https://theintercept.com/2022/10/08/russia-putin-ukraine-war-crimes-accountability/) — when one country uses armed force against another without legal justification. The Hague, Netherlands-based court is unique as a permanent judicial organ capable of prosecuting anyone, infantry soldiers and sitting heads of state alike, for humanity’s gravest crimes if they are committed in the territories of its 125 member states. The ICC is critically a court of last resort that will only intervene when domestic jurisdictions either fail to hold their own service members and political leaders accountable, or when state parties to the court call for an investigation.

While the Trump administration’s timing in sanctioning the ICC was notable, this latest strike against the court is just one facet of the Trump administration’s yearslong campaign to — in the words of Rubio’s State Department — “[dismantle](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/07/state-department-launches-campaign-to-dismantle-international-criminal-courts-threat-to-american-sovereignty)” it. The effort dates back to 2020, when the first Trump administration imposed [sanctions](https://ccrjustice.org/factsheet-us-sanctions-international-criminal-court) on ICC officials after the court opened an investigation into alleged U.S. war crimes and crimes against humanity [committed in Afghanistan](https://theintercept.com/2021/10/05/afghanistan-icc-war-crimes/).

[Related Trump’s Sanctions Against the ICC Are Unconstitutional, Rights Groups Say](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/15/trump-sanctions-international-criminal-court/)

Overturned by the Biden administration in 2021, the first round of U.S. sanctions against the court were replaced last February by a new series [targeting](https://asil.org/ilib/trump-signs-executive-order-sanctioning-icc/) the court’s chief prosecutor, its two deputy prosecutors, and six of its judges. All of these judges had either investigated the actions of U.S. nationals in Afghanistan or were part of the ICC’s decision to [issue arrest warrants](https://theintercept.com/2024/05/20/icc-arrest-warrant-israel-hamas/) for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for their co-perpetration of “the war crime of starvation” and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Though the litany of prior U.S. sanctions against the court impacted the lives of those nine individuals and their families — cutting them off from their bank accounts, emails, and blocking their travel — the actions were piecemeal and did not fully upend the work of the court.

Now, all of the ICC’s U.S.-based partner organizations have six months to completely cut ties with the court or face legal retribution. What’s more, since the current global economic system is built upon the U.S. dollar, international — particularly European — organizations often preemptively abide by U.S. sanctions even if their workings fall completely outside of America’s jurisdiction. For example, when the French company Axa [terminated](https://www.reuters.com/world/icc-cuts-ties-with-axa-over-us-sanctions-ft-reports-2026-10-01/) its life and health insurance contracts with the ICC on October 1, the insurer reportedly cited the escalating campaign by the U.S. against the court.

Absent the implementation of effective countermeasures — like amending and enforcing the [EU Blocking Statute](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/1996/2271/oj/eng), which can shield EU individuals and businesses from “unlawful” third-country sanctions — this latest move by the U.S. may not kill the ICC, but it will cut off the judicial organ’s blood supply.

## Victors’ Justice?

For over 80 years, the U.S. has enjoyed the privilege of proscribing — and not necessarily abiding by — international law. American representatives served as the chief [arbiters](https://history.state.gov/milestones/1945-1952/nuremberg) of the post-World War II Nuremberg and Tokyo military tribunals that prosecuted Nazi and Japanese war criminals, which are seen by many in the field as the birthplaces of modern international criminal law. American arbiters, notably U.S. Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, led the victors of the Second World War as they tried and prosecuted their former adversaries for novel notions of wrongdoing, including crimes against peace and crimes against humanity. These newly defined criminal acts form the bedrock of the ICC’s jurisdiction.

At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, all 25 major Japanese leaders were convicted, with seven receiving death sentences. Judge Radhabinod Pal of India argued for the acquittal of all 25. In his [dissent](https://www.worldcourts.com/imtfe/eng/decisions/1948.11.04_IMTFE_Judgment_Pal.pdf), he complained that the tribunal dispensed victors’ justice. He said that America’s atomic strikes on [Hiroshima](https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/atomic-bomb-hiroshima) and [Nagasaki](https://theintercept.com/2023/11/12/america-wars-bombing-killing-civilians/) were among the most criminal acts of the conflict, yet immune from prosecution.

Indeed, the international criminal justice system was never intended to hold the U.S. or its allies accountable. And in the decades since, consecutive U.S. administrations have wielded the nation’s political and military strength to [avoid any semblance](https://theintercept.com/2023/04/04/donald-trump-indictment-war-criminals/) of international legal oversight.

[Related How the U.S. Derailed an Effort to Prosecute Its Crimes in Afghanistan](https://theintercept.com/2021/10/05/afghanistan-icc-war-crimes/)

Although relations with the court have oscillated over the course of Democratic and Republican administrations, the U.S. has always been wary of the court’s potential jurisdiction over American nationals. From the court’s conception, in which the U.S. played a role, the global hegemon has continuously shown its disdain for the court’s territorial jurisdiction. While the ICC cannot prosecute any American nationals for their actions in the U.S., it does have jurisdiction over acts undertaken, by U.S. nationals or otherwise, within the territories of its member nations including Afghanistan, Libya, and Palestine.

> The international criminal justice system was never intended to hold the U.S. or its allies accountable.

Under the Clinton administration in the 1990s, the U.S. was one of only seven drafting nations to initially veto the Rome Statute — the international treaty that created the ICC — due to its concerns over the court’s territorial jurisdiction. Later, in 2002, the same year the ICC was established, the George W. Bush administration signed the [Hague Invasion Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/107th-congress/house-bill/4775) into law. The act, which is still in effect, grants the president the legal backing to use military force against the court in order to free any U.S. or allied person held or imprisoned by the ICC. The Bush administration subsequently [pressured](https://www.globalissues.org/article/490/united-states-and-the-icc) dozens of countries to agree to never transfer U.S. nationals to the ICC, and threatened to cut military assistance, cease counterterrorism operations, or cut humanitarian aid if these states did not comply. Though relations with the ICC thawed somewhat under the Obama administration in the 2010s, the U.S. has [never shown a substantial interest in joining the court](https://theintercept.com/2021/08/23/samantha-power-icc-sudan/) and has worked for years to restrict its jurisdiction.

The Trump administration’s courtwide sanctions on the ICC are, however, a far leap beyond the pressure campaigns against the court and its member states by prior U.S. administrations. While the Trump administration cares little for the thin veneer of justice that prior U.S. administrations sought to maintain, the ongoing campaign to “dismantle” the ICC is just one piece of a larger effort by the current administration to ensure the U.S. military can act with impunity.

Soon after taking office, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered a mass [purge](https://www.military.com/daily-news/2025/02/24/people-are-very-scared-trump-administration-purge-of-jag-officers-raises-legal-ethical-fears.html) of senior judge advocates general. Among their many functions, JAGs historically educated military leaders on the [laws](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/posse-comitatus-act-explained) that prohibit the use of the U.S. military in domestic law enforcement and ensured commanders were aptly informed of the international legal obligations to protect civilians and prisoners of war. When asked about the mass layoffs in February 2025, Hegseth explained that the action was taken to remove potential “roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief.”

[Related U.S. Military Killed Boat Strike Survivors for Not Surrendering Correctly](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/23/boat-strikes-venezuela-hegseth-bradley-legal/)

In a concerted effort to further “[maximum lethality](https://www.hks.harvard.edu/centers/carr-ryan/our-work/carr-ryan-commentary/epic-fury-pete-hegseth-his-comments-harvard-and),” Trump and Hegseth additionally gutted the Pentagon’s [Civilian Protection Center of Excellence](https://theintercept.com/2026/05/15/pentagon-civilian-harm-casualties-war-hegseth/) and the broader [Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response](https://theintercept.com/2025/04/15/pete-hegseth-pentagon-civilian-casualties-harm/) program in the early months of 2025. The budding program, which the majority of U.S combatant commanders [urged](https://www.propublica.org/article/hegseth-civilian-harm-mitigation-response-trump-defense-department) Hegseth to maintain, was [established in 2022](https://theintercept.com/2022/08/25/pentagon-civilian-harm-mitigation-plan-forever-wars/) to prevent, reduce, and respond to civilian casualty incidents. Stark cuts to the program’s manpower and funding coincided with a rise in civilian [casualties](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-defense-department-iran-hegseth-civilian-casualties) reported in U.S. military operations in [Iran](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/18/iran-war-civilian-deaths-families-infant/), [Yemen](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/12/pete-hegseth-yemen-war-civilian-harm/), Somalia, and in the [Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea](https://theintercept.com/collections/license-to-kill/).

When taken together, the administration’s cuts to internal legal mechanisms and policy programs intended to maintain law and protect civilians, as well as its ongoing attempts to dismantle the ICC, can be seen as two aspects of a larger campaign to eradicate all avenues of military oversight.

Read Our Complete Coverage TomDispatch

## The Fight for Justice Will Continue

The sweeping courtwide sanctions against the ICC are formidable for the same reasons they are survivable: They aim to isolate the court from its broad system of support. The international criminal justice system depends on evidence. This evidence is not found in The Hague; it is [brought to it by an array of](https://theintercept.com/2023/06/12/icc-war-crimes-digital-evidence-reconstruction/) local, national, and international investigators, researchers, watchdogs, and atrocity survivors.

The evidence needed to confirm the genocide in Palestine; the U.S. bombing of the [elementary school](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/minab-school-massacre-iran-war-children-families) in Minab, Iran; and the extrajudicial killings of fisherman in the Caribbean would not exist without the networks of dedicated researchers, local journalists, and courageous survivors. And the work of these people, while critical to the court’s functions, will continue, even if the court is dismantled brick by brick.

“The Trillion Dollar War Machine,” by William D. Hartung and Ben Freeman. Available on [Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/p/books/the-trillion-dollar-war-machine-how-runaway-military-spending-drives-america-into-foreign-wars-and-bankrupts-us-at-home-ben-freeman/e7d4a2e1b1867765?ean=9781645030638).

The ICC has strongly [condemned](https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/icc-strongly-rejects-us-sanctions-against-institution) the U.S. sanctions. ICC President Tomoko Akane has said that the court will “continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” Pillay has also used the publicity stemming from her Nobel Peace Prize to showcase the court’s work. She further [dedicated](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cm9wz5kng0x1o) her award to “all the survivors of international crimes” as well as the international jurists “whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign.”

In his speech on Friday, Rubio took aim at those very jurists, declaring that the U.S. would never submit to the “sterile vision of radical judges or soulless global bureaucrats.” He claimed that this “global elite” was using international law as “an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles.” This was, in fact, a stark about-face for Rubio, who was an advocate for international law during his 14 years as a U.S. senator. He even co-sponsored a resolution encouraging other nations to support the ICC’s investigations of Russian war crimes in Ukraine.

[Related Trump Sanctions Palestinian Human Rights Groups for Doing Their Job. Anybody Could Be Next.](https://theintercept.com/2025/09/16/trump-sanctions-palestine-human-rights-israel/)

Rubio claimed that those who advocate for the restraint of law over all nations are anti-American. “For these people — the fundamental purpose of the law, American law and international law alike, is to weaken the United States,” he claimed. “It is to hinder the American government’s ability to defend American interests at home and abroad.” He continued, “There is nothing — there is nothing — in our history or the history of any other great nation that requires us to recognize the authority or legitimacy of any of these ridiculous ideas.”

Prior to Rubio’s speech, however, Pillay offered up a differing vision of America. [In her estimation](https://www.democracynow.org/2026/10/20/navi_pillay), Americans are not the singularly self-interested, lawless, reprobates envisioned by Rubio but a people who eschew limitless violence and value humanitarian principles. “I know,” she said, “that Americans support the principle of ending impunity for these serious crimes and that they support justice and accountability.”
