articleBody:
Architect Simon Robinson has been leading calls for the Victorian state government to rethink its plan to demolish all of [Melbourne](https://dezeen.com/tag/melbourne/)’s public [housing](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/housing/) towers. In this [interview](https://www.dezeen.com/interviews/), he sets out why he believes retrofit is the smarter approach.

Simon Robinson (centre) is the director of Office

Announced by the Labor-run state government in 2023, [Homes Victoria](https://www.homes.vic.gov.au)’s High-Rise Redevelopment Program (HRRP) will see all 44 of Melbourne's public housing towers and many other lower-rise blocks razed and replaced with new housing by 2051.

Officials [argue](https://www.premier.vic.gov.au/next-phase-australias-biggest-urban-renewal-project) that the buildings, constructed between 1962 and 1975, have reached the end of their useful lives. They claim the towers do not meet modern standards and cost too much to maintain, and that the redevelopment programme will triple housing capacity and improve the quality of homes.

But the policy has proved highly controversial, with critics particularly angry about a lack of transparency or consultation with residents, who are being relocated.

It is now subject to an ongoing legal dispute, has [prompted concern from the UN's special rapporteur on housing](https://imcl.org.au/news/media-releases-1/state-government-should-follow-un-body%E2%80%99s-call-and-suspend-public-housing-demolitions), and become a political issue in the build-up to the Victorian state election later this month.

Flemington Estate has not yet been demolished while a class file action filed by the residents is in progress

Among the voices leading calls for a change of course is Melbourne not-for-profit research and design practice [Office](https://office.org.au).

Office has worked pro bono to make the case for refurbishing the towers, after learning from residents that the government has not published feasibility studies for keeping any of the condemned estates.

“We thought that was pretty odd that you wouldn't do a refurbishment study on these estates," Office director Simon Robinson told Dezeen.

"So we took it upon ourselves to start to do these feasibility studies, along with public housing residents."

“We're not saying that they're in perfect condition," he added. "We’re also not saying that all of them should be refurbished – perhaps some are beyond repair. All we are saying is that these rapprochement studies need to occur."

## Cost of relocating residents "very significant"

In fact, feasibility studies have been conducted by the government but not been made public, despite requests by the Victorian Legislative Council.

"As all the estates are occupied, the cost of relocating and housing the residents during construction work needs to be included in the project cost; this is consistently excluded and never disclosed," said Robinson.

"We have estimated that these costs are very significant, with reports indicating that the government is spot purchasing or head-leasing properties from the private market."

Office's says its proposal to renovate the Flemington Estate would save around $300 million

The practice has put together a counter-proposal based on a strategy that it calls [Retain Repair Reinvest (RRR)](https://office.org.au/project/retain-repair-reinvest-flemington-estate/).

RRR focuses on retaining buildings without displacing residents, carrying out renovation work to improve housing comfort and energy efficiency while reducing construction waste and carbon impact.

Robinson agrees that most of Victoria’s existing public housing buildings are currently not fit for purpose – buildings are rundown, cold in winter, and sweltering in summer. But he believes comfortable living standards can be achieved through renovations.

Office has applied its RRR strategy to three Melbourne estates in hypothetical case studies – Ascot Vale Estate, Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.

## "There's no public housing being rebuilt"

Formerly home to approximately 10,000 people, Flemington Estate's four towers make up about 10 per cent of Victoria's public housing stock.

Only about 32 households remain, though an injunction prevents Homes Victoria from serving further eviction notices while legal challenges are pending.

Office has proposed retaining the estate's 720 dwellings and building an additional 577 infill [social housing](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/social-housing/) units to increase density.

New facades and private balconies would be added, with other upgrades including integrated underground parking, a central communal green space, new heating and cooling systems, improved insulation, new kitchens and bathrooms.

Energy efficiency is another key focus. Double-glazed windows, photovoltaic cells, and water conservation systems would provide a 55 percent reduction of global warming potential compared to the demolition approach, according to Office.

Office will focus on doing more public talks and exhibitions to raise awareness of the issue

Despite the seemingly obvious benefits, the Victorian government has so far been unmoved by the studies presented by the practice.

Robinson believes the reason lies in the fact that the state government no longer wants to manage public housing.

“When the state government manages public housing, they are responsible for maintaining the buildings and organising new tenants – all the admin that comes with owning a building,” he said.

As well as the demolitions, also attracting concern is the type of housing proposed for redevelopment under the HRRP.

Rather than like-for-like public housing, the new homes will be "community housing" – developed by private developers, and split between below-market and market-rate rental homes.

### Interested in stories about architecture and public housing?

[Click here](https://www.dezeen.com/social-housing-revival/) to check out our Social Housing Revival series.

Despite still being classed as social housing by the state government, community housing is slightly more expensive, and the tenancy is less secure from eviction.

Robinson believes the term was created to misdirect the public.

“What they're building is community housing, not public housing, so there's no longer any public housing being rebuilt in Victoria,” he said.

"The government is now calling everything social housing, because they don't want the public to know that it's no longer public housing,” he continued.

“Victoria has the lowest percentage of public housing stock in Australia, and we're currently demolishing it all and turning it into private and community housing.”

## "Public housing is foundational social infrastructure"

The issue is particularly charged in the context of [Australia](https://dezeen.com/tag/australia)'s housing-affordability crisis. There are currently over 60,000 people on the waitlist for social housing in Victoria, where social housing accounts for three per cent of all dwellings, below the national average of 4.2 per cent and the OECD average of 7 per cent.

"Public housing serves as foundational social infrastructure that treats shelter as an essential human right," said Robinson.

"By offering rents permanently capped to income and delivering unmatched security of tenure, it provides an unconditional safety net for society’s most vulnerable households."

Office’s work has gained political attention. In November 2023, the Victorian Legislative Council debated the merits of the RRR approach, with the council's Legal and Social Issues Committee [urging](https://www.parliament.vic.gov.au/4aa6fa/contentassets/d7a5adc5826c4f31859289e90016c087/mr-02122025-government-must-release-public-housing-tower-documents-committee-finds.pdf) the government to reconsider demolition and explore all refurbishment options.

The team can already claim a small victory. At Ascot Valley Estate, the first RRR case study released by Office, the development was quietly removed from the planned demolitions list on the Homes Victoria website and part of the estate has since been refurbished.

Ascot Valley Estate was removed from the demolition list by the government and has since been refurbished

The estate is a collection of 57 three-storey brick housing blocks, built in 1947 and designed by renowned modernist architect and public housing advocate Best Overend during his time with the Housing Commission.

This gave Robinson and his team hope that the government would consider the alternatives if presented with the option.

“We have presented to Homes Victoria, we've presented to different ministers as well, and we've kind of heard that they are starting to look at retrofit some of their existing building stock,” said Robinson.

“It kind of suggests that perhaps they're gonna prefer we show all of them. So we released the following studies on Barak Beacon Estate and the Flemington Estate.”

However, Barak Beacon Estate has since been demolished, and the construction of the redevelopment is due to complete by the end of the year.

Now the fate of Flemington Tower awaits a ruling from the High Court of Australia following a hearing last month.

[A class action](https://imcl.org.au/class-action/) filed by Inner Melbourne Community Legal on behalf of public housing residents in North Melbourne and Flemington is on its last appeal, after the Supreme Court of Victoria and Victorian Court of Appeal ruled in favour of demolition.

Barak Beacon Estate was demolished, the redevelopment is set to finish by the end of the year

Meanwhile, the Liberal opposition has pledged to pause the HRRP if it wins office at the upcoming state election.

Robinson hopes he and his team have done enough, and continue to raise awareness about the issue.

“We've gotten to a point where we feel we can't just keep putting out these reports," he said.

“The papers we produced are quite dense and not for the general public. So what we're now doing is translating that work into a series of publications, putting it in bookshops, and making it more accessible for the general public.”

“We continue interviews with different residents, different advocates, different professionals, speaking with journalists and doing lectures. The idea is to bring awareness to what's occurring, rather than us doing more reports.”

He is also calling for a frank discussion in the architecture community about the redevelopment projects, which many of Australia's prominent studios are working on.

“All the big-name architects are working on these estate renewals, some have even won awards as exemplar projects for these architects to promote their practice in terms of doing public good,” said Robinson.

“It's really hard to find anyone who's willing to talk about why they're doing it, or is it good, the displacement and environmental issues. We're alone.”

Dezeen put Robinson's claims to the Victorian state government, but was told it could not respond in the lead-up to the election.

**Dezeen In Depth**

title: Did Democrats blow it in Florida?
subtitle: Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida.
feedText: Joe Raedle/Getty Images. Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson in Florida. articleBody:
Angie Nixon speaking at a rally in Kissimmee, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images.

Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, [netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_elections) by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican [Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_Senate_election_in_Florida) in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a [death spiral for Florida Democrats](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) that had begun years earlier.

When I [wrote about the Sunshine State back in February](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida), the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “[get out of the](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida) *[superminority](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida)* [in the state legislature](https://www.natesilver.net/p/can-democrats-escape-their-florida).”

But back then, no one knew that [2026 would be a blue tsunami](https://www.natesilver.net/p/after-an-extraordinary-wave-what) where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net *nine* Senate seats.1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting [post-election recriminations](https://x.com/hollyotterbein/status/2117796466551066896) that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win.

So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, [Ashley Moody will be up for re-election](https://www.natesilver.net/p/an-extremely-unofficial-first-look).

title: Putting a spotlight on AI, society, and humanity
subtitle: MIT students are going to office hours less often.
feedText: They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education, and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another. For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Insti…
articleBody:
MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on [artificial intelligence and education](https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/report/), and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another.

For the [MIT Human Insight Collaborative](https://mithic.mit.edu) (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the[Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing](https://computing.mit.edu/cross-cutting/social-and-ethical-responsibilities-of-computing/) (SERC), to help MIT address them.

Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported [67 projects across 31 MIT units](https://mithic.mit.edu/impact/), offering a total of $5.5 million in funding.

Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead [Heather Paxson](https://anthropology.mit.edu/people/faculty/heather-paxson) says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative.

“When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we [relate](https://news.mit.edu/2026/when-we-talk-to-machines-sherry-turkle-book-0929) to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS).

**Eroding “creative friction”**

Building upon this focus, an [AI and Society Forum](https://news.mit.edu/2026/exploring-societal-impacts-of-ai-0623) took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the[MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium](https://genai.mit.edu/) (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI.

On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it.

MITHIC faculty co-lead [Seth Mnookin](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/seth-mnookin/), a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”

“When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.”

**Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers**

MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its [SHASS+ Connectivity Fund](https://mithic.mit.edu/shass-connectivity-fund/), in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT.

In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors [Adam Berinsky](https://polisci.mit.edu/people/adam-berinsky) and [Charles Stewart III](https://polisci.mit.edu/people/charles-stewart-iii) and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor [Chara Podimata](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/faculty/directory/chara-podimata) are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge.

The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently [featured in The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/business/media/ai-chatbots-election-misinformation.html?unlocked_article_code=1.IVE.8Kr5.eEpKyyfrOLzA&smid=url-share).

“AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the *Times*.

In another project, CMS/W Professor [Eric Klopfer](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/eric-klopfer/) and brain and cognitive sciences Professor [Pawan Sinha](https://bcs.mit.edu/directory/pawan-sinha) are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition.

Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “[AI and the Brain](https://mithic.mit.edu/how-does-ai-impact-your-brain/).”

In the field of arts and technology, [Anna Huang](https://www.eecs.mit.edu/people/cheng-zhi-anna-huang/), a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, [Joe Paradiso](https://www.media.mit.edu/people/joep/overview/), a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience.

Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together?

As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation.

**Teaching and scholarship in an AI era**

SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society.

[Graham Jones](https://anthropology.mit.edu/people/faculty/graham-jones), professor of anthropology, and [Arvind Satyanarayan](https://www.eecs.mit.edu/people/arvind-satyanarayan/), associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, [6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design)](https://anthropology.mit.edu/21A.S02_21A.S10_Humane_User_Experience_Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech.

“The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the [inaugural MITHIC Annual Event](https://youtu.be/GOToub5Mm8Q?si=mynDMTCtP3-sxlcH). “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.”

Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by [Dwai Banerjee](https://sts-program.mit.edu/people/sts-faculty/dwai-banerjee/), associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the [Computing and Society concentration](https://shass.mit.edu/for-students/undergraduate-study/computing-and-society-concentration/) launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles.

Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate [Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/mariel-garcia-montes/) to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute.

Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by [Michael Trice](https://cmsw.mit.edu/profile/michael-trice/), a lecturer in MIT’s [Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program.](https://cmsw.mit.edu/academics/writing-rhetoric-professional-communication/)

The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.”

Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a [talk](https://youtu.be/CV-S6_jGauc?si=fH9OrRfXQi_JV4Ag) given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026.

**Meeting the moment**

MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks.

“There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.”

Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.”

At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent.

“SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair.

Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation.

“The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”

articleBody:
Milo Priddle at *Commonweal*:

Dylan’s meanderings have always been intentional and exploratory. *Rolling Thunder Revue: A Bob Dylan Story by Martin Scorsese*, the filmmaker’s second “documentary” about Dylan, is another instance of masquerade and misdirection. At least two Dylans appear in the film, which recounts Dylan’s eponymous tour between fall 1975 and spring 1976. There’s Dylan in whiteface playing small venues across the United States and parts of Canada with Joan Baez, Joni Mitchell, Roger McGuinn, and other musicians. There’s also seventy-eight-year-old Dylan chronicling the tour as he wants to remember it, telling tall tales about the real artists and fabricated characters who joined him on the road. Dylanologists dismiss the film as a sham-documentary, a clumsy attempt at self-mythology that plays way too fast and loose with the historical record and reality, even for them. (Many of the made-up characters appear in the film as talking heads, recounting their experiences on the tour.) A real person who appears in the film is Rubin Carter, the prizefighter wrongfully convicted of murder and the subject of Dylan’s 1974 protest song “Hurricane.” He said this of Dylan: “Bob always been searching. Every time I see Bob now…I ask [him], ‘Have you found it yet Bob?’ And Bob say, ‘Yeah, I found it.’ But I know he hasn’t, because he keeps searching.”

articleBody:
## 99-Year-Old Woman Gets Arrested To Check It Off Her Bucket List

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/99-year-old-woman-police-cell-bucket-list/)

Most people spend their lives trying to avoid getting arrested, but for one 99-year-old woman in the Netherlands, it was a dream come true. In February 2017, a woman named Annie finally got to check an unusual item off her bucket list, thanks to some accommodating local police officers.

While typical bucket list items might include traveling the world or trying an adventurous activity, Annie had a slightly different goal: experiencing what it was like to be locked up in a jail cell. Luckily, she didn’t have to commit a crime to make it happen.

After learning about her aunt’s unusual wish, Annie’s niece reached out to the police department in Nijmegen-Zuid, Netherlands, to see if they could help. Although civilians aren’t normally allowed inside police holding cells, an officer named Maarten decided to make a special exception.

Annie got the full experience, complete with a ride to the police station, handcuffs, and a brief stay behind bars. And judging by the photos shared online, she couldn’t have been happier. The 99-year-old was all smiles as she posed in handcuffs and waved from inside her cell.

Of course, Annie wasn’t actually in trouble with the law, and the entire experience was arranged just for her. Still, it’s safe to say that she got a taste of life on the other side of the bars, without having to worry about a criminal record.

It just goes to show that you’re never too old to try something new, even if that something happens to be getting arrested.

articleBody:
*What tracks get Dave Seaman moving? We asked him.*

Dave Seaman has been a fixture of dance music for close to 40 years. As one half of Brothers in Rhythm he co-wrote and produced Kylie Minogue's 'Confide in Me', the record that marked her break from Stock Aitken Waterman pop, and his remix and production credits take in Pet Shop Boys, New Order, Michael Jackson and David Bowie. Alongside that sits a long DJ career built on Global Underground mixes, his *Back to Mine* compilation and Selador, the label he co-runs with Steve Parry.

Remarkably, he has never released a solo studio album until now. [Mirrorball Sleaze](https://found.ee/MirrorballSleaze) landed on Selador on 13 November. With the album now out, we put our Top Tracks questions to him.

### What's the first album you ever bought?

Blondie – [Parallel Lines](https://www.beatport.com/release/parallel-lines/5216975?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). If you were a ten-year-old boy in 1978, Debbie Harry was particularly alluring.

### The first time you remember hearing electronic music?

Tubeway Army – ['Are "Friends" Electric?'](https://www.beatport.com/track/are-friends-electric/13256328?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Gary Numan had a huge impact on me and started a lifelong obsession with synth music.

### Your favourite ever album?

That's a tough one, but if pushed, I'd probably have to say Prince – [Sign o' the Times](https://www.beatport.com/release/sign-o-the-times/6752625?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guaranteed floor-filler?

Donna Summer – ['I Feel Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/i-feel-love/15739558?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c). Unbelievably, it's 50 years old next year!

### The best tune from last year?

From 2025? DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The guilty pleasure?

Olivia Rodrigo.

### The last track of the night?

That very much depends on the context. Too many variables. Early night or late night? Where and with whom? The occasion?

### The best chillout record?

The remit for my *Back to Mine* compilation was literally to collate some of my favourite chillout tracks, all mixed together on one album, so…

### The record everyone loves, but you hate?

Robin S – ['Show Me Love'](https://www.beatport.com/track/show-me-love/1051600?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The best record for a family party?

Earth, Wind & Fire – ['September'](https://www.beatport.com/track/september/11758082?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The soundtrack to a lazy Sunday afternoon?

Sade – ['Pearls'](https://www.beatport.com/track/pearls/4789376?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c), poolside at Pikes Ibiza.

### The worst record you've ever heard?

I try to banish those from my mind as soon as I've heard them.

### The record you're proudest of?

Kylie Minogue – ['Confide in Me'](https://www.beatport.com/release/confide-in-me/5832405?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

### The future classic?

DJ Koze – ['Buschtaxi'](https://www.beatport.com/track/buschtaxi/20017608?a_aid=66b3e36529a3c).

**Find Dave Seaman on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/daveseamandj/?hl=en) and [Soundcloud.](https://soundcloud.com/daveseaman)**

articleBody:
**Mit der Gibson Billy Gibbons Pearly Gates 1959 Les Paul Standard setzt Gibson einem der wichtigsten Rockgitarristen der vergangenen 50 Jahre ein weiteres Denkmal. Das Instrument ist eine besonders authentische Replik seiner berühmten Les Paul Pearly Gates von 1959. Die streng limitierte Sonderauflage erhält ein aufwendiges Murphy-Lab-Ageing und soll dem Original bis ins Detail nahekommen.**

## Wie im Film

Schon die Geschichte des Lieblingsinstruments von Billy F. Gibbons ist filmreif. 1968 waren der Musiker und einige Freunde im Besitz eines Packard-Oldtimers von 1936. Diesen lieh man einer Schauspielerin für eine Reise von Texas nach Hollywood zu einem Vorsprechen, das von Erfolg gekrönt war. Weil das Fahrzeug offenbar Glück brachte, erhielt es den Spitznamen Pearly Gates. Als man später beschloss, den Packard zu verkaufen, erwarb Billy für seinen Anteil von 250 US-Dollar auf dem Gebrauchtmarkt eine nahezu makellose Les Paul Standard aus dem Jahr 1959. Ein weiterer Glücksfall, weshalb das Instrument den Spitznamen des Autos erbte und fortan mit Gibbons auf Reisen ging.

Die Pearly Gates ist seither auf zahlreichen Alben von ZZ Top zu hören. Bedenkt man, dass Gibbons über eine der größten Gitarrensammlungen überhaupt verfügt, ist das ein echtes Statement! Nun legt Gibson Custom eben diese Les Paul Standard als aufwendige weitere Reissue neu auf.

## Murphy-Lab-Aging und historische Details bis ins letzte Detail

Basis der Billy Gibbons Pearly Gates 1959 Les Paul Standard sind detaillierte Analysen des Originals, einschließlich präziser 3D-Scans. Hinzu kommt ein aufwendiges Murphy-Lab-Ageing, das den heutigen Zustand des Instruments widerspiegeln soll: ein über Jahrzehnte gespieltes Instrument mit entsprechend viel Charakter.

Konstruktiv orientiert sich die E-Gitarre eng an der Collector’s Edition, die im September dieses Jahres erschien, jedoch ausschließlich über die Gibson Garage Nashville erhältlich war.

Der Korpus der Billy Gibbons Pearly Gates 1959 Les Paul Standard besteht aus einem leichten, einteiligen Stück Mahagoni. Darauf sitzt eine selektierte, zweiteilige AAA-Ahorndecke mit markanter Maserung, Binding und cremefarbenem Schlagbrett. Die Nitrolackierung erfolgt im Farbton Pearly Gates Burst und erhält ein passendes Aging. Eingeleimt ist ein einteiliger Mahagonihals, dessen Slim-Taper-Profil ebenso wie die Korpuskonturen dem Original präzise nachempfunden wurde. Ziel ist ein möglichst authentisches Spielgefühl.

Das eingefasste Griffbrett besteht aus indischem Palisander – ein Unterschied zur Collector’s Edition, die auf brasilianischen Palisander setzt. Auf der klassischen Gibson-Mensur von 24,75″ verteilen sich 22 Medium-Jumbo-Bünde und gealterte Trapezoid-Inlays aus Zellulose.

Auch die gealterte Hardware orientiert sich konsequent am Original. Dazu gehören eine ABR-1-No-Wire-Brücke mit Stopbar-Saitenhalter sowie Kluson-Deluxe-Mechaniken im Single-Ring-Reissue-Stil.

## Neu aufgelegte P.A.F.-Humbucker für den Sound des Reverend

Jared Brandon, Leiter der Tonabnehmer-Abteilung von Gibson, hat laut Hersteller die berühmten Gibson P.A.F.-Humbucker intensiv analysiert, um eine möglichst authentische Reproduktion der beiden Original-Tonabnehmer zu realisieren. Die Billy Gibbons 1959 P.A.F. Reissues arbeiten mit Alnico-5-Magneten am Steg und Alnico 3 am Hals und sind mit gealterten Nickel-Abdeckkappen versehen. Darunter verbergen sich weiße Spulenkörper und historisch korrekter Wickeldraht.

Das Ergebnis soll den Sound des Meisters auf den Punkt treffen. Die Auswahl der Humbucker erfolgt klassisch über einen 3-Wege-Toggle-Schalter. Hinzu kommen individuelle Lautstärke- und Tonregler für jeden Pickup.

## Haute Couture oder Konfektion?

Das Musikhaus Thomann konnte sich vier Exemplare der Gibson Billy Gibbons Pearly Gates 1959 Les Paul Standard sichern. Der Preis für das edle Instrument liegt dabei ganz klar in der Sammlerklasse: 17.649 Euro inklusive Lifton-Koffer und Echtheitszertifikaten. Linkshänder werden hier nicht fündig. Die Lieferzeit wird mit zwei bis fünf Tagen angegeben, Verfügbarkeit vorausgesetzt!

Wem das eine Nummer zu hoch ist, der kann auch zur Billy Gibbons Pearly Gates Les Paul Standard greifen, die vor allem auf das aufwendige Murphy-Lab-Ageing verzichtet. Diese Version ist hochglänzend in Slow Iced Tea Fade Vintage nitrolackiert. Ansonsten finden sich auch hier die beiden Signature-Humbucker von Billy Gibbons sowie ein konventioneller ABR-1-Tune-O-Matic-Steg. Der Preis für diese E-Gitarre liegt bei 3.299 Euro. Laut Thomann ist sie sofort lieferbar.

title: They Suffered Brain Injuries After Riding a Six Flags Roller Coaster. Regulators Pinned the Blame on Them.

articleBody:
An aerial view of the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in September Jae C. Hong/AP Photo

A 17-year-old boy died after riding the extreme X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California this summer, just weeks before two more people suffered severe brain injuries after riding the same attraction, ProPublica and L.A. Material have found.

A homicide detective investigating Christopher Gibson’s death in June sent an email to the California official responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety. But records show that the official did not reply until nearly two months later. The lack of action raises the question of whether the brain damage suffered by the two riders the following month could have been avoided.

Christopher’s death, which has not been previously reported, also raises questions about Six Flags, its flagship X2 ride and the way in which California regulates roller coasters.

Billed as a “fourth-dimension” roller coaster, the X2 drew more than 16 million riders attracted to extreme thrills. It featured seats that swiveled in all directions as the ride hurtled and twisted along the track, sometimes at a rate of up to 76 mph.

Guests ride the X2 roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain theme park in Valencia, California, in 2023. Eric Thayer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The X2 was shut down temporarily after two separate brain hemorrhages in July. In August, [CNN reported](https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/27/us/six-flags-rollercoaster-brain-injury-invs) that the X2 had been “linked to more than a dozen reports of serious injuries” and two deaths over nearly two decades.

Christopher’s is a third.

A ProPublica and L.A. Material investigation has found that state regulators have repeatedly failed to take swift action in the face of reported deaths and head injuries on the X2. On at least 70 occasions since 2010, Magic Mountain reported head injuries to the little-known unit within the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health responsible for ensuring roller coaster safety.

But rather than responding to those reports with vigorous inspections or safety checks, the regulators often did minimal or no investigation, according to a ProPublica and L.A. Material analysis of court filings, public records and internal regulatory documents.

“How many more people have to die before you think, ‘Well, maybe we should look at that?’” said Mariusz Ziejewski, a biomechanical engineer who has worked with the military to reduce brain injuries and was an expert witness in a lawsuit against Magic Mountain. “I think one is already way too much.”

CalOSHA and Magic Mountain instead frequently blamed riders for their injuries and in more than 35 cases alleged that people had somehow ridden the attraction incorrectly by failing to hold their heads in the right position. In one case, when a 14-year-old was hospitalized last year after losing consciousness on the ride, officials attributed it to the teenager’s menstrual cycle.

Six Flags and CalOSHA did not respond to detailed questions from ProPublica and L.A. Material. However, Denisse Gómez, a spokesperson for the state department that oversees CalOSHA, said in a statement that when theme park injuries are reported, regulators evaluate whether the ride was operating correctly and according to state safety rules. The agency is “committed to public safety,” she said, adding that “because that investigation is ongoing, we are not commenting on matters involving X2 at this time.”

Six Flags provided a statement that noted that the X2 had consistently passed safety tests, and its parks undergo preventative maintenance and a comprehensive, third-party inspection program. They also said their investigation of the ride remains ongoing, and that they are fully cooperating with CalOSHA. “Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do,” a spokesperson said.

When Six Flags has been sued for wrongful death or injuries related to the X2, it has maintained that injuries are rare and the ride is highly regulated by CalOSHA. In a recently settled lawsuit related to 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 in 2022, Magic Mountain’s director of public safety said in a declaration that the state has never notified the park of any “patron safety-related concerns related to the acceleration forces on the X2.”

Christopher Gibson was an autistic but healthy teen when he and his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, drove from their Colorado home to California to celebrate his high school graduation at Magic Mountain.

The pair rode roller coasters for several days starting on May 31, including the X2 and the Viper, which Christopher called a “neck breaker,” according to a sheriff’s report. On their fourth day at the theme park, the teen once again rode the X2 and then the Great American Revolution before complaining of a headache. By early afternoon, they returned to the hotel.

That night, the pain grew worse. His mother gave him Advil. Eventually, he moved to the hotel room’s closet, where it was darker, and went back to sleep. His mother assumed he was just exhausted, but around 2 p.m. the next day she noticed that he had stopped snoring. She looked into the closet and saw that his lips were blue and his face was covered with “white and pink foam.” She called 911. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 3:16 p.m. on June 4.

Within a month, a sheriff’s homicide detective reached out to the California state office that regulates roller coasters, writing that “it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.” The detective did not receive a reply until she contacted the office again two months later.

It’s been a deadly year for Six Flags. In addition to the California incident, an Atlanta school worker died in October after riding one of the theme park’s “hypercoasters” at Six Flags Over Georgia, prompting the company to temporarily close nine attractions at six theme parks across North America.

Theme park rides are regulated by states, not the federal government. In 2000, the legislature gave CalOSHA, the agency responsible for worker safety in California, oversight of roller coasters. Millions of people flock to the state’s theme parks each year, and the move came after a series of high-profile accidents in the 1990s. Under the law, state officials were given [new power to conduct annual inspections](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-jan-05-me-8740-story.html), and theme parks must report accidents that result in serious injury to the agency.

But ProPublica and L.A. Material found that officials in CalOSHA’s Amusement Ride and Tramway Unit have frequently determined that investigations are unnecessary when accidents happen on the X2.

Excerpt from a “Notification of Reportable Accident” form in which a patron was sent to the hospital after riding the X2 in 2016, but no follow-up investigation was performed Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and L.A. Material

In 16 instances involving people who wound up in the hospital after riding the X2 between 2009 and 2022, CalOSHA invoked identical or similar language after checking a box on accident reports that said state action was not called for. “At this time, this accident does not warrant an investigation,” said one typical form. “The condition which developed while the patron was riding does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride.” The report was filed in response to a woman who was hospitalized in 2016 with a head injury after riding the X2.

This also held true in cases where people lost their lives. When Hilda Farias suffered a massive brain hemorrhage after riding the X2 in October 2010, CalOSHA officials adopted similar language and conducted no inspection. The state regulator’s report did not even note that the 28-year-old mother of a 5-year-old had died, according to records obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material. Farias’ family sued the theme park, and the case settled in 2015.

When Hawley died in June 2022 after riding the X2, Magic Mountain initially told CalOSHA that the cause appeared to be heatstroke, according to a state report. The coroner later determined that Hawley, like Farias, had died of a massive brain hemorrhage. On that occasion, CalOSHA shut the ride down briefly while Six Flags conducted tests to measure the impact of g-forces on the rider and examined maintenance records. It ultimately determined that the ride was operating normally, according to a CalOSHA inspection obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Christopher Hawley, center, at a baseball game with his father and brother Courtesy of the Hawley family via Newsroom Public Relations

Christopher Gibson wore a Batman hoodie to school almost every day.

Diagnosed with autism when he was 5 or 6, Christopher was “high-functioning and verbal,” his mother told a sheriff’s detective. He had recently graduated high school and was headed to Colorado Mesa University to study theater.

As part of a family tradition, the teen’s mother let each of her five children pick the location of a celebratory senior trip. Chistopher wanted to ride roller coasters, and mother and son discussed a trip to Disneyland or Disney World. After some online research, Christopher chose Six Flags Magic Mountain, known for its thrill rides and DC Comics characters.

“He wanted to see Six Flags,” said Chadwick McGrady, an attorney representing the family in Christopher’s death. “The marketing worked.”

Magic Mountain sits about 35 miles north of downtown Los Angeles, in Valencia, the last notable stop before Interstate 5 climbs a steep stretch known as the Grapevine and drops down into the San Joaquin Valley. The park is aptly named: Roller coasters built into the mountainous terrain hurtle riders down hillsides and through trees, with disorienting turns taken at high velocity.

Christopher rode the X2 on June 2 and again on the morning of June 3. Soon after, reeling from a headache, he texted his mother from a park restroom: “I don’t think I can do any more today. My head is hurting me.”

They went back to the hotel. He had two days to recover before one of the big draws of the trip: DC Heroes and Villains Fest. Christopher “was a huge fan of DC Comics and was looking forward to meeting Batman on Friday, when DC Comics characters would be at the park,” sheriff’s detective Yoon Nam would later write in her report. Friday, June 5, was its opening day, and Christopher was determined not to miss it.

Christopher Gibson, left, with his mother, Leanndra Fascaldo, at a medieval-themed show in Las Vegas, days before his death during a trip to Six Flags Magic Mountain Courtesy of Leanndra Fascaldo

But on the morning of June 4, his head was still hurting him. He had taken refuge in the hotel room’s closet. His mother wasn’t unduly alarmed, because Christopher often retreated to dark spaces at home, a longstanding self-soothing ritual. She listened to the sound of his snoring — until at some point in the afternoon, the sound stopped.

In a statement released through her lawyer, Fascaldo said that her son “had so many dreams, and had his whole life ahead of him.”

After an autopsy, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner found a large subdural hemorrhage. The cause of death: “blunt force head trauma.” The reason for the injuries was noted as a “history of theme park rides.”

Nam and the medical examiner spoke by phone with Fascaldo, Christopher’s mother, on June 6.

According to a source familiar with the investigation, Fascaldo was composed, recounting a precise chronology of the rides Christopher had ridden. Among them were Full Throttle and the Viper, and, at least twice, the X2.

Nam contacted CalOSHA. She knew that it was responsible for regulating the state’s roller coasters and wanted to make sure the agency was aware that the Magic Mountain rides could have contributed to Christopher’s death.

“I cannot attribute his death to his roller coaster ride experiences with 100% certainty,” Nam wrote in a July 2 email to Bobby Park, who runs the CalOSHA unit regulating roller coasters. “However, at this time, it is possible that he suffered an injury during his visits to the theme park.”

The detective offered to help. “Please let me know if this case warrants additional follow-up by your office,” she wrote. “Feel free to call, text, or email with any questions or concerns.”

In the days after that unanswered email, more parkgoers suffered injuries after riding the X2.

On the evening of July 5, three days after the homicide detective sent her email, Pamela Guillen, 39, rode the coaster with her daughter.

When the car she was riding in trundled back into the station, Guillen’s daughter saw that her mother was “sitting with a vacant stare and her mouth open,” according to a lawsuit the family recently filed. Six Flags has not yet filed a response.

Guillen, who was visiting from Hawaii, managed to stumble off the ride, but a few minutes later park EMTs found her lying unconscious at the exit ramp. Two hours later, Gary Newman, the park’s vice president of maintenance, phoned CalOSHA to report the accident, relaying that a relative had said: “My cousin seemed out of it when she got off the ride so we took her to a bench and she went unconscious.”

The next morning, Scott Prather, a senior safety engineer with CalOSHA’s theme park unit, emailed his boss. According to a state official who has viewed the email, Guillen had been diagnosed with a brain bleed and was going into surgery. The email also said that the ride had been closed for inspection and g-force testing to ensure it was operating as intended.

Excerpt from the complaint filed by Pamela Guillen and her daughter, Camille Marquez, after Guillen sustained injuries at Magic Mountain Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and L.A. Material

Six Flags hired a firm that specialized in amusement park rides to conduct the test, according to a CalOSHA source familiar with the investigation.

State officials reviewed the results and authorized Magic Mountain to reopen the ride, the source said.

Then, on July 9, there was another incident, according to CalOSHA records reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. A woman from Nevada was visiting Magic Mountain with her family and others. They were roller coaster enthusiasts and had saved the X2 for their last ride of the day.

As soon as the ride started, the woman sensed something was wrong, according to an email she later sent to CalOSHA’s general inbox.

“The back of my head was repeatedly and forcefully slammed against the back of the seat,” she wrote in the email, which was reviewed by ProPublica and L.A. Material. “I tried holding my head forward and tried pushing it back against the seat to stop the banging, neither worked.”

When the ride stopped, she wasn’t sure whether she could stand. She couldn’t turn her head from side to side. She had nausea, sensitivity to light and a headache that reached “approximately 9 out of 10.”

She wasn’t the only one. “Three of the eight people riding together experienced similar difficulty with their heads repeatedly striking the backs of their seats,” she wrote in August.

Naomi Greer-Wilkinson suffered a traumatic head injury after riding the X2 in July. Facebook

She also filed a formal complaint with Six Flags in July but has not received a response, she told ProPublica and L.A. Material.

Two days after the Nevada woman rode the X2, there was another, more serious injury.

Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, a healthy 25-year-old from Los Angeles, rode the X2 on the night of July 11.

According to a lawsuit her family filed in September against the park, Greer-Wilkinson came off the ride “confused and having difficulty walking.” She stumbled off and then lost consciousness. She has since had multiple emergency brain surgeries. The lawsuit says she “remains bedridden, ventilator dependent, unable to speak.” Six Flags has not responded to the lawsuit.

On July 12, the X2 was temporarily shut down. It has not reopened.

Excerpt from a complaint filed by the family of Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, who sustained injuries on the X2 only six days after another incident on the same ride Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica and L.A. Material

In the wake of the ride’s closure, many amusement park patrons are asking how regulators could have missed so many signs of danger.

California law requires CalOSHA [to audit records](https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/344_8.html) related to every permanent ride each year, including reports of accidents. When amusement park patrons are seriously injured on rides, the theme park [must notify regulators immediately](https://www.dir.ca.gov/title8/344_15.html).

And yet, again and again, records show, regulators accepted Six Flags’ assertions that the injuries people suffered were not the fault of the X2. ProPublica and L.A. Material reviewed the state’s reports on X2 riders who were taken to the hospital from 2009 to 2022. In more than two-thirds of the cases, or 17 out 23, CalOSHA checked “no” on the form that would determine whether an investigation was warranted.

In September 2022, less than three months after Hawley died, a 28-year-old woman passed out as she exited the ride and hit her head, according to Magic Mountain’s account of the accident in a report filed with the state Paramedics took her to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.

Two days after the woman’s injury, Park determined no investigation was necessary. Park wrote: “Patron has pre-existing TBI [traumatic brain injury], diabetes, and has not eaten or consumed anything throughout the day.”

The woman, who survived the incident, sued Six Flags, which denied fault. The case settled in 2025.

The pattern of regulators citing preexisting conditions or rider behavior went back years. In 2011, the state noted that a 21-year-old woman had “a history of panic attacks,” so no investigation of the ride was necessary after she complained of a head injury.

In 2016, a 49-year-old woman hit her head against the headrest and asked for an ambulance. CalOSHA noted that her condition “does not appear to be related to the maintenance or operation of the ride,” adding that she “did not keep her head back” as riders are instructed.

Park declined to comment.

Some of the failures appear related to staffing shortages at CalOSHA. According to a 2025 staffing study by a Sacramento consulting firm commissioned by the state, audits of amusement park rides can be brief. The annual audit for a ride in X2’s class — a review meant to cover accident reports, training and maintenance reports and inspections — lasted an average of 3.7 hours.

The study also found that CalOSHA’s ride unit had been short-staffed for at least three years, with vacancies for its top job and two of four supervisor posts. There were “insufficient” supervisors for “thorough field supervision” and “inspection report review,” the report found.

Documents obtained by ProPublica and L.A. Material show Park had voiced frustration about staffing for his division since at least 2019. In an email he sent last week to his supervisor and the state department that oversees CalOSHA, Park wrote: “We have done workload studies, classification studies, begged, pleaded, and warned of the impending doom, and we are still no further along than we were 11 years ago.”

He continued: “We have failed. I have tried to do this, but I cannot continue as the dwindling supply of tools has run out.”

Park had been the CalOSHA official who received the news of Christopher Gibson’s death from Nam, the homicide detective, in early July.

In late August, after the X2 had been closed for more than a month, the detective sent a follow-up email to Park about the teen’s death.

“I never heard back from you regarding my previous email,” Nam wrote. “I saw news about multiple injuries involving the X2 ride at the Six Flags. Is there anything else I need to do?”

Park finally wrote back: “Apologies, I thought we responded.”

Park told the detective that since Christopher had died in a hotel room, there was no way to confirm which roller coasters the teen had ridden and “it would be difficult to determine which ride to assign this to or if it even is associated with a ride.”

The X2 roller coaster is seen after its closure at Six Flags Magic Mountain in September. Jae C. Hong/AP Photo

Still, a few weeks later, state officials ordered a more sophisticated g-force test of the ride, citing a series of injuries and a death over the summer. CalOSHA said in a statement that there are limits to commonly used ride testing. The standard test focuses on the torso and does not “necessarily establish the full range of movement or physical impacts experienced by an individual rider, including the potential effects on the head and neck,” the agency said. The order for new g-force testing didn’t mention anyone by name, but it did refer to an incident on June 3, the day Christopher left the park with a headache and eventually retreated to his hotel room’s closet, where he died.

The test results are pending.

Later in September, Six Flags announced the ride’s permanent shuttering without acknowledging the injuries or deaths connected with the roller coaster. “While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain president Brian Oerding said [in a statement](https://www.sixflags.com/blog/retiring-x2-magic-mountain). “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”

articleBody:
Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents.

Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems.

In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity.

Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens, who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030. And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.”

Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced.

This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website, a podcast series, and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact.

Eight guiding principles

The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality, but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools.

The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators.

The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote.

A suite of standards

The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process (IEEE 7000-2021), AI system transparency (IEEE 7001-2021), data privacy (IEEE 7002-2022), algorithmic bias considerations (IEEE 7003-2024), the impact on people’s well-being (IEEE 7010-2020), machine-readable personal privacy requirements (IEEE 7012-2025), and systems that mimic human empathy (IEEE 7014-2024).

AI ethics certifications

IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd, which includes two certifications: one for individuals and one for products.

The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria.

“Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative

The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program, which can certify it and issue the certification mark.

IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program. This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements.

New industry connections group

The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members.

The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle.

The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability.

Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues.

“The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.”

Podcasts and blogs

To mark the 10-year anniversary, IEEE SA created the five-part “Ethically Aligned Design: 10 Years of Impact” podcast series. It launched on 21 October. New episodes are being released every two weeks.

The episodes center around the vision for EAD, the process for selecting its foundational principles, and how they were translated into the IEEE 7000 standards.

The first podcast, “Origins of Ethically Aligned Design,” explored early efforts to make ethics a practical part of AI and autonomous system design. The experts discussed challenges, debates, global collaboration, and the real-world impact that helped move responsible technology from ethical principles toward actionable standards and practices.

The second podcast, “The Chapters and Committees” focuses on the multidisciplinary groups that worked on turning broad human values into practical guidance for AI and autonomous systems.

The podcast discussions serve as material for a thought leadership program that also includes blog articles about the IEEE 7000 series and educational resources to continue to raise awareness and support of this groundbreaking work.

articleBody:
> Here is a queer new puzzle that I know will interest my readers considerably. The four draughtsmen are shown exactly as they stood on a square chequered board — not necessarily eight squares by eight — but the ink with which the board was drawn was evanescent, so that all the diagram except the men has disappeared. How many squares were there in the board and how am I to reconstruct it? I know that each man stood in the middle of a square, one on the edge of each side of the board and no man in a corner. It is a real puzzle, until you hit on the method of solution, and then to get the correct answer is absurdly easy.

Select Click for Answer

> Draw a line from A to D. Then draw CE perpendicular to AD, and equal in length to AD. Then E will be the centre of another square. Draw a line from E to B and extend it on both sides. Also draw a line FG through C and parallel to EB and the lines through A and D perpendicular to EB and FG. Now, as H is the centre of a corner square, we can mark off the length HE all round the square and we find the board is 10 × 10.
> If the size of the men were not given we might subdivide into more squares, but the men would be too large for the squares. As the distance between the centres of squares is the same as the width of the squares, we can now complete the board with ease, as shown in the diagram inset.

[The inset diagram is hard to read, but if rows are numbered and files lettered, I believe the men are on e1, a5, j7, and d10.]

From [Modern Puzzles and How to Solve Them](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Modern_Puzzles_and_how_to_Solve_Them/FS8PAAAAQAAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA54&printsec=frontcover), 1926.

articleBody:
Adam Engst, writing at TidBITS:

> This past August, I did something I had never done before:
> released a full-fledged Mac app. Prompted by tech ghost stories
> about settings mysteriously changing during operating system
> updates, I spent months working with Claude Code to create a
> utility called SetShot that would reveal what settings change
> during macOS updates (see “[SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes](https://tidbits.com/2026/08/19/setshot-tracks-macos-settings-changes/),” 19 August 2026). So far, I haven’t caught Apple
> red-handed, although I still hear chatter about configuration
> changes after users install updates.
> Practically speaking, SetShot offers something never previously
> available to Mac users: the capability to identify and log
> settings changes over time, whether made by you, macOS, or some
> app. To that end, it takes and compares snapshots of numerous
> settings deep within macOS, reporting on what changed between
> them. It never changes any settings, so the worst it can do is
> tell you something you didn’t want to know.

[SetShot](https://tidbits.com/setshot/) is a very cool app, and so very Adam Engst-flavored. Free of charge and [open source](https://github.com/adamengst/setshot-app) to boot.

There’s an anecdote involving me in Engst’s post, and while SetShot couldn’t fix my problem directly, it was very helpful in showing me where to look to fix it myself. The backstory: I set a custom “Text highlight color” in System Preferences: Appearances many years ago — I mean like maybe 20 years ago — and had not changed it in years. It’s just the perfect shade of blue. But one night two months ago I went screwing around to see what the modern default text highlight colors are, and, son of a bitch, when I tried to change my color back to the custom one I’d been using for decades, I couldn’t. The way the color picker stores color values from the modern Appearance settings panel must have changed. It still honors the old value I had if it’s in the defaults system that way, but it writes a different style of value if you change it in the Appearance panel in System Settings.

Here’s a short version of how I got my old color back. Using System Settings, I changed the custom color to the exact RGB values 0.2 / 0.4 / 0.6. Then I read them from the command line:

❯ defaults read -g AppleHighlightColor
0.200000 0.400000 0.600000 Other

That’s not the color I wanted; I just wanted to prove that that’s the global key for a custom text highlight color. When I read those same values from a backup version of my *~/Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist* file (always have backups, kids), with my beloved custom color, it looked liked this:

❯ defaults read /path/to/.GlobalPreferences.plist AppleHighlightColor
0.698039 0.760784 0.835294

So the old value was a string with three floating point RGB values. The new value was a string with those three values *plus* the word “Other”. This command, writing back my custom RGB values without the word “Other”:

❯ defaults write -g AppleHighlightColor "0.698039 0.760784 0.835294"

restored the color I’ve been using since George W. Bush was still president. It’s a really good color, trust me.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/17/setshot-1-0)

title: BundID: Massenhafte Login-Versuche führen zu Kontosperren, Passwort-Zugang eingeschränkt
subtitle: Nach einer Welle automatisierter Anmeldeversuche hat der Bund beim zentralen Bürgerkonto die Reißleine gezogen.
feedText:

articleBody:
**Nach einer Welle automatisierter Anmeldeversuche hat der Bund beim zentralen Bürgerkonto die Reißleine gezogen. Wer in den vergangenen Tagen eine Sperrmail zu seinem BundID-Konto bekommen hat, ist nicht allein. Das zentrale Bürgerkonto des Bundes, über das ihr unter anderem BAföG beantragen oder ein Fahrzeug zulassen könnt, war Ziel eines groß angelegten Angriffs. Das Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) hat den Vorfall inzwischen bestätigt.**

## Recht veraltete Angriffsmethode zwang BundID in die Knie

Nach Angaben der Behörde via [heise online](https://www.heise.de/news/BundID-Massenhafte-Angriffe-fuehren-zu-Kontosperrungen-11526376.html) kam es zu automatisierten, massenhaften Anmeldeversuchen auf BundID-Konten. Die vielen Fehlversuche lösten automatische Sperren aus, Betroffene erhielten E-Mails mit der Aufforderung, ihr Passwort zurückzusetzen. Erste Berichte über solche Mails tauchten bereits am 13. und 14. November auf. Hinweise darauf, dass Angreifer tatsächlich Konten übernommen haben, liegen dem BSI derzeit nicht vor. Wie viele Konten gesperrt wurden, ließ die Behörde offen.

## Keine konkreten Details

Zur Angriffsmethode gibt es bislang nur inoffizielle Angaben. Das [Handelsblatt](https://www.handelsblatt.com/politik/deutschland/bundid-hackerangriff-auf-buergerkonten-mit-massenhaften-log-in-versuchen/100270238.html) berichtet unter Berufung auf Regierungskreise von Credential Stuffing. Dabei probieren Angreifer Kombinationen aus E-Mail-Adresse und Passwort aus früheren Datenlecks bei anderen Diensten durch und hoffen darauf, dass Nutzer dieselben Zugangsdaten mehrfach verwenden. Offiziell bestätigt hat das BSI diese Einordnung nicht.

## BundID seit gestern gesperrt

Seit Montag ist die Anmeldung per Benutzername und Passwort eingeschränkt. Laut einem Hinweis auf der BundID-Seite wurde dieser Zugang wegen zahlreicher unberechtigter Anmeldeversuche deaktiviert. Der Online-Ausweis und andere Zugangsmittel funktionieren weiterhin. Wann der Passwort-Login wieder vollständig zur Verfügung steht, ist noch unklar. Einigen Berichten zufolge soll er künftig nur noch mit einem zusätzlichen Sicherheitscode per E-Mail funktionieren. Eine pauschale Entsperrung der betroffenen Konten ist offenbar nicht geplant.

Für euch heißt das: Ist euer Konto gesperrt, müsst ihr das Passwort zurücksetzen oder euch mit dem Online-Ausweis beziehungsweise einem ELSTER-Zertifikat anmelden. Habt ihr dasselbe Passwort auch bei anderen Diensten genutzt, solltet ihr es dort ebenfalls ändern. Zudem lohnt sich ein Blick in die Kontoeinstellungen unter „Zugänge & Daten“, wo ihr die Zwei-Faktor-Anmeldung aktivieren könnt.

## Kommt zur ungünstigsten Zeit

Der Vorfall trifft die BundID in einer Phase, in der der Bund die digitale Verwaltung ausbauen will. Zuletzt zählte das Bürgerkonto rund 4,9 Millionen Konten, knapp 1.800 Onlinedienste sind angebunden. Im Zuge des Onlinezugangsgesetzes 2.0 soll es künftig als „DeutschlandID“ weiterlaufen. Am 2. Januar 2027 startet zudem mit d-you die staatliche EUDI-Wallet. Kritiker bemängeln seit Längerem, dass jedes BundID-Konto zwangsläufig einen Passwort-Zugang erhält, der sich nicht vollständig entfernen lässt. Die Sicherheitsforscherin Lilith Wittmann hatte bereits 2024 Schwachstellen bei der Einbindung der BundID in kommunale Verwaltungsportale aufgezeigt.

title: Tripod Is the Best New Podcast App I’ve Tried in a Long Time (With an Excellent Queue System)
subtitle: Over the years, I’ve realized that I’m a particular type of podcast listener: I do not listen to every single new episode that comes in from the sh…
