articleBody:
Tripod for iPhone.

Over the years, I’ve realized that I’m a particular type of podcast listener: I do not listen to every single new episode that comes in from the shows I’m subscribed to; I want to see them in a list, then pick and choose the episodes I want, and arrange them in a queue. The interactions need to be simple and the queue tactile, ideally with drag and drop to move specific episodes up and down. I do not personally care about transcripts and video (although [we support both with our shows](https://www.macstories.net/news/macstories-podcasts-now-let-you-switch-between-video-and-audio-in-apple-podcasts/), and I think they’re great additions). I do not need an Apple Watch app. I do not need playlists. And I want to have audio effects – pioneered by [Marco Arment in Overcast](https://marco.org/apps), now found in the most popular indie podcast apps – to trim silence and boost volume. I listen to most podcasts at 1.5x speed, but some at 1.8x. I play podcasts from my iPhone, and I want to use an *extremely* native app that also comes with a CarPlay version.

The intersection of all these preferences is surprisingly hard to find in a single, well-rounded iPhone app. I find [Overcast](https://overcast.fm/) to have the best audio effects and performance, but I do not understand its queuing system. For the longest time, I used [Pocket Casts](https://pocketcasts.com/), but the design wasn’t great, and it was often slow at refreshing my feeds. I would have used [Castro](https://castro.fm/), which had the closest version of the queue management system I wanted, but the app’s future has always been somewhat up in the air…and [it just changed ownership, again](https://mjtsai.com/blog/2026/11/06/castro-sold-yet-again/).

With this context in mind, you can imagine my surprise when, seemingly out of the blue, [indie developer Ben McCarthy](https://benricemccarthy.com/apps/) – a [longtime friend of MacStories](https://www.macstories.net/?s=Ben%20McCarthy) and wildly proficient iOS developer – dropped [Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.com/tripod/), their brand new podcast app designed around an inbox and queue system.

I’ll cut to the chase: Tripod is the best podcast app I’ve tried in a long time. The app looks wonderful on the iPhone Duo, it has the best-designed and most reasonable (for my brain, at least) inbox-queue combo I’ve seen to date, and it is full of little details, hidden Easter eggs, and small quality-of-life features that make it a remarkable option for Castro expats and, for my taste, one of the best app debuts of 2026.

The idea behind Tripod is pretty simple: there is an inbox and a queue. New episodes land in the inbox, which you can configure in terms of notifications, UI (you can optionally show action buttons underneath each episode, or rely on the default context menu for managing them), and behavior. For instance, you can choose to automatically remove episodes older than one week or one month, or just keep a specific number of a show’s recent episodes.

Tripod’s inbox screen.

Immediately in the inbox, there are some details I appreciate. When you long-press to show the context menu for a podcast, the menu items are tinted to match the key color of the podcast’s artwork, which is a lovely detail. But also in this menu, you can choose to either remove an episode or mark it as played (not a lot of apps get this right!), jump to the podcast’s main page, and either add it to the queue or ‘Someday’ list (more on this later).

Menu items are tinted per podcast.

In the inbox, you can group episodes by date or show – the latter option being especially effective if you just want to see how many inbox episodes you have for a specific podcast in your library, so you can quickly triage them. Speaking of the library: you can long-press a show to easily choose where new episodes should land from a context menu, but you can also tweak a podcast’s dedicated settings. These include notifications as well as separate limits for the inbox and queue.

You’ll also notice a scrollable list of filters at the top of the library. These UI elements are available on this page as well as the queue, but I find them to be best suited for the queue, where they make the most sense to me. The queue is a list of episodes where, as previously seen in Castro, episodes can be delightfully rearranged with drag and drop. Various grouping and sorting options are available here as well, but it’s the filter row at the top that I love. With filters, you can sort Tripod’s queue by in-progress episodes (boring, but necessary), favorites, and my three favorite options: short episodes, episodes by category, and “someday” episodes.

Tripod’s queue.

With the ‘Short’ filter, I can quickly get through episodes that don’t last too long; categories are fetched from Apple Podcasts’ database, and they’re an ingenious way to triage episodes based on what I’m in the mood for without having to create smart playlists upfront (something I used to do in Pocket Casts). The ‘Someday’ list (which seems to be inspired by [the namesake feature originally seen in Things](https://culturedcode.com/things/support/articles/4001304/)) is a surprisingly useful way to save evergreen episodes I know I want to get to, well, *someday*, but don’t have to be part of my daily rotation. For example, [Myke Hurley’s ‘State of the Workflow’ series](https://www.theenthusiast.net/state-of-the-workflow/) on [Cortex](https://relay.fm/cortex) is perfect for the Someday list since those episodes aren’t time-sensitive or news-heavy, and hold their value months after their release date.

Filters in the queue.

The result of all these decisions is that when I spend time interacting with Tripod, everything clicks and works with the way my brain thinks of managing podcasts. The app is also a great example of how to design for the iPhone Duo: every device pose is supported, and when the Duo is unfolded, the Now Playing screen lives in a left sidebar so you can both navigate the app and manage your listening session.

Different iPhone Duo poses for Tripod.

Features seen in other podcast apps are also seen here: swipe up on the artwork, and you’ll get pages in the sidebar for chapters (you can select which ones you want to skip), a real-time transcript (which is generated on-device and seems comparable to Overcast’s in terms of quality), and audio settings.

Pages in Tripod’s Now Playing screen, including the ability to generate clips for social media.

And it is, in fact, when comparing Tripod to Overcast that I need to air some of my complaints about this early version of the app (Tripod launched last week, and a 2026.4 update – which I tested for this review – is launching soon on the App Store). Tripod does not support streaming episodes yet, and it’s a download-only affair for now. That is not a dealbreaker for me, but I don’t care about keeping episodes offline and dislike having to wait a few seconds before an episode begins, so I hope McCarthy supports streaming in the near future. Second, while Tripod does have audio effects for trimming silence between words and adjusting volume (it’s an equalizer with different options), they don’t sound nearly as good as Marco Arment’s effects to my ears. Arment has been tweaking and optimizing those effects for years, and it shows. That said, Tripod’s effects are certainly better than some sloppy podcast clients I’ve tried this year, and they get the job done.

What Tripod may lack in maturity (the app is not on the iPad or Mac either, for example), it compensates for with fun details that are a testament to McCarthy’s taste and deep knowledge of iOS. Promo codes for sponsors are automatically extracted from episodes you listen to and their show notes, and made available for quick copy in the Search screen. Links you open from show notes are also temporarily saved, so you can easily find them later. There are two stunning Six Colors and Trans alternative app icons; you can review your entire activity in the app in a dedicated screen; and there are listening stats that – I have to assume – will be made easier to share, Spotify Wrapped-style, at some point.

Tripod can automatically find promo codes for sponsors of your favorite shows.

It’s always been hard to stand out in the App Store, but even more so these days because of the [increasing number of new app releases](https://www.macstories.net/linked/app-store-chaos/) made possible by AI coding agents. However, as someone who’s been doing this for 17 years, I can tell you that – and excuse my French – it’s still quite easy to tell a shitty app apart from one that is thoughtful, designed with care, and considered with the restraint that is necessary to ship a quality product.

[Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.com/tripod/) is both the sum of its parts and the parts it *doesn’t* have. It’s an opinionated podcast app created for a particular type of podcast listener that, however, pulls off the tricky balancing act of blending its creator’s opinions with customization features for a wider audience.

If you’re the kind of person who would enjoy listening to podcasts with this kind of app, I think [you already know what to do](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tripod-podcast-player/id6824844745).

articleBody:
**Eventide SplitEQ 2 löst die Vorgängerversion des Plugins ab, das tatsächlich schon vor fünf Jahren veröffentlicht wurde. Und immer noch stecken hier Funktionen drin, die andere Hersteller so nicht mal im Ansatz umgesetzt haben. Version 2 erweitert nun sogar die Möglichkeiten.**

## Alles über Eventide SplitEQ 2:

- Was macht Eventide SplitEQ 2 so besonders?
- Welche Neuheiten stecken in SplitEQ 2?
- Verfügbarkeit und Preis
- Weitere Infos

## Was macht Eventide SplitEQ 2 so besonders?

Eventide SplitEQ 2 · Quelle: Eventide

Im Gegensatz zu vielen anderen EQ-Plugins setzt auch Eventide SplitEQ 2 wieder auf einen ganz besonderen Trick. Das Audiomaterial lässt sich über die eigens entwickelte und *Structural Split* benannte Methode in Transienten und tonale Anteile trennen, um beide dann individuell zu bearbeiten.

Das ist immer noch ein ungewöhnlicher Ansatz, der in der neusten Version mit einigen Funktionen ausgebaut wird. Version 2 bietet sich damit wieder als Werkzeug für Mixing-Aufgaben an, bei denen manchmal mit chirurgischer Präzision gearbeitet werden muss. Und ebenso ist dieser Equalizer ein interessantes Plugin für Sounddesign.

## Welche Neuheiten stecken in SplitEQ 2?

Bei SplitEQ 2 handelt es sich weiterhin um ein EQ-Plugin mit insgesamt acht Bändern. Diese Bänder lassen sich nicht nur in Transienten und tonale Anteile splitten, sondern ebenso stereo, links, rechts oder Mid/Side bearbeiten. Für das Trennen des Signals stehen jetzt neue Einstellungen für die Wahl des Ausgangsmaterials bereit.

Sechs Bänder bieten umfassende Optionen und funktionieren nun sogar dynamisch. Du kannst hier also zusätzlich mit einem Threshold-Wert arbeiten, um vergleichbar zu einem Kompressor oder Expander die Dynamik der Bänder zu manipulieren. Das ist gerade in Kombination mit dem Trennen in Transienten und tonale Anteile sehr interessant. Wohlgemerkt kannst du natürlich auch das gesamte ausgewählte Frequenzband mit dem Plugin vornehmen. Dann verhält sich das Plugin eben mehr wie ein „traditioneller“ dynamischer Equalizer.

Zusätzlich gibt es eine globale Dynamikbearbeitung, die wahlweise vor oder nach einzelnen EQ-Bändern eingesetzt werden kann. Und auch hier lässt sich das Signal bei Bedarf vorher in Transienten oder den tonalen Anteil trennen.

Praktisch ist in dem Zusammenhang, dass Eventide SplitEQ 2 sechs Optionen für Sidechaining anbietet, ebenfalls im Split oder mit dem gesamten Signal auf einem Band. Und optional lassen sich auch externe Signale als Sidechain nutzen. Im Zusammenspiel mit dem dynamischen EQ-Bändern ist das ein sehr nützliches Feature.

Eventide SplitEQ 2 · Quelle: Eventide

Wie bei fast allen modernen EQ-Plugins zeigt auch dieses den gesamten Frequenzbereich im Stil eines Analyzers an. Dabei lassen sich ebenfalls solche Frequenzbereiche darstellen, die sich auf unterschiedlichen Tracks gegenseitig maskieren. So entdeckst du auch visuell die Problemzonen in einem Mix, wenn du diesen schnell aufräumen und transparenter machen willst.

Laut Angaben des Herstellers arbeitet das Plugin nun mit einer höheren Auflösung und einem verbesserten Filter im Höhenbereich. Über Tracking Bypass kann das Plugin jederzeit „ausgeknipst“ werden, um beispielsweise bei Aufnahmen keine unnötige Latenz zu erzeugen.

Unterm Strich stellt Eventide hier nicht radikal das Plugin auf den Kopf, sondern verbessert vielmehr an den wichtigen Stellen. Gefällt mir!

## Verfügbarkeit und Preis

Eventide SplitEQ 2 läuft als **VST3, AU und AAX**auf**macOS**(10.14 oder neuer) sowie**Windows** (10 oder neuer). Für die Lizenzierung ist ein kostenloser iLok-Account erforderlich.

Bis zum 03. Januar 2027 ist das Plugin für 107 Euro (statt 199 Euro) zu haben. Wer die erste Version besitzt, findet im User-Account den Preis für ein Upgrade. Du bekommst das Plugin auch [hier bei Plugin Boutique](https://www.pluginboutique.com/product/2-Effects/16-EQ/18386-SplitEQ-2?a_aid=5d08a894507cb&data1=gnde)*.

title: Metallpartikel könnten den Impaktwinter nach dem Chicxulub-Einschlag verlängert haben
subtitle: Der Chicxulub-Einschlag vor rund 66 Millionen Jahren schleuderte große Mengen geschmolzenen Gesteins in die Atmosphäre.
feedText: In erstarrten Tröpfchen dieses Materials sind winzige Kristalle mit Iridium, Osmium und Platin nachgewiesen worden. articleBody:
**Der Chicxulub-Einschlag vor rund 66 Millionen Jahren schleuderte große Mengen geschmolzenen Gesteins in die Atmosphäre. In erstarrten Tröpfchen dieses Materials sind winzige Kristalle mit Iridium, Osmium und Platin nachgewiesen worden. Die Partikel könnten zusätzlich zu Staub und Ruß die Bildung lichtabschirmender Aerosole begünstigt und so den nachfolgenden Impaktwinter verlängert haben.**

**Lund (Schweden).** Der Einschlag des Chicxulub-Asteroiden auf der heutigen Halbinsel Yucatán setzte vor rund 66 Millionen Jahren gewaltige Mengen Material frei. Geschmolzenes Gestein wurde in die Höhe geschleudert, kühlte ab und fiel zum Teil als winzige Glaskügelchen auf die Erde zurück. Gleichzeitig verdunkelten Staub, Ruß und andere Schwebstoffe den Himmel, sodass die Photosynthese über längere Zeit beeinträchtigt war.

Eine markante Spur des Einschlags ist die weltweit verbreitete, mit Iridium angereicherte Grenzschicht zwischen Kreidezeit und Paläogen. Wie die seltenen Metalle in den ausgeschleuderten Partikeln gebunden waren, blieb jedoch weitgehend unklar. Auch die Frage, welche Stoffe den [lang anhaltenden Impaktwinter](https://www.scinexx.de/news/geowissen/der-tag-an-dem-die-dinos-starben/) verstärkten, ist noch nicht abschließend geklärt.

### Iridium steckt in winzigen Kristallen

Ein internationales Team um Prof. Vivi Vajda vom Swedish Museum of Natural History hat außergewöhnlich gut erhaltene Glaskügelchen aus der Kreide-Paläogen-Grenzschicht auf der kolumbianischen Insel Gorgonilla untersucht. Dort sind ursprüngliche Auswurfprodukte des Einschlags in marinen Sedimenten bewahrt geblieben, ohne vollständig zu Tonmineralen umgewandelt worden zu sein.

In einem ersten Schritt wurden 610 Kügelchen mittels Röntgenmikroskopie erfasst und 16 besonders gut erhaltene Proben ausgewählt. Drei davon untersuchte das Team anschließend mit einer hochauflösenden Röntgenfluoreszenz-Methode an der Synchrotronanlage MAX IV in Lund. Bei einzelnen Messungen lag der Abstand der Messpunkte bei nur 100 Nanometern.

Die Elementkarten zeigen, dass Iridium, Osmium und Platin in den Glaskügelchen nicht gleichmäßig verteilt sind, sondern kleinste, örtlich konzentrierte Strukturen bilden. Iridium kommt sowohl in nadelartigen als auch in würfelförmigen Gebilden vor, während Osmium vor allem in den Nadeln und Platin eher in würfelförmigen Bereichen auftritt. Hinzu kommen auffällige gemeinsame Vorkommen mit Kobalt, Nickel, Kupfer, Zink und Blei.

> „Mit der extrem hochauflösenden Kartierung am NanoMAX konnten wir das Iridium als winzige Splitter in Form von Nadeln und Dreiecken sehen“, erklärt Prof. Vivi Vajda.

### Beim Einschlag entstanden wohl neue Mineralphasen

Die Kügelchen bestehen aus unterschiedlich zusammengesetzten Gläsern, in denen sich vor allem siliziumreiche und kalziumreiche Bereiche unterscheiden lassen. Diese Mischung weist darauf hin, dass beim Aufprall auf die karbonatreichen Gesteine Yucatáns Material des Asteroiden und des Untergrunds aufgeschmolzen und miteinander vermischt wurde.

In den würfelförmigen Nanostrukturen treten Platin und Iridium vor allem zusammen mit Kobalt, Nickel und Blei auf. Nadelartige Gebilde zeigen dagegen enge räumliche Beziehungen zwischen Osmium, Iridium, Kupfer und Zink. Diese Kombinationen sprechen für bisher nicht genauer charakterisierte Mineralphasen, die unter den extremen Bedingungen des Einschlags entstanden sein könnten.

Welche chemischen Verbindungen die seltenen Metalle im Einzelnen bilden, lässt sich aus den Messungen noch nicht sicher bestimmen. Auch die quantitative Analyse der winzigen Strukturen ist mit Unsicherheiten behaftet. Einzelne chemische Veränderungen können zudem erst nach der Ablagerung im Sediment erfolgt sein.

### Metallsplitter als Keime für Aerosole?

Die Funde könnten auch für die Folgen des Einschlags wichtig sein. Winzige feste Teilchen können als Ausgangspunkte dienen, an denen sich Aerosole bilden, die Sonnenlicht streuen oder abschirmen. Die Studienautoren vermuten deshalb, dass schwer reaktive Metallsplitter zusätzlich zu anderen Auswurfprodukten die lang anhaltende Verdunkelung der Atmosphäre begünstigt haben könnten.

Nachgewiesen wurde bislang allerdings nur, in welchen Formen die Metallpartikel in den erstarrten Glaskügelchen erhalten sind. Ob ähnliche Splitter damals tatsächlich in der Atmosphäre schwebten, wie wirksam sie als Aerosolkeime waren und welchen Anteil sie am Impaktwinter hatten, wurde in dieser Untersuchung weder direkt gemessen noch in einem Klimamodell berechnet.

Um die mögliche Rolle dieser Partikel besser zu beurteilen, sollen die chemischen Bindungsformen der iridium-, osmium- und platinhaltigen Strukturen genauer untersucht werden. Ein Vergleich mit Glaskügelchen aus weiteren Fundregionen wie Belize, Haiti und Dänemark könnte zeigen, wie die feinen Metallpartikel beim Einschlag entstanden und verteilt wurden.

- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [MAX IV Laboratory](https://www.maxiv.lu.se/article/the-great-planetary-reset-mapping-glass-pearls/)

title: iPhone Duo: Entwickler liefern, die Hardware macht Sorgen
subtitle: Die Software-Unterstützung für Apples faltbares iPhone entwickelt sich schneller als erwartet.

articleBody:
Die Software-Unterstützung für Apples faltbares iPhone entwickelt sich schneller als erwartet. Apples Marketingchef Greg Joswiak meldet inzwischen mehr als 200.000 Anwendungen, die für das iPhone Duo optimiert wurden. Innerhalb von etwas mehr als einer Woche habe sich diese Zahl verdoppelt. Der Manager [zeigt sich auf X](https://x.com/gregjoz/status/2122393925080252469) entsprechend zufrieden mit der Resonanz unter Entwicklern.

#### Die Apple-Store-App: Gestern noch nicht für das Duo optimiert

Ganz ohne Spott blieb die Erfolgsmeldung allerdings nicht. Nutzer wiesen [umgehend darauf hin](https://x.com/MichalLangmajer/status/2122398652169654531), dass ausgerechnet Apples eigene [Store-App](https://www.ifun.de/app/375380948) noch nicht an das neue Bildschirmformat angepasst war. Die entsprechende Aktualisierung hat Apple inzwischen nachgereicht.

## Claude testet Apps auf dem faltbaren iPhone

Dass Anpassungen inzwischen deutlich schneller gelingen, dürfte auch mit KI-Werkzeugen zusammenhängen. Wir haben [bereits über die zunehmende KI-Unterstützung bei der App-Entwicklung berichtet](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/ki-app-flut-apples-app-store-wird-zum-nadeloehr-fuer-alle-290001/). Nun erweitert Anthropic die Möglichkeiten seiner Entwicklungsumgebung Claude Code um die direkte Unterstützung des iPhone-Duo-Simulators.

#### iPhone Duo im Simulator: Jetzt auch in Claude Code

Wie Anthropic in seiner [aktuellen Anleitung](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-ios-simulator#test-your-app-on-an-iphone-duo) beschreibt, kann Claude Anwendungen im Simulator selbstständig bedienen und deren Darstellung überprüfen. Die KI klickt sich durch Menüs, betätigt Schaltflächen und sucht nach abgeschnittenen Inhalten, fehlerhaften Bedienelementen und unerwartetem Verhalten.

#### Claude bietet den neuen Simulator aktiv an

Beim iPhone Duo lassen sich dabei drei Gerätestellungen überprüfen: geschlossen, halb geöffnet und vollständig aufgeklappt. Auch Zwischenstellungen des Scharniers können simuliert werden. Claude kann erkannte Probleme mit Bildschirmfotos dokumentieren und konkrete Änderungen vorschlagen. Voraussetzung sind Claude Desktop ab Version 4.29.0 und Xcode 27.1 oder neuer.

## Neue Displaybrüche und Vorwürfe gegen Apple

Während die Software zunehmend auf das Duo zugeschnitten wird, reißen die Berichte über Hardwareprobleme nicht ab. Ein [neues Reddit-Video](https://www.reddit.com/r/iPhoneDuo/comments/1xy66x7/she_was_opening_the_iphone_duo_and_it_cracked/) zeigt erneut einen Displaybruch beim Aufklappen. Ähnliche Aufnahmen hatten [bereits Anfang November](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/iphone-duo-video-zeigt-displaybruch-beim-aufklappen-290084/) auf mögliche Probleme mit dem Scharnier hingewiesen.

#### Ein weiterer im Video dokumentierter Display-Bruch beim iPhone Duo

[↗ Primärquelle: reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com/r/iPhoneDuo/comments/1xy66x7/she_was_opening_the_iphone_duo_and_it_cracked)

Hinzu kommen Vorwürfe gegen Apple. Nach Recherchen der koreanischen Fachpublikation [The Elec](https://www.thelec.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=64923) soll der Konzern einen Zulieferer dazu gedrängt haben, eine öffentliche Stellungnahme zurückzuziehen. Der Hersteller Fine M-Tec liefert Metallkomponenten zur Unterstützung des faltbaren Bildschirms und hatte Ende Oktober erklärt, dass seine Bauteile nicht für die gemeldeten Schäden verantwortlich seien.

Anfang November verschwand die Erklärung von der Webseite des Unternehmens. Laut The Elec soll Apple die Veröffentlichung beanstandet haben. Eine Bestätigung durch Apple liegt nicht vor. Der Konzern hat [die Displayprobleme bereits eingeräumt](https://www.iphone-ticker.de/crackgate-beim-iphone-duo-apple-bestaetigt-displayprobleme-289183/) und bietet betroffenen Kunden Ersatzgeräte an. Welche technische Ursache hinter den Brüchen steckt, bleibt weiterhin offen.

articleBody:
On 13 November 2026, the Norwegian Supreme Court, sitting as an eleven-judge Grand Chamber, delivered a landmark judgment in the [North Sea Fields](https://www.climatecasechart.com/document/greenpeace-nordic-and-nature-youth-v-energy-ministry-the-north-sea-fields-case_52a4) case. The Court held that environmental impact assessments (EIAs) must address downstream emissions from burning extracted oil and gas (Scope 3). By a 6–5 majority, it also required the emissions of Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil to be assessed alongside those of other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. Finding that the Ministry of Energy had failed to meet this requirement, even in its subsequent assessments, the Court declared the development approvals invalid ([HR-2026-2428-S](https://www.domstol.no/no/hoyesterett/avgjorelser/avgjorelser-2026/hoyesterett---sivil/HR-2026-2428-S/), paras 225, 234, 244), short of ordering operations to stop. The decision’s constitutional significance lies in the role of procedural environmental rights, which ultimately require thorough and independent assessments, as well as the inclusive participation of the public in how the State assesses climate harm.

Greenpeace Nordic and *Natur og Ungdom* (Nature and Youth) brought the proceedings against the Norwegian State. Save the Children Norway intervened through written submissions on children’s rights. The Norwegian Association of Local and Regional Authorities and the Norwegian National Human Rights Institution also submitted observations.

The three developments hold an estimated 875 million barrels of oil equivalent. Yet, the ruling matters beyond this scale: it challenges the assessment of petroleum projects in isolation.

## The Road to the Supreme Court

In June 2023, the environmental organisations challenged the approvals of the three Plans for Development and Operation (PDOs), arguing that the EIAs had omitted emissions from the eventual combustion of the oil and gas. They also sought interim relief.

In January 2024, the Oslo District Court declared the approvals [invalid](https://verfassungsblog.de/is-the-norwegian-paradox-coming-to-an-end/)and granted interim relief. In the appeals brought by the State, the Borgarting Court of Appeal suspended the injunction and sought an advisory opinion from the EFTA Court, which held in May 2025 that the EIA Directive required downstream combustion emissions to be assessed ([Case E-18/24](https://eftacourt.int/cases/c-wp-9768)).

Meanwhile, the operators submitted supplementary environmental reports, followed by public consultations. In August and December 2024, the Ministry decided not to revoke the approvals. In November 2025, the Court of Appeal declared those decisions [invalid](https://www.greenpeace.org/static/planet4-norway-stateless/2026/08/ff64a3a1-judgment-and-injunction-order-of-14-november-2025_unofficial-english-translation.pdf): although it considered the supplementary reports sufficient, the Ministry’s own assessment was deemed deficient, and the State appealed.

While the appeal was pending, the government in May 2026 issued a Royal Decree declining to revoke the approvals, but the appeal decided by the Supreme Court concerned only the Ministry’s 2024 decisions.

This Norwegian case has already travelled. The Oslo District Court judgment was cited by the UK Supreme Court in [Finch v Surrey County Council](https://www.supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2022-0064) ([2024] UKSC 20, paras 169–172). *Finch*, in turn, was later relied upon by the Scottish Court of Session in [quashing](https://www.scotcourts.gov.uk/media/v0zkbsxy/2025csoh10-petitions-by-greenpeace-limited-and-uplift-for-judicial-review.pdf)the Jackdaw and Rosebank consents ( *Greenpeace Ltd v Advocate General for Scotland*, [2025] CSOH 10). Meanwhile, in Norway, the Borgarting Court of Appeal referred questions concerning downstream emissions to the EFTA Court ([Case E-18/24](https://eftacourt.int/cases/c-wp-9768)), whose advisory opinion was cited by Judges Bhandari and Cleveland in their joint declaration attached to the ICJ’s Advisory Opinion on *Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change* ([Joint declaration](https://icj-web.leman.un-icc.cloud/sites/default/files/case-related/187/187-20250723-adv-01-06-en.pdf), para 16 with reference to Case E-18/24, para 17), as well as by the [Danish Energy Board of Appeals](https://www.climatecasechart.com/documents/greenpeace-v-danish-energy-agency-decision_662c), which required reconsideration for the approval of the Hejre oil field.

## The Supreme Court’s Decision

At first glance, the judgment turns on whether Article 3(1) of the EU EIA Directive (2011/92/EU) encompasses downstream combustion emissions among a project’s significant direct and indirect effects. But its reasoning reaches further, engaging with causation, cumulative harm and the constitutional value of environmental procedure, and is historic in both breadth and depth.

In breadth, the majority, led by Justice Poulsen, situated the Directive within a wider legal landscape. It referred to the ICJ’s view that customary international law requires States to exercise due diligence to prevent significant climate harm and to consider cumulative effects of activities under their jurisdiction or control (paras 177). The Court also drew on the ECtHR’s [Greenpeace Nordic v Norway](https://www.climatecasechart.com/document/greenpeace-nordic-and-others-v-norway_0687), under which authorities must consider whether petroleum developments are compatible with national and international obligations to protect against climate harm (paras 184–191).

In depth, the decision is anchored in consequential reasoning. Once extracted, oil and gas will almost inevitably be burned, generating emissions unless carbon capture intervenes (paras 149–150). This reasoning can be called the logical inseparability of extraction and combustion, and it reflects IPCC science, whose findings Norway had already recognised, alongside its domestic and international climate commitments (paras 99–107, 151).

According to the Court, the EIA Directive’s requirement that gross combustion emissions be not only described, but also assessed in an EIA before approval of a PDO is consistent with the wording of Norway’s Petroleum Act and the Petroleum Regulations, and could be gleaned already from the first climate case against the Norwegian state, [Peoples v Arctic Oil](https://www.climatecasechart.com/document/greenpeace-nordic-assn-v-ministry-of-petroleum-and-energy-people-v-arctic-oil_508f), which was decided in 2020, whereby “global climate effects” are to be subject to an EIA in connection with an application for PDO approval ([HR-2020-2472-P](https://lovdata.no/dokument/HRSIV/avgjorelse/hr-2020-2472-p), paras 212, 214, 216, 218 and 241 as cited in para 155).

Further, the court held that neither the EIA Directive nor international and regional law impose a more extensive obligation to carry out an EIA in proceedings concerning PDO approval that also considers the global climate budget or consequential effects. On the global carbon budget, the court referred to the Paris Agreement Article 4 (as referenced in para 189) and Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) on the obligation to carry out “adequate, timely and comprehensive” EIAs ([People v Arctic Oil](https://cdn.climatepolicyradar.org/navigator/NOR/2016/greenpeace-nordic-assn-v-ministry-of-petroleum-and-energy-people-v-arctic-oil_c4546edcd30d144ba35805a6ce08fe26.pdf), para 318, as quoted in para 184). Similarly, when describing the project’s “direct effects and any indirect, secondary and cumulative effects”, the EIA Directive does not impose the carbon budget approach as account *should,* rather than *shall,* be taken of “the environmental protection objectives established at Union or Member State level which are relevant to the project”(point 5, para 2, of Annex IV to the EIA Directive, as referenced in paras 181 and 182). In contrast, the Court of Appeal had held that assessments were to be carried out in light of the remaining global carbon budgets, that is, the maximum amount of CO ₂ that can be released into the atmosphere before the temperature rises to a given level (para 179).

On consequential effects, the Norwegian Supreme Court stated that there is no doubt that an EIA must cover the project’s effects on all the factors listed in Article 3(1) of the EIA Directive, namely human beings, human health, biodiversity, land, soil, water, air, climate, material assets, cultural heritage and landscape, as well as the interactions between these factors (para 194). The Court clarified, however, that the question at issue was a different one: whether the assessment must also encompass the *consequential* effects that the project’s impacts on one or more of these factors may have on other factors, and answered in the negative (paras 196ff).

## The Norwegian Continental Shelf, and Its Dissent

The disagreement between the majority and minority judges concerned cumulative assessment. The majority holds that the EIA Directive requires an impact assessment to describe and assess the combustion emissions both of the project at hand and, cumulatively, of other existing and approved projects on the Norwegian shelf, together with their effect on global temperature rise (paras 178 and 214ff). The State argued that cumulation matters only to prevent “salami-slicing”, that is, splitting a project to dodge the assessment threshold. The majority rejected this: cumulation governs not only whether an assessment is triggered, but also what it must contain (paras 164–165). Two limits frame this duty: the continental shelf, because Norway can license petroleum nowhere else (para 167) and the petroleum sector, since adding every other sector would make the assessment disproportionately burdensome (para 168). The majority also stressed that the duty can be easily fulfilled by reference to reserve data for every field, which is public, and simple computations on gross emissions and their warming effect (para 176). Therefore, in light of Articles 3 and 8 of the EIA Directive and the relevant Norwegian implementing legislation, the authorities must carry out an independent assessment of the effects described in the EIA report. Furthermore, the authorities must assess whether conditions should be imposed with a view to limiting and mitigating significant adverse effects (paras 219 ff).

The dissent, penned by Justice Sivertsen, did not challenge the inclusion of downstream combustion emissions within the EIA Directive. Rather, it disputed the majority’s extension of the assessment to cumulative emissions from other existing and approved petroleum projects on the Norwegian continental shelf. For the dissenting justices, an assessment of each project’s gross combustion emissions and their climate effects was sufficient. Accordingly, they found no grounds for invalidating the Ministry’s 2024 decisions (paras 260–264).

The narrow 6–5 majority in the 2026 judgment invites comparison with the Norwegian Supreme Court’s first climate ruling in 2020, when the Court upheld the contested petroleum licences by 11 votes to four. While the outcome differed, there is a striking pattern of judicial continuity.

Seven judges participated in both decisions. Three of the four dissenting judges in 2020 – Webster, Falch and Østensen Berglund – joined the majority in 2026. Conversely, three members of the 2020 majority – Falkanger, Høgetveit Berg and Steinsvik – joined the 2026 dissent. Chief Justice Øie sided with the majority in both cases.

This alignment is particularly interesting because the 2020 dissent was already concerned with the adequacy of EIAs and the need for meaningful judicial scrutiny of procedural requirements. Justice Webster, writing for the minority, argued that judicial restraint in reviewing the substantive environmental choices of the political branches made effective scrutiny of the decision-making procedure all the more important (HR-2020-2472-P, para. 256).

Although the two judgments concern different stages of petroleum authorisation, different legal questions, and an evolving legal framework, the voting patterns suggest a degree of continuity in individual judicial approaches to environmental assessment, institutional deference and the consequences of procedural shortcomings. This observation resonates with [Jørn Øyrehagen Sunde](https://intrechtdok.de/pow-challenge?redirect_url=%2Fservlets%2FMCRFileNodeServlet%2Fmir_derivate_00009727%2FRechtskultur%25201.pdf%3Futm)’s historical account of the Norwegian Supreme Court. Øyrehagen Sunde connects the Court’s increasingly active role in judicial review with broader institutional developments and internationalisation. In particular, he describes the growing role of legal norms originating beyond Norway’s borders in plenary and Grand Chamber decisions. Viewed through a judicial politics perspective, the 2026 judgment therefore raises a question extending beyond the immediate dispute: How does the internationalisation of law reshape the balance between judicial restraint and effective scrutiny of executive decision-making?

Procedural review, in this sense, is neither procedural formalism nor [procedural fetishism](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4624702). What appears as a [procedural turn](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.5235/205088413808821363?needAccess=true) in climate adjudication may reflect a deeper institutional transformation. The internationalisation of legal norms, instead of allowing courts to “make” climate policy, has empowered their capacity – and [responsibility](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-lawsocsci-061824-074150) – to scrutinise the legal conditions under which such policy is implemented.

## Constitutional Rights and Effective Judicial Review

EIA obligations must be understood in light of Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution, as recognised in the first Norwegian climate case (HR-2020-2472-P, paras 182–183, as cited in para 221). As the majority writes, “[f]or judicial review to be effective, it is essential that reasons be given”, clearly demonstrating that combustion emissions and their effects on global temperature rise have been taken into account and assessed (para 222).

The royal decree passed by the Norwegian government in May 2026, which reassessed the petroleum approvals, offered a more detailed justification than its 2024 decisions, including an assessment of the emissions’ contribution to climate change. Yet, it still failed to consider the cumulative combustion emissions from existing and approved petroleum fields on the Norwegian continental shelf. Even more importantly, the cumulative climate impacts also should have been addressed in the *developers* ’ environmental impact reports and subjected to public consultation (paras 233–234).

The majority then explains why such an omission invalidates the decisions. Rules on impact assessment for interventions in nature are procedural rules to be enforced strictly, in light of Section 112 of the Constitution and the intensive review it calls for. Their purpose is not only to identify the political trade-offs for the authorities. It is also to give the population knowledge of what planned interventions will do and to secure real public participation in the decision (paras 236–238). The path to invalidity appears therefore short. A decision approving a project within the Directive’s scope that rests on an assessment omitting significant effects meets, by its very nature, the requirement that the error may have affected the outcome (paras 239–240). The democratic rationale for impact assessment is thus written into the remedy.

As the Court explained, the petroleum operators were not parties to the proceedings, and the declaration of invalidity was therefore not binding on them. Consequently, the approvals did not automatically cease to have effect vis-à-vis the licence holders. Rather, the judgment requires the Ministry to reconsider the approvals in accordance with the applicable environmental assessment requirements, potentially confirming, amending or withdrawing them following a legally compliant procedure.

## Democracy and the Separation of Powers Principle

Drawing on its 2020 *Peoples* v *Arctic Oil* judgment, the Supreme Court reaffirmed that Section 112 of the Norwegian Constitution guarantees environmental rights and access to environmental information. While democratic considerations require judicial restraint in reviewing the political choices underlying environmental decisions, procedural compliance calls for closer scrutiny: the greater a project’s potential consequences, the more rigorous both the environmental assessment and judicial review must be, and the *North Sea Fields* case concerned procedural errors, rather than the substantive limits of governmental authority (paras 108–111). Writing in the wake of *People v Arctic Oil*, [Minnerop and Røstgaard](https://ir.lawnet.fordham.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2819&context=ilj) had already argued that constitutional environmental rights would let courts scrutinise the cumulative effects of global emissions. The Grand Chamber has taken that insight from the field to the shelf.

## Who Carries the Risk

The financial stakes are substantial: approximately NOK 21 billion invested in Breidablikk, NOK 7 billion in Tyrving and NOK 177 billion estimated for Yggdrasil (paras 6, 9, 13). Yet the judgment does not decide who would bear the losses if an approval were ultimately revoked. The legal risk was not wholly unforeseeable. US and Australian courts had already addressed combustion emissions ( *WildEarth Guardians* v *Zinke* and *Gloucester Resources* v *Minister for Planning*, both 2019), and Norway’s Supreme Court had indicated in 2020 that global climate effects would be assessed at the PDO stage (paras 4, 7, 10, 155). The Court itself kept the present case alive because it concerned ‘an area under legal development’ of great importance to operators (para 97). Sophisticated licensees could price that risk and arguably should have.

## Concluding Remarks

The three Norwegian fields alone are projected to generate close to 400 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent from combustion over their lifetimes (paras 4, 7, 11). This is nine times Norway’s emissions in 2025.

It is worth noting that [the global carbon budget will be depleted in less than four years](https://globalcarbonbudget.org/fossil-co2-emissions-decrease-in-2026/), at current emissions levels, and [overshooting 1.5°C is now inevitable](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/limiting-overshoot-navigating-exceedance-15degc-and-pathways-towards-return). Yet, [it remains possible to achieve a ‘lowest possible’ pathway and limit global warming to 1.7–1.8°C before returning to 1.5°C](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/emissions-gap-report-2026). This allows for a slightly greater budget that future negative emissions may be able to compensate for. EIA can then be considered in relation to scenarios – or their carbon budgets – of the highest possible ambition, the closest to the Paris Agreement objectives.

Just as the ICJ reframed States’ responsibility for climate change in what has been called [the Great Reset](https://www.ejiltalk.org/the-great-reset-the-icj-reframes-the-conduct-responsible-for-climate-change-through-the-prism-of-internationally-wrongful-acts/), the Norwegian Supreme Court’s judgment may mark a reset of its own. The Norwegian reset shows how constitutional procedural rights – as well as interpretation informed by science, regional law and international law – can discipline a (petro-)state’s decisions by amplifying, rather than displacing, democratic choices. Whether more demanding procedure will ultimately change those choices remains open.

articleBody:
### 💬 Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as Nvidia CEO

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/17/jensen-huang-says-he-would-be-honored-if-allowed-to-return-as-nvidia-ceo/)

- Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's founder and CEO, said in his first public statement since leaving that he would be honored to return to the top job if the board decides it serves the company's interest.
- Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1 and said he is committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation, while Nvidia formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
- An open letter calling for his return drew over 10,000 current and former Nvidia staff plus figures like Elon Musk, but a board source told the Washington Post yesterday there were no plans to reinstate him.

### 🦹 Popular websites subverted in bid to steal crypto

[↗ Primärquelle: firstpost.com](https://www.firstpost.com/tech/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-14060570.html)

- Attackers planted malicious JavaScript on the websites of 178 organizations, including Zoom, HSBC, Equifax, CNN, Salesforce and IKEA, trying to steal cryptocurrency and infect iPhones, security researcher Scott Helme said yesterday.
- The scripts reached visitors through Optimizely, a website optimization platform, and tried to swap crypto payment addresses with the attacker's wallet, skim credit card numbers, grab cookies and screenshots, and drop exploit code onto iOS devices.
- Salesforce said it was investigating unauthorized Optimizely script changes and disabled them as a precaution, while Equifax looked into the problem, stopped using Optimizely, and reported no evidence that its systems were compromised.

### 📱 Meta launches Direct, a standalone messaging app

[↗ Primärquelle: engadget.com](https://www.engadget.com/2318452/meta-is-testing-direct-a-standalone-messaging-app-for-instagram/)

- Meta has begun testing Direct, a standalone Instagram messaging app that pulls the photo-sharing service's inbox into its own app and, notably, lets people use it without an Instagram account.
- Direct mirrors Instagram's inbox layout and carries over existing chats, Notes, and custom thread backgrounds, but people who sign up with just an email or phone number must add contacts manually through a username or QR code.
- Available only in Thailand and Turkey for now, Direct blocks chats with unconnected accounts, lets parents monitor teens through Meta's controls, and claims technology to spot inappropriate interactions with young users.

### 🛡️ Nvidia forms export-control board after Huang exit

[↗ Primärquelle: theregister.com](https://www.theregister.com/systems/2026/11/17/nvidia-places-chip-exports-under-boardroom-supervision-after-huangs-exit/5310429)

- Nvidia's board has set up a national security and export control committee following the resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang and claims that Singapore customer Megaspeed sent GPUs to China.
- Chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, the panel will meet at least quarterly to watch Nvidia's export compliance and trade risks, with existing compliance teams reporting to it and interim CEO Colette Kress.
- Huang quit last week after admitting an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities reportedly suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, while Commerce and Justice confirmed they had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024.

### 🔐 macOS warns against giving AI apps full Mac control

[↗ Primärquelle: macrumors.com](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/11/16/macos-27-3-full-desk-access/)

- Apple's macOS 27.3 beta gives Mac users tighter control over what apps can touch, with new safeguards aimed at AI agent apps that could expose files, mail, messages, and browsing history.
- Apple is splitting the old Device Control and Data Access setting into System & App Protection Override and Accessibility, and will push users to grant access only to the specific apps or folders a task actually needs.
- Users can set apps to ask each time instead of handing over blanket access, and a menu bar indicator will appear whenever a requesting app is controlling another app through System & App Protection Override.

### 🛡️ OpenAI gives 24-hour bans for child abuse prompts

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/openai-releases-a-new-image-classifier-and-chatgpt-warnings-to-combat-csam/)

- OpenAI rolled out new tools today to fight child sexual abuse material, including warning screens in ChatGPT that suspend accounts for 24 hours when users try prompts aimed at sexualizing children.
- A new image classifier, built with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, detects abuse images including AI-generated ones, and in testing flagged 48% fewer images while catching the same number of abusive ones.
- Repeated offenses could get accounts removed for good, and OpenAI is sharing the classifier free through its API with select companies while publishing child-safety guidelines for developers and giving law enforcement investigative tools.

articleBody:
[Thomas Nagel](https://as.nyu.edu/faculty/thomas-nagel.html) is the 2026 winner of the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture.

The Berggruen Institute called Nagel, professor emeritus of philosophy and law at New York University, “one of the most significant philosophers of our time,” and praising his “long-lasting contributions through his scholarly work and commentary in the public sphere,” referencing his work in moral philosophy, legal and political theory, metaphysics, and philosophy of mind, and his contributions to our understanding of consciousness, existence, altruism, equality, justice, and free will.

In a [press release](https://berggruen.org/news/usd1-million-berggruen-philosophy-prize-awarded-to-thomas-nagel), Nicolas Berggruen, the chairman and founder of the Berggruen Institute, says, “The Institute is pleased to recognize Thomas Nagel for his interrogation of the human experience and for expanding consciousness and our capacity to understand ourselves.”

The Berggruen Prize, according to the Institute, “seeks to place philosophical thought of the highest caliber on center stage of the public discourse and to amplify its significance to society.” It was created in 2016 and is awarded annually.

([Previous posts about the Berggruen Prize.](https://dailynous.com/?s=berggruen+prize))

articleBody:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

## Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\ \left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ {\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\ \left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \ \left(t\right) = \ \left(t\right) \times \ {|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \ \left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\ \left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\ \left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\ \left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\ \left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\ a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\ $$

Where:

$$
\ {lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\ (0) \times \ (1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\ (1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\ $$

This captures a few things:

- The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.
- The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.
- The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\ $. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \ {\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \ {\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, because these represent situations where the tangents have been flipped by 180º.

In most cases, there will only be one valid solution, and this works pretty well:

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

## Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0 < 0$ or $l_1 < 0$, it's about to vanish, so its weight should go to zero there.

2) When two opposite-bending parabolas are about to become tangent, two solutions will move towards each other, before both vanishing at the same time:

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\ = \ 2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\ \\[0.3em]
\ = \ b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\ $$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \ \cdot \ }{\displaystyle |\ ||\ |}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\ |$ i.e. $\ $, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \left(\ {\displaystyle |\ |^2}\right)^2
$$

- By applying $\arccos \left(-\cos \theta\right)$, we remap the dot-product range $(-1..1)$ to $(0..π)$ which effectively neutralizes the unstable solutions
- Large $|\ |$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option
- When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
\left(\ \right) = \ {|\ - \ |^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

## Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

*The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/unconed/bezbox/-/blob/master/src/graph/bez.ts?ref_type=heads#L61).*

title: Helen Garner Will Receive Our 2027 Hadada Award
subtitle: In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Mel…

articleBody:
Photograph by Darren James.

In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Melbourne, the first of several share homes they would live in during that decade. The house was noisy and chaotic but offered Garner a creative freedom that she hadn’t found in her first marriage. While her daughter played with the other children, Garner read Proust and Tolstoy, wrote in her diary, and began a passionate love affair with a man who was addicted to heroin. As the relationship went on, she began to see her experiences as a narrative. “Story is a chunk of life with a bend in it, and I could feel this one coming,” Garner tells Thessaly La Force in **[The Art of Fiction No. 255](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/7929/the-art-of-fiction-no-255-helen-garner)**, published in issue no. 241. “I suddenly thought, Maybe I could write about this while it’s still happening, as it’s coming into its bend.”

The resulting novel, Garner’s debut, *Monkey Grip* (1977), created a rupture in the landscape of Australian literature, winning Garner first prize in the National Book Council Awards while also provoking consternation among critics for its depictions of unconventional domestic life, sex, and female desire. Some accused Garner of merely publishing her journal—which is, in fact, more or less what she had done. In an essay published in 2002, she asked why this should be a bad thing. “As if there were no work involved in keeping a diary in the first place,” she wrote. “It’s as if a diary wrote itself, as if it poured out in a sludgy, involuntary, self-indulgent stream.” (Her extraordinary diaries have been published in three volumes spanning from 1978 to 1998.)

Garner was born in 1942 in the coastal city of Geelong, Victoria, the eldest of six. “In a big family you’ve got to find a way of getting away from everybody to a place where you can quietly exist, and that’s what reading was for me,” she tells La Force. “It was my way of being absent. I used to kneel by the side of my bed so I could keep reading even while I was pulling my clothes on.” The family unit—particularly under strain or in free fall—has frequently been a subject of her novels, including *The Children’s Bach* (1984), in which the circumscribed lives of a couple are upturned by a visit from an old friend’s bohemian family, and *The Spare Room* (2008), in which the narrator hosts an old friend who is undergoing alternative treatment for cancer, and which deals with the frustrations of care with brutal honesty.

Family has been central, too, in Garner’s nonfiction, most notably in two books about her experience of following murder trials: *Joe Cinque’s Consolation* (2004), about a young woman who killed her boyfriend, and *This House of Grief* (2014), about a father who drove himself and his three children into a dam, killing the children. “The thing is, despite being told that my concerns were too domestic, I’ve always known that the family is where everything is played out,” Garner tells La Force.

Over the past five decades, in her fiction, journalism, and essays, Garner has continually brought the fullness of her self to bear on the page: her scrupulous honesty, emotional intelligence, clarity, and imagination. She has been awarded the Windham-Campbell Prize, the Melbourne Prize for Literature, and the Walkley Award, and has been inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women. We are delighted to add to this list the Hadada, our award for lifetime achievement, which has previously been awarded to writers including John Ashbery, Anne Carson, Deborah Eisenberg, Jamaica Kincaid, N. Scott Momaday, Edward P. Jones, and James Salter. We are tremendously excited to present Garner with the Hadada on **[April 6](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** at the Spring Revel, our annual gathering of writers, artists, and friends to celebrate and raise funds for the *Review*, which is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Tickets are now available, and all proceeds from the event will help us continue to seek out the best new work and share it with readers in print and online. We hope you’ll **[join](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** us.

articleBody:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.

When the “[Monument Against Fascism](https://jochengerz.eu/works/monument-against-fascism?ref=hyperallergic.com)” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque.

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.
