articleBody:
Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a **neolab**— at least according to a presentation at [AI Engineer Code Summit](https://ai.engineer/code/2026/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) by**Michelle Chen**, who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side.

We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two [System One models](https://latent.space/p/jev/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), to be precise: **Clef and Clairic.**As Chen explained in her talk,**Clef is a decision model**directly inspired by [TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model](https://latent.space/p/jev-revolution/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), while**Clairic**is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls**an “extract” model**.

In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t *just* be producing system one models. **There will be large language models, too.**

“We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.”

Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but **potentially reasoning models** that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.”

However, she added that these probably **won’t be pre-trained models** built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce.

“I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.”

She noted that **“most of our team really just does post-training,”** so that will be the focus in model development.

## What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one?

The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November [by](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/investors-chase-neolabs-outflank-openai-anthropic?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)[Stephanie Palazzolo](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/investors-chase-neolabs-outflank-openai-anthropic?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.”

**Deedy Das**, a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs [a big list of neolabs](https://debarghyadas.com/neolabs/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv). It includes companies like**Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI** itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), *don't* have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money.

*Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20.*

Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s **a public company with significant revenue traction**. In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare [announced record earnings](https://www.cloudflare.com/press/press-releases/2026/cloudflare-announces-third-quarter-2026-financial-results/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv). “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO**Matthew Prince**. “We crossed**$3 billion in annualized revenue** with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.”

So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, **building models is part of a natural progression for the company**: from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to [serving open weight models](https://blog.cloudflare.com/workers-ai-large-models/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models.

## Jev as the “east wind”

Chen readily admits that **Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot** to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models.

“And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? **We don't have to send every request to an LLM.** We can send some of it to a System One model.”

In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build **Clef — which is a copy of Jev** — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model.

“All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and **inventing something new here**, that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.”

**Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company**— speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow**more work to be done by smaller, faster models**, where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds.

## Clairic and what extraction models do

While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with **an original twist on System One with Clairic**, [launched last month](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clairic-extraction-model/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.”

“What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation.

In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer.

One of the problems they settled on was that **LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input.** Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON.

“So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.”

*Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare.*

She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number.

“When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, **the number's right there, you just have to read it!** ”

So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass.

## Why Cloudflare is in the lab now

Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models.

**“Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,”** Chen said in her presentation.

In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations.

**“I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space**, because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.”

If you look at [Cloudflare’s product page](https://www.cloudflare.com/products/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there!

But there’s still room for several more models.

articleBody:
nbin4

A norns mod that routes four MIDI channels to n.b. voices and saves complete configurations for reuse across scripts.

I made nbin4 because I wanted to play several n.b. voices from a single MIDI input while keeping my current norns script running. The existing nbin mod was close to what I needed, but I wanted to assign separate MIDI channels to multiple n.b. voices at once.

nbin4 lets you select one MIDI input and configure four channel-to-voice routes. Each part can use a different n.b. voice, and multiple parts can also use the same one. In that case, they play the same player instance and share its internal parameters.

It handles note on/off and velocity, pitch bend, channel pressure and polyphonic key pressure. It also keeps the loaded script’s MIDI handler active on the selected input. I’ve tested it on my norns setup, where it’s working.

nbin4 now also supports complete, reusable profiles. A profile saves the MIDI input and routing, all four channel and voice assignments, bend and pressure settings, and the internal sound parameters of each selected n.b. voice. Profiles can be named, loaded and deleted from the NBIN 4 parameters menu, and are available across scripts on the same norns. When multiple channels use the same voice, its shared parameters are saved once.

Requirements

monome norns with the mod system

n.b., available through nbout or as a standalone library

The n.b. voice mods you want to use, installed and enabled

A MIDI controller or sequencer connected to a configured norns MIDI input

Documentation

The README includes installation steps, routing details, parameter descriptions, MIDI behavior and instructions for saving and loading complete profiles across scripts (and a test checklist): nbin4 README.

LLM disclosure

I used ChatGPT / OpenAI Codex to help generate and revise parts of the Lua code and documentation. I defined the feature set, guided the implementation and tested the mod on norns.

Download

Current version with complete profile support: https://github.com/giovannilami/nbin4/archive/refs/heads/main.zip

articleBody:
Midterm results showed that men under 30 (a supposed MAGA bulwark) shifted back to voting mostly for Democrats. Louise Perry and I spoke about whether that signals the end of the New Right.

Among other things, we discuss whether perceptions of corruption played a role. Voters will overlook a president lining his pockets, so long as they themselves feel prosperous. But the economy feels shaky for many people. Moreover, we discuss whether the online right on X made the same mistake the online left made back when it was still called Twitter: confusing applause from fellow partisans with the preferences of normal people.

Louise and I also speak about whether it’s true that “the left can’t meme.” We converge on an answer that involves censorship, 4chan, sex differences in humor, esoteric messaging, and why so much political imagery now looks like it was made for toddlers. We also get into what I heard Dave Chappelle recently say at Madison Square Garden about Charlie Kirk.

Finally, I asked Louise a question every man has wondered about women’s group chats. Her answer was not what I expected.

[↗ robkhenderson.com](https://www.robkhenderson.com/p/did-the-new-right-meme-itself-out)

building on the moon with materials already there

articleBody:
## building on the moon with materials already there

Researchers at the University of Arkansas have developed a way to [3D print](https://www.designboom.com/tag/3d-printing/) interlocking building blocks from simulated [moon](https://www.designboom.com/tag/human-fascination-with-the-moon/) dust, using heat to fuse the [material](https://www.designboom.com/tag/material-exploration/) together without glue or cement. Led by mechanical engineering professor Wan Shou and researcher Cole McCallum, the experiment explores how future lunar settlements could be built using materials gathered directly from the Moon’s surface.

The idea could reduce the amount of construction material that needs to make the journey from Earth. Instead of transporting cement and other building supplies into space, astronauts could eventually manufacture structural components using the mineral powder already covering the lunar landscape.

The team has produced a series of small, LEGO-like modules that can be assembled into larger structures and rearranged as needed. Each block is made entirely from a material that mimics lunar regolith, the loose layer of crushed rock and mineral dust covering the Moon.

a 3D printer was used to create bricks of pure lunar dust | image © Cole McCallum, University of Arkansas

## lunar dust is sharper than the dust we know on earth

Lunar regolith might resemble ordinary sand or soil, but its physical properties are quite different. Over billions of years, meteorites and other space debris have struck the Moon’s surface, breaking down rock into increasingly fine particles. Without wind or flowing water to gradually wear away their edges, these fragments remain sharp and angular, with an abrasive texture that NASA has compared to tiny pieces of glass.

The dust also behaves differently under lunar conditions. Its particles can become electrically charged and cling to nearby surfaces, making them particularly troublesome for astronauts and sensitive equipment.

During the Apollo missions, lunar dust damaged spacesuit materials and clogged mechanical components. Engineers planning future missions are still working out how to keep the powder from entering machinery, where its jagged edges can wear down moving parts.

manufactured modular bricks made with lunar simulant | image © Cole McCallum, University of Arkansas

## researchers recreate lunar regolith in laboratories on earth

For their experiments, the [Arkansas researchers](https://news.uark.edu/articles/83229/researchers-turn-moon-dust-into-lego-like-blocks-for-settlements) used Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant, known as LHS-1, a specialized powder developed by the University of Central Florida’s [Exolith Lab](https://news.uark.edu/articles/83229/researchers-turn-moon-dust-into-lego-like-blocks-for-settlements) and supplied by **[Space Resource Technologies](https://spaceresourcetech.com/products/lhs-1-lunar-highlands-simulant)**.

The material is made from terrestrial minerals selected to reproduce the composition and granular texture of lunar highland soil, drawing on samples collected during the Apollo missions.

Creating convincing artificial moon dust has become a field of research in its own right. Specialized laboratories and companies manufacture different regolith simulants to help engineers test lunar excavation systems and study the effects of abrasive particles on spacecraft hardware. These mixtures reproduce selected properties of lunar soil, although the real material has characteristics that remain difficult to replicate on Earth.

Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1) | image via Space Resource Technologies

## a laser fuses the powder together, layer by layer

To manufacture the blocks, the team turned to a 3D printing method called laser powder bed fusion. A thin layer of simulated regolith is spread across a platform, where a focused laser traces the intended shape and heats the mineral particles until they fuse together.

The platform then lowers, another layer of powder is added, and the process repeats until a solid component takes shape. The approach allows the researchers to work with the regolith alone, avoiding the polymer binders or cement mixtures used in some earlier experiments with lunar construction materials.

Instead, thermal energy bonds the grains directly to one another through a process known as sintering. ‘ *There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,* ‘ **explains McCallum,** who was an undergraduate at the university when he began the research. For future construction on the Moon, this could eliminate the need to transport large quantities of adhesives from Earth.

lunar regolith visualization | image via Space Resource Technologies

## LEGO-like bricks take on cross-shaped and H-shaped forms

The researchers also considered how individual printed components might come together to form larger structures. Drawing on the principles of traditional mortise-and-tenon joinery, they developed two complementary brick geometries: one shaped like a cross and the other resembling the letter H.

The cross-shaped piece acts as a projecting connector, fitting into the recessed profile of the H-shaped module. Together, the pieces can interlock without additional fastening materials. While the researchers describe the system as LEGO-like, the comparison refers to its modular assembly instead of the familiar rectangular bricks with circular studs.

The team has demonstrated small wall configurations and shielding units assembled from its cross-shaped and H-shaped pieces. Printing individual components could also offer more flexibility than manufacturing an entire enclosure with a large-scale 3D printer. Blocks could be produced in batches and replaced individually, allowing structures to be rearranged as the needs of a lunar settlement change.

a lunar regolith simulant is designed to match data collected from the Moon | image via Space Resource Tech

## could sunlight replace the laser?

The researchers are also investigating the possibility of using concentrated sunlight to harden lunar regolith. In their published study, they consider how optical devices such as Fresnel lenses or parabolic mirrors could focus solar radiation onto the powder, producing temperatures high enough to fuse the mineral particles together.

Earlier solar-sintering experiments have already demonstrated the potential of concentrated light to harden simulated lunar soil, although the Arkansas team’s own prototypes were manufactured using a laser. The idea could eventually allow construction equipment to draw on two resources already present on the Moon: regolith and sunlight.

The current bricks remain experimental, with porous surfaces and connections that require further refinement. Their strength also needs improvement before they can support substantial structural loads. ‘ *These structures we’re making can be self-supported,* ‘ **says McCallum,** while acknowledging that the technique still needs development for load-bearing construction.

melting a triangular pattern in regolith using a laser | image via [ESA](https://www.esa.int/articles/how-to-make-roads-on-the-moon)

## ESA experiments with laser-melted lunar roads

The idea has already been explored in another lunar construction experiment. In 2023, the European Space Agency (ESA) tested a method for creating roads and landing pads from simulated moon dust, using a powerful laser to melt the powder into a solid, glasslike surface.

The project, called PAVER, aimed to prevent passing rovers and landing spacecraft from kicking up abrasive lunar dust that could clog machinery and damage equipment. Researchers even produced interlocking, triangular paving elements, and proposed using sunlight concentrated through a large Fresnel lens to replace the laser on the Moon.

a single laser-melted layer is about 1.8 centimeters deep | image via ESA

## toward a future of locally built lunar settlements

Further experiments under lunar vacuum and gravity conditions will be essential before the team can begin translating its laboratory experiments into a practical construction system. For now, the printed blocks are only a few centimeters across, and the researchers are continuing to investigate how their mechanical properties can be improved.

Still, the research offers an early glimpse of how future lunar settlements might manufacture their own building materials. With mineral powder gathered from the surrounding landscape and heat supplied by lasers or potentially sunlight, the basic components of a building could eventually be produced directly on the Moon, one layer of regolith at a time.

paved surfaces around a Moon base visualization | image via ESA

**collaborating institutions:** University of Houston; Tampere University

subtitle: Die EU-Kommission hat den Digital Omnibus vorgeschlagen, ohne zuvor eine umfassende Folgenabschätzung durchzuführen.
feedText:
Eine Studie des Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts untersucht die möglichen Folgen. Nach Einschätzung der Autoren schwächt der Vorschlag die Datenschutzrechte von Beschäftigten in der EU. articleBody:
Die EU-Kommission hat den Digital Omnibus vorgeschlagen, ohne zuvor eine umfassende Folgenabschätzung durchzuführen. Eine Studie des Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts untersucht die möglichen Folgen. Nach Einschätzung der Autoren schwächt der Vorschlag die Datenschutzrechte von Beschäftigten in der EU.

Uber-Fahrer nutzten DSGVO-Datenzugriffsanfragen, um ihre Arbeitnehmerrechte zu verteidigen. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: NurPhoto via Imago

Verlust der Kontrolle über persönliche Daten, übermäßige Überwachung, ungerechte automatisierte Entscheidungen, verborgene Kennzahlen und undurchsichtiges algorithmisches Management: All dies sind Formen von Datenmissbrauch am Arbeitsplatz, die künftig erheblich schwerer nachzuweisen sein könnten. Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt eine Studie des [Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts](https://www.etui.org/publications/conditions-legal-protection), die den vorgeschlagenen Digital Omnibus untersucht.

Der [Digital Omnibus](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-a-new-plan-for-europe-s-sustainable-prosperity-and-competitiveness/file-digital-package) wird derzeit im Europäischen Parlament diskutiert. Das von der Europäischen Kommission vorgeschlagene Gesetzespaket betrifft unter anderem die [Datenschutz-Grundverordnung](https://gdpr-info.eu/) (DSGVO), das zentrale EU-Gesetz zum Schutz personenbezogener Daten. Der Vorschlag könnte beispielsweise Auskunftsanfragen nach der DSGVO einschränken, wenn sie Zwecken dienen, die über den Datenschutz hinausgehen, etwa um Beweise für einen arbeitsrechtlichen Streit zu sammeln.

Die Kommission präsentiert den neuen Rechtsrahmen als Maßnahme zur Vereinfachung und Steigerung der Wettbewerbsfähigkeit. Nach ihren Schätzungen könnte das Paket bis 2029 Verwaltungskosten von bis zu 5 Milliarden Euro einsparen. Mehr als 100 zivilgesellschaftliche Organisationen bezeichneten den Vorschlag hingegen als [„Versuch, Europas stärkste Schutzmaßnahmen gegen digitale Bedrohungen heimlich abzubauen“](https://noyb.eu/sites/default/files/2025-11/The%20EU%20must%20uphold%20hard-won%20protections%20for%20digital%20human%20rights.pdf).

Was könnten diese Änderungen für Beschäftigte bedeuten, die sich dagegen wehren wollen, wie ihre Daten verwendet werden? Da die EU-Kommission für den Digital Omnibus keine Folgenabschätzung durchgeführt hat, erstellten die Autoren Aida Ponce Del Castillo und Thomas le Bonniec im Auftrag des Europäischen Gewerkschaftsinstituts diese Studie.

Um die möglichen Auswirkungen der Änderungen zu untersuchen, wandten die Autoren sie rückwirkend als hypothetisches Szenario auf vier Fälle aus der Arbeitswelt an. Diese hatten zuvor zu behördlichen Maßnahmen oder erfolgreichen Klagen gegen Datenmissbrauch am Arbeitsplatz geführt. [Darunter waren Fälle, an denen die Fahrdienstplattformen Uber und Ola beteiligt waren.](https://netzpolitik.org/2020/uber-fahrer-wollen-transparenz-ueber-daten-und-algorithmen/)

## Beweislast verschiebt sich zu Beschäftigten

In einem der Fälle verlangten sechs Uber-Fahrer Zugang zu personenbezogenen Daten und Informationen darüber, wie sich die Systeme der Plattform auf ihre Arbeit auswirkten. Dazu gehörten Informationen über die Vermittlung von Fahrten, die Preisgestaltung und Bewertungen. Sie wollten nachvollziehen, wie Ubers algorithmische Managementsysteme Entscheidungen über sie trafen oder beeinflussten. Ein ähnliches Verfahren wurde gegen Ola angestrengt, ein Fahrdienstunternehmen mit Sitz in Indien.

2023 gab das Berufungsgericht Amsterdam den Forderungen der Fahrer schließlich statt und verpflichtete Uber und Ola dazu, bestimmte personenbezogene Daten und aussagekräftige Informationen über bestimmte automatisierte Entscheidungssysteme offenzulegen.

Die Fahrer nutzten ihre bestehenden Auskunftsrechte nach der DSGVO, um für ihre Klage wichtige Informationen zu erhalten. Die Autoren der Studie argumentieren, dass vergleichbare Ergebnisse durch die Änderungen des Digital Omnibus künftig schwieriger zu erreichen sein könnten.

Unter anderem würden die Änderungen Arbeitgebern oder Plattformen mehr Möglichkeiten geben, Auskunftsersuchen von Beschäftigten zu ihren personenbezogenen Daten abzulehnen. Ein Arbeitgeber könnte beispielsweise argumentieren, dass ein Beschäftigter eine DSGVO-Auskunft nicht zur Ausübung seiner Datenschutzrechte nutzt, sondern für einen anderen Zweck, etwa um Beweise für einen arbeitsrechtlichen Streit zu sammeln.

Diese Unterscheidung ist wichtig, weil Arbeitgeber und Plattformen häufig genau die Daten, Algorithmen und Aufzeichnungen kontrollieren, die Beschäftigte benötigen, um nachzuvollziehen, was mit ihnen geschehen ist. Beschäftigte haben oft keinen eigenen Zugang zu den Beweisen, die sie benötigen, um ihre Ansprüche zu stützen.

Der Studie zufolge könnten die Änderungen daher einen größeren Teil der Beweislast auf die Beschäftigten verlagern. Sie müssten möglicherweise präzisere Auskunftsersuchen formulieren, Ablehnungen anfechten oder rechtliche Hilfe in Anspruch nehmen, um Informationen zu erhalten, über die ihr Arbeitgeber oder die Plattform bereits verfügt.

Zu den vorgeschlagenen Änderungen sagte Studienautorin Aida Ponce Del Castillo: „Ein Beschäftigter kann mit seinem Verdacht auf rechtswidrige Überwachung richtig liegen und trotzdem nicht in der Lage sein, dies zu beweisen. Wenn die EU es schwieriger macht, Informationen von einem Arbeitgeber zu erhalten, wird es für Menschen auch schwieriger, gegen das vorzugehen, was ihnen am Arbeitsplatz widerfährt.“

## Automatisierte Entscheidungen schwerer anzufechten

In einem zusammenhängenden Fall wehrten sich vier Uber-Fahrer gegen die Deaktivierung ihrer Konten, nachdem Uber-Systeme einen Verdacht auf betrügerische Aktivitäten gemeldet hatten. Die Fahrer argumentierten, dass es sich dabei um folgenreiche Entscheidungen gehandelt habe, die ausschließlich durch automatisierte Verarbeitung und ohne nennenswertes menschliches Eingreifen getroffen worden seien.

Bei dreien der vier Fahrer kam das Gericht zu dem Schluss, dass Uber kein nennenswertes menschliches Eingreifen nachgewiesen hatte. Die Fahrer waren nicht angehört worden. Zudem hatte Uber nicht nachgewiesen, dass die Personen, die die Entscheidungen überprüften, über ausreichende Informationen und Befugnisse verfügten, um das automatisierte Ergebnis zu ändern.

Die DSGVO bietet Schutz vor bestimmten Entscheidungen, die ausschließlich auf automatisierter Verarbeitung beruhen. Derzeit kann bei der Prüfung, ob eine automatisierte Verarbeitung tatsächlich notwendig war, relevant sein, ob eine ebenso wirksame menschliche Alternative zur Verfügung stand.

articleBody: Protein–protein interfaces encode molecular recognition through spatially organized contacts, yet their buried, curved surfaces are difficult to inspect as a whole. Flattening these surfaces can expose interface organization but introduces geometric distortion and may divide individual residues into disconnected regions. We present TopoPPI, a geometry-aware platform that converts interaction surfaces into low-distortion two-dimensional atlases while retaining links to source atoms, residues and contacts. TopoPPI extends OptCuts with a contact-weighted penalty for seam-induced fragmentation of residue footprints—the surface regions assigned to individual residues—jointly balancing continuity, seam length and distortion. In a leakage-controlled benchmark of 2,236 experimental complexes, the geometry-only OptCuts foundation achieved 88.39% lower family-weighted scale-fair distortion than the next-best tested parameterization across 2,209 complete comparable outputs. Across 2,204 exact-domain comparisons, TopoPPI reduced family-weighted residue-footprint fragmentation by 12.81% (95% confidence interval, 11.50–14.05%), with a 2.60% increase in normalized seam length and a 0.061% increase in scale-fair distortion. Continuity gains extended to 1,180 fixed-pose pairs of AlphaFold monomer models and 145 predicted complexes, with fragmentation reductions of 18.60% and 11.65%, respectively. Functionally annotated antibody and colicin–immunity interfaces demonstrated reconnection of the footprints of experimentally characterized binding and specificity residues. Further applications mapped published binding and folding free-energy estimates onto the KRAS–RAF1 interface and compared shared receptor residues across two growth-hormone recognition sites. Available through graphical and command-line interfaces, TopoPPI provides a residue-aware visualization framework for integrating structural contacts and functional annotations within geometrically controlled interface maps.

articleBody:
Today, *TIME Magazine* has published their list of [100 “must-read” books of 2026](https://time.com/collection/must-read-books/2026/), including *[Yesteryear](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780593804216)* by Caro Claire Burke, who is also featured on the magazine’s cover.

The last novelist to be featured on the cover of *TIME* was [Taylor Jenkins Reid](https://time.com/7284944/taylor-jenkins-reid-atmosphere-interview/), in 2025; before that there hadn’t been a novelist on the cover since [Akwaeke Emezi](https://time.com/collections/next-generation-leaders/6047430/akwaeke-emezi-next-generation-leaders/) was featured as part of the magazine’s “Next Generation Leaders” package in 2021 (Amanda Gorman was also [featured in a solo cover](https://lithub.com/amanda-gorman-is-on-the-cover-of-this-weeks-time/) that year). Novelists *used* to show up in this spot all the time, but they have rather fallen off in the magazine’s modern history. In 2010, Jonathan Franzen famously became the first living novelist to be featured on the cover of *TIME* in a decade, followed by [Colson Whitehead, in 2019](https://lithub.com/colson-whitehead-is-the-first-novelist-to-grace-the-cover-of-time-since-2010/). So at least things are picking up this decade.

See Caro Claire Burke’s cover below, and read the cover story [↗ time.com](https://time.com/article/2026/11/17/caro-claire-burke-interview/). (You can also read Lit Hub’s interview with Burke [↗ lithub.com](https://lithub.com/caro-claire-burke-on-tradwives-the-performance-of-selfhood-and-the-good-old-days/).)

Photograph by Tonje Thilesen for TIME @tonjethilesen

## Remembrance of proteins past (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/17/mississippi-gosh-darn/#wheres-the-beef)

Without a doubt, the best piece of media from the 2026 midterms was Scott Colom's "Pick another senator instead" ad from his triumphant Mississippi senate campaign against GOP incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith:

[https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&t=2219](https://youtu.be/zpUnm09lTUk?si=3ApbHida5_VpQCLB&t=2219)

Some background: Colom is the first Black Mississippi senator elected since Reconstruction gave way to Jim Crow. He's also the first Democratic Mississippi senator since 1982. Colom's campaign shifted the statewide vote leftward by 19 points, and he won a quarter of the state's white votes.

Colom ran a great campaign and promoted great policies, but also: he ran one of the great political ads of all time. That ad skewered Hyde-Smith's "let them eat whey powder" remark to WLOX Biloxi host Hugh Keeton, who asked her about the cost of living crisis and the high price of beef, to which she replied that people "have so many proteins to choose from":

[https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/](https://www.mississippifreepress.org/americans-who-cant-afford-beef-have-so-many-proteins-to-choose-from-says-us-sen-cindy-hyde-smith/)

Colom's ad plays a montage of Mississippians expressing disgust with Hyde-Smith's response, saying "I'd rather choose another senator instead." Colom was quick to credit content creator Ryan Sayles, who joined the campaign after doing some freelance work for them, as the ad's mastermind:

[https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/12/ryan-sayles-scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-01163508)

Much has been said about the ad's style, especially the viral "s-h-e-e-e-i-t" voiced by US Army vet Russ Hudson, who stepped in to do the ad when his father declined to curse on camera:

[https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/scott-colom-viral-protein-ad-mississippi-senate)

But the most important analysis on the ad is of its *substance*, specifically how it repudiates one of the key doctrines of neoliberal, austerity economics, as David Dayen writes for *The American Prospect*:

[https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/](https://prospect.org/2026/11/16/how-the-mississippi-senate-win-exposed-austerity-logic/)

Neoliberalism is the signature achievement of the "law and economics" movement that came out of the University of Chicago. The central conceit of law and econ is that economics is a "hard science" (not a social science) and that its domain is a deterministic, quantifiable physics of human behavior. Economists went so far as to create a fake "Nobel Prize" in economics in a bid to elevate their work out of the social sciences:

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics](https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics)

This "science" claims it can replace squishy, qualitative questions with mathematical models that can output the objectively correct answer to every thorny political question, thereby substituting an obscure form of mathematics for political deliberation:

[https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful](https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/03/all-models-are-wrong/#some-are-useful)

This is a remarkably cheap and transparent stunt. To produce this "mathematics of human behavior," you must first quantize all the qualitative questions so that they can be plugged into variables in econ equations. But here's the problem: *assigning a numeric value to a qualitative factor is a qualitative exercise!*

When an economist decides that the pain you'll experience as a result of their policy prescriptions is worth "7" while the benefit is worth "8," they are not doing objective work, they're just declaring their own judgments (and biases) to be empirical observations, while demoting *your* judgments to mere "feelings" (and biases):

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics](https://pluralistic.net/2024/09/18/falsifiability/#figleaves-not-rubrics)

Economism doesn't just eliminate qualitative questions from policymaking: it *incinerates* all of those qualitative factors so that economists can perform mathematics on whatever dubious quantitative residue remains in the crucible:

[https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/](https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-qualia/)

This is where Scott Colom's brilliant campaign ad comes in. As Dayen points out, when Hyde-Smith made her "many other proteins to choose from," gaffe, she was referencing a key piece of economic theory that has been thoroughly weaponized by the neoliberals: "substitution."

On its face, substitution is just the commonsense proposition that when prices for one good or service go up, some consumers will substitute another. When gas prices go up, more people ride the bus. When Instagram increases its ad-load, more people switch to Mastodon or Bluesky. When your ISP jacks up your price, you might switch to another carrier.

So far, so good. Indeed, one of the best things about digital products and services is how low digital "switching costs" (the cost you bear when switching from one service to another) can be. The lower the switching costs are, the easier it is to substitute one thing for another.

This means that, in a state of nature, tech bosses have to be careful about enshittifying their products, lest their users defect to a rival. This is why tech bosses have spent decades doing everything they can to jack up those "switching costs." They want to convert all their users into hostages:

[https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2021/08/facebooks-secret-war-switching-costs)

Substitution is real and it makes sense. The problem comes when neoliberal economists use this idea in *policy*. In the early 2010s, Barack Obama proposed applying substitution to the American welfare system through something called "Chained CPI."

"CPI" stands for the "Consumer Price Index": this is a measurement of the cost of a "basket of goods" (a bunch of supposedly representative household items) that is used to make inflationary adjustments to a variety of payments. When the CPI goes up, so do social security, welfare and disability payments. Otherwise, inflation would continually reduce the living standards of everyone who receives these entitlements.

"Chained CPI" takes the CPI and applies substitution to it. Rather than asking whether *hamburger* just got more expensive, the economists who calculate CPI ask whether the cheapest protein at the grocery store got more expensive (because hamburger can be swapped out for another protein).

Chained CPI's intent and effect is to reduce payments to retirees, disabled people, and poor people. Chained CPI is always going to be lower than CPI, because chained CPI only rises when the cheapest "substitute" for one of the items in CPI's "basket of goods" gets more expensive. In effect, the "basket of goods" becomes a *transdimensional* basket, one that contains every substitute good that might have gone into the basket in all possible parallel universes. Economists get to universe-shop for the dimension where that basket has the lowest cost, and then we all have to live in their chosen universe.

Obama tried to adopt it 2013 as part of a "grand bargain" to reduce the deficit, but was thwarted by the Tea Party Caucus, who refused the grand bargain on the grounds that it contained an infinitesimal tax rise for the richest Americans:

[https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/](https://abcnews.com/blogs/politics/2013/04/obamas-chained-cpi-throws-off-pols-and-heres-how-it-works/)

But chained CPI is one of the most cherished ideas of neoliberal thinktanks, so it came back in 2017 for Trump's tax giveaway to the super-rich, whose costs were partially offset by using chained CPI to calculate tax brackets, the standard deduction, and the Earned Income Tax Credit:

[https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan](https://newrepublic.com/article/145688/biggest-trojan-horse-republican-tax-plan)

As Dayen writes, "[This created] a regressive tax increase by eroding deductions and credits and pushing people into higher tax brackets. The wealthy were unaffected by this since they were already in the highest tax bracket and itemized rather than using the standard deduction."

Which brings me back to Cindy Hyde-Smith's foot-in-mouth remarks about "so many proteins." Whether or not Hyde-Smith knew it, she was referencing this substitution/chained CPI doctrine when she told people that beef inflation didn't matter because other proteins were available. In doing so, she was performing economism's cheapest trick: pretending that *her* opinions are objective facts, while other people's opinions are just *feelings*.

As Dayen writes, "[W]ho decides whether the cheaper product they switch to is 'similar' to the one that’s become so expensive that the consumer must give it up?…The logic is, approximately: You're not doing as badly as you think, so pick another protein and quit your whining."

People *do* substitute one thing for another as a matter of economic necessity. But the idea that a "substitute" is an "equivalent" can only be accepted if you first buy into the economist's conceit that all qualitative matters can be safely incinerated, leaving the expert to do math on the quantitative ash.

In this conceit, if you can't afford hamburgers and end up substituting chicken or fish, then you've found a new protein and have lost no "welfare." If you think otherwise, then you are expressing an irrational preference (unlike economists, whose preference for having a Nobel prize of their own is so empirically correct that it could be detected by a Martian peering at Earth through a telescope).

It's not only Cindy Hyde-Smith who unconsciously metabolized the idea of substitution as "rationality"; it's the voters, too, who recognized in Hyde-Smith's remarks the arrogance of policy elites who've spent decades discounting their views as "feelings" while declaring their own views to be experimental validated facts. Not only do voters recognize this move: they *hate* it.

They know that elites are perfectly capable of expressing strong views about qualitative matters and moving heaven and Earth to achieve a life that fits with their aesthetics. They know that the same Ivy League economists who dismiss their preferences as "irrational" will revel for *4,000 pages'* worth of Marcel Proust expounding on the spiritual, intangible reasons for choosing his favorite baked goods.

Economics is the study of why people do things, but somewhere along the way it became a club used to *force* people to do the things that powerful people prefer. The (alleged) "rationalism" of economism has worn out its welcome. You don't need an economics degree to understand why that "rationalism" is a cheap trick: after 50 years of neoliberalism, a Martian with a telescope could spot it.

title: Most Teens Care, So Why Don’t They Always Help?
subtitle: A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone.
feedText: Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why? articleBody:
A student notices a classmate eating lunch alone. Another sees a peer being excluded from a group chat. Someone knows a friend has been struggling but hesitates before reaching out. Why?

Most adults assume the challenge is getting young people to care. But after spending years studying adolescent compassion, I have come to believe that caring may not be the central problem.

Many adolescents care deeply.

The question is what happens next.

We often imagine compassion as a straightforward process: Notice suffering, feel concern, take action. Yet anyone who has worked with adolescents knows that the path is rarely so simple. Young people are navigating friendships, social hierarchies, identity development, and concerns about belonging, all while learning how to manage their own emotions. In these moments, compassion is not simply a feeling. It is a decision unfolding within a complex social world.

In our [recent research developing the Youth Compassion Measure](https://doi.org/10.1177/01650254261485170), an assessment of compassionate responding, we find that most adolescents recognize when a peer is struggling. What varies is whether that recognition translates into helping. Across hundreds of students, four factors consistently shape whether compassion becomes action: peer dynamics, social risk, emotional regulation, and intrinsic motivation.

Understanding these factors may help parents, educators, and youth-serving professionals better support compassionate action in young people.

## 1. Compassion has to survive peer dynamics

One of the clearest findings from our work is that adolescents were more likely to help when the person experiencing distress was someone they knew well.

At first glance, this may seem obvious. Most of us are more likely to check on a close friend than a stranger. Yet this finding points to a deeper truth about adolescence: Compassion unfolds within relationships.

During adolescence, friendships become central to daily life. Young people are figuring out who they are, where they belong, and how they fit into their social worlds. Relationships provide security, identity, and connection. Unsurprisingly, those same relationships shape compassionate responding.

This means that compassion is not simply an individual trait. It is also social.

When educators talk about creating compassionate schools, they often focus on [teaching empathy or kindness](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_educators_are_using_kindness_to_transform_schools). Those efforts matter. But our findings suggest that fostering strong, supportive relationships may be just as important. Young people appear more willing to take compassionate action when they feel connected to the people around them.

In other words, belonging may do more than improve well-being. It may help create the conditions that allow compassion to flourish.

## 2. Compassion involves social risk

If relationships explain who adolescents help, social risk helps explain why they sometimes do not.

Consider a common scenario. A student witnesses a peer being teased. They know the behavior is hurtful. They may even want to intervene. Yet stepping forward could carry consequences. They may worry about being judged, excluded, or embarrassed, or becoming a target themselves.

Our findings suggest that adolescents are often weighing these possibilities, consciously or unconsciously, before deciding how to respond.

This is one reason public conversations about bullying can be so frustrating. When videos circulate online, attention quickly turns to the bystanders. Why didn’t anyone help?

The question assumes that recognizing suffering naturally leads to action. But social reality is more complicated.

Young people are often assessing multiple things at once: the seriousness of the situation, who is involved, who is watching, what might happen if they intervene, and what might happen if they do not. What appears from the outside as indifference may actually be a moment of conflict between compassion and self-protection.

This perspective does not excuse harmful behavior or passivity. But it does encourage us to understand helping as a social act rather than a purely moral one.

If we want young people to act compassionately, we need environments where compassionate action is socially supported instead of socially costly.

## 3. Compassion requires emotional regulation

Perhaps the most surprising finding from our study is that recognizing suffering alone did not consistently predict helping.

Many students understood that someone was struggling. The difference was what happened after that recognition occurred.

One of the strongest predictors of compassionate action is distress tolerance, the ability to remain engaged in the presence of emotional discomfort. This matters because witnessing another person’s suffering is often uncomfortable. We may feel sadness, anxiety, uncertainty, helplessness, or fear of saying the wrong thing. Adolescents experience these emotions, too.

Imagine a teenager whose friend is crying. The challenge is not simply recognizing that the friend is upset; it’s navigating the delicate space between overidentifying with another person’s suffering and distancing oneself from it. Too much emotional absorption can lead to overwhelm and withdrawal. Too much distance can lead to disengagement. Compassion requires something different: remaining connected to another person’s experience while maintaining enough emotional balance to respond effectively.

People sometimes assume that compassion and empathy are the same thing. They are not. [Empathy](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/empathy/definition#what-is-empathy) allows us to resonate with another person’s experience. [Compassion](https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/topic/compassion/definition#what-is-compassion) involves channeling that awareness into a desire to alleviate suffering. Doing so requires emotional regulation. Without it, concern can become overwhelm, uncertainty, or avoidance. Instead of moving toward suffering, we move away from it.

Our findings suggest that compassionate action depends not only on recognizing another person’s distress, but also on the ability to stay present with that distress without becoming consumed by it. In this sense, emotional regulation is not separate from compassion; it helps make compassion possible.

For parents and educators, this finding has important practical implications. Teaching young people how to navigate difficult emotions may strengthen their capacity for compassionate action. Skills such as mindfulness, emotional awareness, reflection, and distress tolerance are not simply tools for managing stress. They may also be the very capacities that help adolescents transform caring into action by staying engaged when helping feels uncertain, vulnerable, or emotionally difficult.

## 4. Compassion needs motivation

Even when adolescents care and have the emotional skills to stay engaged, one additional factor matters: motivation.

In our study, intrinsic prosocial motivation was one of the strongest predictors of helping. Simply put, adolescents who genuinely wanted to help others were more likely to translate concern into action.

This may sound self-evident, but it carries important implications.

Adults often try to encourage helping through external incentives, praise, rewards, or behavioral expectations. While these approaches can influence behavior, our findings suggest that compassionate action is especially powerful when it emerges from internal values and genuine concern for others.

Young people are constantly asking themselves what kind of person they want to be. When helping becomes connected to identity, meaning, and purpose, compassionate action appears more likely to follow.

This suggests that fostering compassion is about more than encouraging kind behavior. It is also about helping young people develop a sense of responsibility toward others and a meaningful connection to shared humanity.

## What gets in the way of compassion?

Taken together, these findings challenge a common assumption.

There is a tendency to treat moments of inaction as moments of moral failure. We see a young person remain silent, fail to intervene, or walk past another person’s suffering, and we assume we understand what happened.

Yet our research suggests that these moments are often more complicated than they appear.

They unfold within social worlds shaped by belonging, friendship, identity, uncertainty, vulnerability, and the deeply human desire to remain connected to others. They are influenced by relationships, social risks, emotional capacities, and personal motivations.

What looks like indifference from a distance may sometimes reflect a struggle between compassion and the realities that make compassionate action difficult.

This perspective shifts the conversation from a question of character to a question of conditions.

Rather than asking whether adolescents are compassionate, we might ask: What conditions help compassion become action?

## Helping caring become action

The encouraging message from this research is that the factors influencing compassionate action are not fixed traits.

Relationships can be strengthened.

School climates can be improved.

Emotional regulation skills can be taught.

Prosocial values can be nurtured.

When we think about compassion this way, the goal becomes larger than helping young people recognize suffering. The goal is helping them develop the capacities that allow caring to become action.

Perhaps this is what adolescence reveals so clearly. The distance between caring and acting is rarely empty space. It is filled with questions about belonging, uncertainty, responsibility, and risk.

Young people are learning to navigate that space every day.

Our responsibility as the adults who support them is not simply to teach them to care. It is to create the relationships, communities, and opportunities that help them act on the care they already possess.

articleBody:
*The following article was written as a companion piece for Lewis Richmond’s upcoming* Tricycle *class, “A Buddhist Response to AI: Studying Samsara, Practicing Kindness.”* [Sign up today](https://tricycle.org/events/ai-buddhism-email-program/#signup) *.*

The Dalai Lama has often said that Buddhist practitioners should study samsara. Samsara means the everyday world of ignorance and delusion. His advice is foundational and practical; he is encouraging us to know the sea in which we swim. And because today’s technology is so inescapable and powerful, there is probably no greater magnifier of samsara today than technology, which now includes artificial intelligence. So, like it or not, we Buddhists need to deal with AI; at least we need to study it. As a lifelong Buddhist practitioner and teacher, as well as a former computer professional, I have my doubts as to whether AI is truly intelligent, but, regardless, its influence and power are sweeping the world, and, try as we might, none of us can avoid it. I am proposing that the practices and teachings of Buddhism can be a counterpoint to some of AI’s seductions and a protective shield from some of its dangers. But how, as Buddhists, can we accomplish that? What can we do?

Today, there is a near-war going on between two opposing camps: the realm of living things, and the realm of digital technology. The outcome of this conflict is likely to define every aspect of our long-term future—even whether we survive as a species at all. At least that’s what Nobel prize winner Dr. Geoffrey Hinton—known as the “father of AI”—has warned; other tech gurus have echoed his words. This is serious business. I have given names to these two camps: I call the world of technology “Byteworld,” and the world of living things “Lifeworld.” Byteworld and Lifeworld—these two are arm in arm, marching headlong into unknown territory. Of course Lifeworld (that is, ourselves) created all of Byteworld (as well as Buddhism), but Byteworld is breaking free of its human bonds and going its own way, like some golem-like clay doll magically come to life.

Computer technology arguably began with the invention of the mainframe computer in the 1950s, followed by the personal computer, the internet, smartphones, social media, and, finally, “artificial intelligence.” The biosphere, in contrast, has existed for untold millennia, evolving from single-celled organisms to dinosaurs, parrots, dolphins, elephants, the great apes, and us. Our human achievements are legion: fire, the wheel, great epics and dramas, symphonies and songs, towering cities and civilizations, sailing ships and rockets, myriad forms of civilization and social organization, religion and spiritual life, and, of course, Byteworld itself. Of these I think Lifeworld’s greatest accomplishment is religion and spiritual life—paths leading to inner transformation and an awakened state of compassionate awareness. Buddhism, which has been my life’s study, is such a path.

I know technology from the inside; beginning in 1994, for twenty-five years, I owned and managed a software company whose product was a business-to-business software application that I wrote myself. But before that I spent thousands of hours in meditation on my black cushion, as well as studying Buddhism with some of the best living teachers. So I’ve had a foot in both worlds. I know the thrill that comes from writing a block of computer code and watching it perform its magic in the real world. I also know how urgently our world needs the spiritual healing and compassionate perspective that paths such as Buddhism can provide.

Though I understand how Byteworld works, my refuge has always been the biological wisdom of Lifeworld. When I was younger, it was my hope that this coming age would be one of spiritual awakening, but, instead, I see all the attention, power, and money racing in the other direction: toward the godlike power of technology, a glittering secular deity whose silicon chips and farmland-destroying data centers are replicating like a metallic cancer. How can we rein in this explosive machine?

Technology and AI do have limits. I doubt that AI is on its way to being all-powerful, in spite of what some tech gurus say. These machines of our making emulate only some portion of what our brains can do—mostly their verbal and mathematical skills. There is so much more to the human psyche. Psychologist Howard Gardner has proposed a theory of eight forms of human intelligence. In addition to words and mathematics, he adds music (Mozart), spatial awareness (architects), physical ability (athletes and surgeons), naturalistic knowledge (gardeners), interpersonal intelligence (therapists, ministers, and mediators), and *intra* personal intelligence (the awareness of our inner states and processes). AI excels in words and numbers. But it lacks feeling and true emotion—the relational skills of which Gardner speaks—and an intimacy with the natural world of plants and animals. It’s worth mentioning that “intrapersonal intelligence” is also the domain of meditation, which involves paying attention to our inner physical and mental states. Intrapersonal intelligence, on which Buddhism is built, may be in time a hidden resource that could counterbalance the empires of Byteworld. If so, each of us as Buddhists may have a role to play.

AI offers power, wealth, and control to those few who create and deploy it, but its capacities are narrow compared to the biological wisdom that incorporates emotion, intuition, faith, and religion, the five physical senses, and our 64 trillion cells, each with its own DNA-powered intelligence that we share with the whole biosphere. AI is a kind of miracle, to be sure. There is no question that Byteworld has game, but Lifeworld has so much more. What AI entity could ever experience the grandeur of Beethoven’s musical heart? And, for that matter, what robot could pray?

I suspect that our fascination with the glories of AI will sour in time as its darker capabilities, including weaponization and environmental pollution, come to the fore. To summarize the core message of the Buddha’s path: Each of us is a living Buddha at heart, only waiting to emerge like a butterfly from a cocoon. We don’t need any additional machines or vast data centers in farmland or in space to achieve that. We already have what we need. We are the heirs of the whole biosphere’s intelligent rainforest. Awakening is a birthright for every one of us. Lifeworld offers us untold gifts, including the dharma. That said, the human realm is not an unalloyed good, and technology is not an unalloyed bad. Each domain is complex; each has its gifts as well as dangers.

## Gifts and Dangers of Lifeworld

*Living relationships.* Everything in the world of the living is intrinsically related, but not by bits and bytes. We share with every living thing the pulse of aliveness; we share their DNA, their evolution and adaptability. In a more profound sense we share a living connection with all of reality. Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh calls this connectivity “interbeing,” and it is described in detail in Buddhist scriptures such as the *Avatamsaka Sutra*. Human community and family, the kind we can touch and feel in the presence of others, is foundational; in some ways it is our deepest intelligence. In Buddhism we call that sangha.

*Slowness.* Speed is our new god these days, but the pace of living things is of a different order. Lifeworld is optimized for survival and evolution. Lifeworld is actually neither slow nor fast; it simply marks the pace of being alive. A human baby takes nine months to gestate. It can’t be speeded up. A majestic redwood tree takes a hundred years to grow, or a thousand. It will never be digitized. The vibrancy of all living things, the unfolding of a whole human life from beginning to end, the blossoming of love and of family, each require their appropriate season and timing. Speed will not improve them. Deepfake emulation will not replace them. Life evolves and replicates in slow time.

*Kindness.* The world of the living tends toward kindness; kindness is an artifact of interbeing. Human beings can be cruel, too, but kindness is our higher goal. Digital intelligence can emulate kindness; already chatbots have been trained to tell us how good we look and how great our ideas are. But true kindness occurs through aliveness. It arises from the interpersonal intelligence that Howard Gardner describes, and it is intrinsic to sangha. The kindness we have can never be replaced by a machine. What is most true about kindness is that we need more of it.

*Dangers of the human realm.* Long ago the Buddha identified the dark side of the human psyche with his teaching of the “three unwholesome roots”—greed, aversion, and egoistic delusion. These “three poisons” have sullied and darkened every human generation, including ours. Just because we are Buddhas in the making doesn’t mean that we are blameless. Innately we are good, but that quality is too often clouded.

## Dangers and Gifts of Byteworld

AI is not just chatbots. AI is rapidly being integrated in every aspect of human life. In business, AI is taking over marketing, customer service, and hiring; it is also now doing much entry-level computer programming. In banking, AI does fraud protection, lending, and customer service. Its military uses are rapidly increasing too. Candidly, AI is everywhere. These new AI roles present many dangers; here are just a few of them.

*Addiction.* Social media is already addictive, and harms children; AI is making it more so. Criminals using AI have discovered new ways to defraud, to steal, to harass, to invade privacy, to destroy reputations, even to kill. Terrorists may soon use AI to create a weaponized virus with no cure. Has all this AI-enhanced digital connectivity been worth it, just so we can ask our chatbot for the best recipe for banana bread?

*Jobs.* The fear that AI and humanoid robots driven by AI will replace jobs is everywhere. People say they are afraid for their livelihoods and their very future due to AI. The deeper issue is that for the most part the creators of AI and the politicians who make the rules don’t seem to care that much about people’s worries. Are we on the cusp of major social discontent, even disorder in the streets? AI riots?

*Environmental Impact.* In order to do its work, Byteworld requires huge data centers, many the size of fifteen football fields. They are sprouting up everywhere: in previously quiet suburbs; on farmland that once grew crops for food; on the edge of big cities where there is power and water to satisfy their cooling needs. There are already thousands of these centers supporting the digital “cloud”; it is estimated that in the next ten years, to support AI, 3,000 more of these monster construction projects will be built just in the US, with many more in other countries. Each of them requires vast amounts of water and electricity; many also have huge diesel- or gas-powered turbines that pollute the air. These centers are also noisy; those who live near them say that their sound is a loud sleep-disturbing hum. Some local governments are fighting back, but there are billions of dollars to be made by building out this AI infrastructure. When there is that kind of money to be made, ethics and care tend to go out the window.

*Technology’s Gifts.* To be fair, AI has also brought many new benefits. In the realm of medicine alone, AI is already contributing lifesaving technologies such as early cancer detection. It is speeding all manner of research and helps with weather prediction, eldercare, education, and so much more. These benefits are bound to expand with each passing year.

## My Religion Is Kindness

The Dalai Lama has often said, “My religion is kindness.” Because this is such a simple statement, people may not realize how profound it is. He doesn’t only mean “Kindness is valuable and good.” He means that Buddhism as a wisdom practice transforms us into people who are unconditionally kind. The Buddhist term for that type of person is bodhisattva. Lifeworld is the crucible where this kind of compassion can be nurtured.

Once, when the Dalai Lama was asked if he was angry at the Chinese, he replied, “The Chinese have taken so much from us. I won’t let them take my state of mind.” Even in the face of that pain, he maintained his kind heart. I was, for a time, the personal attendant of renowned Vietnamese Buddhist monk Thich Nhat Hanh. He spoke softly and carefully, as though each word were a treasure. The sound of his voice itself, and the way he lifted the cup of tea I had poured for him, radiated kindness.

For my own teacher, Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, kindness was second nature. I witnessed, so many times, when he reached out to help someone or touch a person who needed his care. One time, I came to meditation early in the morning, and there, on the front steps, was Suzuki, quietly talking to a homeless man. As I stepped past them to enter the building, he didn’t look up. He was doing his work.

This unconditional kindness is, I think, the most precious thing in the world. I fear that the implacable march of technology will crush this treasure. I fear that Byteworld will toss it aside as unnecessary, seeing it as a weakness, dismissing it as unable to make money or wield power—an obsolete quality that human beings will no longer need.

I don’t want that to happen. I want kindness to survive, and not just to survive but to prosper. I want everyone to see through the false promise of a light speed digital future and remember what binds us together and connects us to all life—kindness. Without kindness, I fear, we will become wan and hollow. As the Dalai Lama has said, our religion as Buddhists is kindness. Kindness is the best of who we are. It is our not so invisible power.

## Breathwalking with Byteworld

In the course of pondering Lifeworld and Byteworld, I have created a library of contemplative exercises to help us experience the difference between them. Here is one called “Breathwalking with Byteworld.” It uses a smartphone to illustrate how Byteworld takes us away from ourselves, and how we can return to ourselves by walking in awareness—a venerable Buddhist practice.

To begin, stand in a quiet uncrowded place—a hallway in your house or an unpopulated outdoor path—and lift up your smartphone. Open the phone’s camera app so that you can see the scene in front of you. To start, let the phone drop to your side and begin walking slowly, feet a shoulder-width apart, one step for each exhale, so that your whole body flows with movement and your mind observes it with attention and awareness. In ancient days, Buddhist monks would spend hours each day walking just like this on their verandas or in forests.

Now, lift up your phone and look at it. Watch the scene in your camera unfold while you continue to walk. Notice how the pixel version of what you are seeing gradually absorbs all your attention, while the awareness of your body slowly recedes. The scene you see is almost the same as without your phone, but it is an emulation, a deepfake, if you will. Everywhere, these days, we see people absorbed in that phone world—in airport lobbies, restaurants, classrooms, on sidewalks, even in a moving car—people glued to their phone, watching the alternate universe it presents. Have we all become phone zombies, walking around holding up these shiny rectangles in front of our faces? Sometimes it seems that way.

Now, shift gears again, let the hand that holds your phone drop down, and return to the awareness of breath and your body as you continue to walk. Feel the transition, the bump in the road as the familiar physical world returns and the emulated imagery of the phone screen goes away. The phone is more than a passive copycat. We know now that the apps, texts, photos, and videos on that phone can cause harm. They can hurt children. In the moving car of a distracted texting driver, they can kill. By practicing Breathwalking with Byteworld you can bring the awareness exercise of Buddhist practice to the fore and disempower this deceptive device.

More and more people are becoming aware of how technology is distorting their reality. There are now paid phone apps that lock your phone out for a time, forcing you to give it up when you lack the willpower to do it yourself. You can also go on vacation to an expensive resort that offers a phone-free environment; you give them your phone when you register. These remedies are salves and medicines; look for there to be more of them in the future.

## Looking Ahead

It is hard to say what will happen with all this mad swirl of technological change. There are as many predictions as there are savants to utter them. The truth is no one knows. Meantime, to return to the question that began this essay, *what should we as Buddhists do?*

One possibility is to escape, to remove ourselves as much as possible from the influence of technology and AI. Buddhism’s monastic tradition seems to offer that option. Monastic life is one form of “living off the grid,” staying far from the buzz of the big city, in hidden valleys where everyone knows your name, where people have put away their phones, unplugged their devices from the internet while they tend their own vegetable gardens and write notes to each other in longhand simply because it is more beautiful.

But there is another option besides escape. To paraphrase Pope Leo, “We shouldn’t reject technology but prevent it from dominating humanity.” Buddhists can have a role in that. Bodhisattvas may train in the monastery, but they don’t stay there forever. The vow of the bodhisattva says, “However many beings there are in the world, I vow to liberate them, to care for them all, be kind to them all.” This vow is a commitment not to escape but to engage. As Buddhists we can study the samaras of technology to become more skillful at helping, even as we continue the transformative practices of studying ourselves. We can choose to live in the light of kind action. When there is an opportunity to help, we do not hesitate; when an opportunity doesn’t immediately present itself, we practice patience, tend to our practice and wait. That opportunity will come soon enough.

We can, each in our own way, become exemplars of a life that upholds the highest human values and the deepest inter- and intrapersonal human intelligence, even as AI and its manic golems sweep the world. The bodhisattva vow manifests an awareness and an intelligence that no machine or digital brain can match. We Buddhists dedicate our lives to it, and uphold it as long as we can until others rise to take our place. Even in the face of the loudest criers of technological doom—who may, in the end, be wrong—we keep confidence in that vow.

May it be so.

articleBody:
The Roman baths of Cimiez originally belonged to the ancient Roman city of Cemenelum, located in the modern district of Cimiez, Nice.

The ruins of the frigidarium of the northern baths have always been visible, never having been covered over since Roman times.  The frigidarium of the northern baths was long mistakenly called the "Temple of Apollo".

Three thermal complexes were eventually uncovered; the north, east and west complexes.  The three groups follow the same layout, with the axis and the order of the rooms are identical.

The ancient city's aqueducts brought water to the thermal complex.  The comprehensive water drainage system consists of a complex network of sewers and canals which is still visible around the site.

At the beginning of the 5th century, the first bishop of Cimiez, Saint Valerian, established the episcopal complex here made ip of a cathedral, baptistery, outbuildings, and the bishop's residence located north of the baths.  The basilica was built on the Roman walls using reused materials.  The columns from the northern baths were used in the construction of the baptistery.

Only a tiny part of the ancient city of Cemenelum has been excavated so far.  As such there is still debate about the exact dates of the bath complexes.

title: When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)

articleBody:
“ *La ciudad es más que la gente.* ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in *Invasión*, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when *Invasión* came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as[Jorge Luis Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Luis_Borges) — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to *Invasión* ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters [Adolfo Bioy Casares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_Bioy_Casares). Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled [Borges](https://link.amazon/B0dw5EXR9)) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own *ficciones*, it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that *Invasión* was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in [one version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JbJZHB8Ce4E) with optional English and French subtitles, and [another, higher resolution version](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QxP1ftEepoE) with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding [foley work](https://www.openculture.com/2018/05/how-the-sounds-you-hear-in-movies-are-really-made-discover-the-magic-of-foley-artists.html) and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, *Nouvelle* *Vague*, political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about *Invasión*, there is no one answer.

title: Wie Politik Wissenschaft in Debatten einsetzt
subtitle: Auf welche Art und Weise beziehen sich Parteien auf Wissenschaft?
feedText: Welche Themen und Argumente spielen dabei eine Rolle? Das hat der Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner von der Universität Wien untersucht. Es zeigt sich: Rechtspopulist*innen nutzen am seltensten wissenschaftliche Bezüge, Grüne und Liberale am häufigsten.
