articleBody:
Auf welche Art und Weise beziehen sich Parteien auf Wissenschaft? Welche Themen und Argumente spielen dabei eine Rolle? Das hat der Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner von der Universität Wien untersucht. Es zeigt sich: Rechtspopulist*innen nutzen am seltensten wissenschaftliche Bezüge, Grüne und Liberale am häufigsten.

**Sie haben mit** **Jakob-Moritz Eberl und Sophie Lecheler von der Universität Wien [untersucht, wie Parteien in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten](https://jcom.sissa.it/article/pubid/JCOM_2506_2026_A09/) auf Wissenschaft Bezug nehmen. Wie sind Sie darauf gekommen, dass das ein lohnendes Forschungsthema wäre?**

**Daniel Wiesner** ist Doktorand in der Forschungsgruppe für Politische Kommunikation (POLCOM) an der Universität Wien. In seiner Dissertation befasst er sich mit der Rolle von Wissenschaft in politischen Diskursen. Foto: Jakob-Moritz Eberl

In meiner Dissertation geht es darum, wie Wissenschaft im politischen Diskurs eingesetzt und repräsentiert wird. Parlamentsdebatten sind spannend, weil in dieser Arena die unterschiedlichen Parteien miteinander kommunizieren. Es gibt ein argumentatives Hin und Her, das man in anderen Kanälen nicht findet. Gleichzeitig sind diese Debatten sehr nah am Policymaking-Prozess, also an konkreten politischen Gestaltungsprozessen. Man kann daran erkennen, welche Partei Wissenschaft wie zitiert, um ihre Entscheidungen zu rechtfertigen.

**Welche Verbindungen haben Politik und Wissenschaft idealerweise?**

Grundsätzlich ist beides stark miteinander verbunden. Wissenschaft ist wichtig für politische Entscheidungen, aber natürlich hat auch Politik Einfluss auf Wissenschaft – zum Beispiel über die Finanzierung oder eine bestimmte Agenda, die vorgegeben wird. Im konkreten Kontext der parlamentarischen Arbeit gibt es diese Idealvorstellung des evidenzbasierten Policy-Makings im Sinne von „Follow the Science“. Dieses Idealbild hat etwas mit der kultivierten Vorstellung von Wissenschaft als objektiver, rationaler und überlegener Wissensquelle zu tun, die sowohl in der Gesellschaft vorherrscht, aber auch von Politiker*innen vermittelt wird. Dahinter steckt die Idee, dass man dringende soziale und politische Probleme durch wissenschaftliche Evidenz lösen kann. Oft funktioniert das aber nicht ganz so einfach. Am Ende ist es doch oft eine politische Entscheidung, verschiedene Pro- und Contra-Argumente abzuwägen und eine Entscheidung zu treffen, die positive, aber gleichzeitig auch negative Folgen in unterschiedlichen Lebensbereichen der Bürger*innen haben kann. Dieses Spannungsfeld ist interessant.

**Sie haben**mehr als 100.000 Reden**des österreichischen Nationalrates von 1996 bis 2018 analysiert. Dazu mussten Sie erst einmal festlegen, was als Bezug zur Wissenschaft gewertet wird. Wie haben Sie das gemacht?**

Ja, das war eine Herausforderung. Wir haben zwei Hauptkategorien festgelegt. Die erste war „wissenschaftliche Akteur*innen“, also Wissenschaftler*innen und wissenschaftliche Institutionen. Die sind relativ einfach zu erkennen, weil sie meistens namentlich genannt werden. Bei der zweiten Kategorie, „wissenschaftliche Evidenz“, war das ein bisschen schwieriger. Es gibt konkrete Verweise auf spezifische Studien, aber auch abstraktere Konstrukte wie „die Wissenschaft sagt“. Wir haben deshalb ein breites Wörterbuch mit Schlüsselbegriffen erstellt. Large Language Models haben dann kodiert, ob ein Bezug zu einer spezifisch genannten Person, Institution, zu Studien oder Wissenschaft und wissenschaftlichen Erkenntnissen im abstrakten Sinn vorkommen.

### „Es gab keinen allgemeinen Trend zu mehr oder weniger Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Vor allem während der Covid-19-Krise hätten wir erwartet, dass wissenschaftliche Bezüge deutlich häufiger vorkommen. Aber es war fast ausschließlich in Gesundheitsdebatten der Fall.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Art und Qualität der zitierten wissenschaftlichen Belege haben Sie nicht untersucht. Sie können also nicht ableiten, wer die „bessere“ Evidenz hat? **

Wir haben nicht erhoben, um welche Studien es geht, ob es seriöse wissenschaftliche Arbeiten sind und ob die Studien richtig zitiert wurden. Worauf wir uns konzentriert haben, ist das Selbstverständnis der Parteien – also wie sie Wissenschaft für ihre politischen Positionen verwenden und welches Selbstbild sie transportieren. Sind sie besonders wissenschaftshörig oder besonders kritisch?

**Haben Sie die Ergebnisse überrascht?**

Es gab überraschendere und weniger überraschende Aspekte. In etwa 20 Prozent der untersuchten Debatten kam irgendein Bezug zu Wissenschaft vor. Das ist nicht besonders viel oder wenig, das hatten wir ungefähr erwartet. Spannender war die zeitliche Komponente. Es gab keinen allgemeinen Trend zu mehr oder weniger Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Vor allem während der Covid-19-Krise hätten wir erwartet, dass wissenschaftliche Bezüge deutlich häufiger vorkommen. Aber es war fast ausschließlich in Gesundheitsdebatten der Fall – zum Beispiel in Form von Studien zur Wirksamkeit von Impfungen und zu Auswirkungen von Kontaktbeschränkungen. Aber das hat nicht auf andere Politikfelder abgefärbt, in denen die Debatten so weitergeführt wurden wir bisher.

**Während es im Zeitverlauf kaum Veränderungen gab, haben Sie durchaus Unterschiede zwischen den Parteien gefunden. Welche waren die deutlichsten?**

Zum einen haben wir gesehen, dass die kleineren Parteien häufiger auf Wissenschaft verweisen als die großen, etablierten Parteien. Das könnte damit zusammenhängen, dass sie bei bestimmten Themen noch kein eindeutiges Profil haben und deswegen stärker auf Wissenschaft verweisen.

Zum anderen haben wir gesehen, dass es inhaltliche Unterschiede gibt, wie die Parteien Wissenschaft interpretieren. Die rechtspopulistische FPÖ zeigte die geringsten Referenzen zur Wissenschaft. Aber nicht nur in Bezug auf die Häufigkeit, sondern auch auf die Frage, wie eine Partei über Wissenschaft spricht, zeigten sich Unterschiede. Bei der FPÖ sahen wir, dass sie eine starke konfrontative Logik in den Reden verfolgt, in denen Wissenschaft vorkommt. Es wird häufig eine Outgroup benannt – zum Beispiel politische Gegner*innen oder Migrant*innen, von denen man sich abgrenzt.

### „Bei der FPÖ sahen wir, dass sie eine starke konfrontative Logik in den Reden verfolgt, in denen Wissenschaft vorkommt. Es wird häufig eine Outgroup benannt – zum Beispiel politische Gegner*innen oder Migrant*innen, von denen man sich abgrenzt.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Es wird also regelmäßig auf Wissenschaft Bezug genommen – jedoch selektiv und passend zur eigenen Parteilinie?**

Ja, genau. Wir haben uns im zweiten Teil unserer Analyse die „typischen“ und „untypischen“ Wörter im Wissenschaftsdiskurs der jeweiligen Parteien angesehen. Dadurch werden die Themen und Terminologien deutlich, die eine Partei etablieren möchte. Bei den Grünen wurde das Wort „ökologisch“ beispielsweise häufig verwendet und bei den Sozialdemokraten der Begriff „Arbeitnehmer*innen“. Typisch für den FPÖ-Diskurs war der Bezug auf „Linke“ als politische Gegner*innen und „Ausländer“. Begriffe wie Umweltpolitik, Klimaschutz und Energiefonds wurden bei der FPÖ hingegen sehr selten verwendet.

Auffällig war bei den Grünen, aber vor allem auch bei den liberalen Neos, dass sie Begriffe wie „Evidenz“ und „evidenzbasiert“ verwendeten, was der Follow-the-Science-Logik entspricht, weil Politik dadurch wissenschaftlich begründet wird. Die FPÖ verwendete diese Begriffe selten und hatte stattdessen meist einen konfrontativen Claim, den die Ergebnisse einer Studie untermauern sollten – beispielsweise, dass Migrant*innen laut Forschungsergebnissen zu viele Sozialleistungen in Anspruch nehmen würden.

Anteil der verschiedenen Darstellungsweisen von Wissenschaft an der Gesamtzahl der Reden der jeweiligen Partei (1996–2022). Abbildung: [Wiesner et al. (2026)](https://jcom.sissa.it/article/pubid/JCOM_2506_2026_A09/)

**Bei welchen politischen Themen spielte Wissenschaft eine Rolle?**

Vor allem bei Gesundheit, aber auch bei Umwelt, Technologie, Energie und bis zu einem gewissen Grad auch Bildung. Diese fünf Themen kamen am häufigsten vor. Es gab einige Themenbereiche, bei denen Wissenschaft eine sehr geringe Rolle spielte, was uns zum Teil überrascht hat – zum Beispiel bei Wirtschaft und Arbeit. Die wissenschaftlichen Referenzen waren hier selten, obwohl es viele Studien zu wirtschaftlichen und sozialen Themen gibt. Möglicherweise gibt die Parteiposition in diesen Bereichen stärker die Richtung vor, sodass es Wissenschaft schwerer hat, zitiert zu werden als beispielsweise bei Gesundheitsfragen.

**Wissenschaft hat es demnach bei bestimmten Themen schwerer, in parlamentarischen Debatten vorzukommen. Haben Sie überlegt, wie sich das ändern ließe?**

Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass sich die Politik auf ihre Muster verlässt und die Themen gewissermaßen den Bezug zur Wissenschaft vorgeben. Aber ich denke, dass sich einiges ändern ließe. Es zeigt sich zum Beispiel, dass Institutionen wie Scientific Advisory Boards innerhalb der Parlamente einen positiven Effekt haben. 1 Wenn Wissenschaft für Entscheidungsträger*innen aufbereitet und verfügbar gemacht wird, hat das einen positiven Effekt auf evidenzbasiertes Policy-Making. In einem anderen Forschungsstrang schaut man, wie wissenschaftliche Argumente, die politische Implikationen haben, formuliert sein könnten. In der Honest-Broker-Diskussion („ehrliche Vermittler*innen“, Anm. d. Red.) nach Roger A. Pielke 2 lautet eine Annahme, dass es besonders vorteilhaft wäre, wenn Wissenschaftler*innen Evidenz präsentieren, ohne dabei politische Positionen oder Richtungen vorzugeben. Empirische Forschung hierzu zeichnet jedoch kein einheitliches Bild. Die Alternative wäre ein Advocacy-Modell, in dem Wissenschaftler*innen verstärkt Policy-Empfehlungen abgeben. Das ist ein spannendes Feld, und eine Frage, die uns wohl auch in Zukunft noch weiter beschäftigen wird.

### „Es gab einige Themenbereiche, bei denen Wissenschaft eine sehr geringe Rolle spielte, was uns zum Teil überrascht hat – zum Beispiel bei Wirtschaft und Arbeit.“

Daniel Wiesner

**Gibt es ähnliche Studien aus anderen Ländern – beispielsweise Deutschland?**

Zu parlamentarischen Reden gibt es relativ wenig. Eine Ausnahme ist eine Studie 3, in der über einen langen Zeitraum die Rhetorik im US-Kongress analysiert wurde. Es ging um die Frage, ob eher eine evidenzbasierte oder intuitionsbasierte Sprache verwendet wurde. Ansonsten gibt es ein breites Forschungsfeld, dass sich den Policy-Making-Prozess anschaut – also politische Dokumente, in denen bestimmte Quellen zitiert werden. Aber zum parlamentarischen politischen Diskurs gibt es relativ wenig.

**In welche Richtung würden Sie gerne weiterforschen?**

Zum einen zur angesprochenen Frage: Wie akkurat sind diese Darstellungen von Wissenschaft, also mehr im Sinne eines Fact Checkings, ob wissenschaftliche Argumente korrekt repräsentiert werden und welche Arten von Quellen innerhalb des politischen Diskurses herangezogen werden. Auf der anderen Seite interessiert mich auch: Was denken Bürger*innen über diese Argumente? Haben sie eher eine Follow-the-science-Erwartung oder wünschen sie sich abwägende politischen Prozesse, in denen Wissenschaft einbezogen wird, aber die Entscheidung am Ende doch bei der politischen Ebene liegt?

## Raccoon Who Passed Out in Liquor Store Inspires Merch That Raises Over $290,000 for Charity

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/drunk-racoon-trashed-panda/)

> View this post on Instagram
> [A post shared by SBS Bourbon Destination – Best Of Georgia 2025 磊 (@sprayberrybottleshop)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DRz5XqsD6bc/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

On November 29, 2025, one particularly mischievous raccoon made headlines after reportedly breaking into a liquor store in Ashland, Virginia, helping itself to the booze, and passing out on the bathroom floor. Nearly a year later, the raccoon’s drunken antics inspired [Hanover County Animal Protection and Shelter](https://www.instagram.com/hanover_county_animal_shelter/) to launch a merchandise line called *Trashed Panda*, which has raised more than $290,000 for the charity so far.

According to Hanover County Animal Protection (HCAP), an officer was called to the liquor store on that fateful morning. When she arrived, she discovered that the raccoon had somehow made its way inside and pulled several bottles of liquor from the shelves. The party animal was later found sprawled face down on the bathroom floor and was apparently “very intoxicated.”

HCAP shared photos of the chaotic scene on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/hcvaanimalprotection/posts/pfbid0SXn6S2de9rSYxkzPr8LPXuzYGJTxMfMiQEjdviPawuPoNa2EW5h4rWUSLbxqDdbSl) with the caption, “Officer Martin safely secured our masked bandit and transported him back to the shelter to sober up before questioning. After a few hours of sleep and zero signs of injury (other than maybe a hangover and poor life choices), he was safely released back to the wild, hopefully having learned that breaking and entering is not the answer.”

The funny story quickly went viral, and even inspired a [Saturday Night Live sketch](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lFiEKPTaaRc). HCAP decided to turn the raccoon’s embarrassing moment into a fundraising opportunity, so they teamed up with apparel company [Bonfire](https://www.bonfire.com/one-year-of-trashed-panda-1/) to launch a merchandise collection. The series of t-shirts, sweatshirts, hats, stickers, and cups features a playful illustration of the passed-out raccoon alongside the nickname “Trashed Panda” and the tagline, “One bad night. A whole lot of good.” Seasonal designs also featured clever slogans like, “Hot Trash Summer” and “Trick or Trashed.”

While the shelter typically receives less than $20,000 in donations each year, the *Trashed Panda* merchandise has generated more than 10 times that amount, bringing in over $290,000. The funds raised have already helped support animals in care and equip all eight of the department’s animal protection officers with body cameras, which will support their work investigating animal cruelty cases and responding to other calls.

“To everyone who shared the story, purchased merchandise, or simply followed along for the laughs, thank you for turning one raccoon’s poor decisions into something truly meaningful,” said HCAP in a [Facebook post](https://www.facebook.com/hcvaanimalprotection/posts/pfbid0UXYMe6Hr4d3FUbP7g5hA7yV81ewBd6RWVpWiGYSc4AwCwh8sWDJLsc4kgZtcDRohl) announcing the final run of the merch. “As for our furry celebrity, we hope he’s enjoying his quiet retirement and staying out of the liquor stores.”

Check out the [Trashed Panda collection on Bonfire](https://www.bonfire.com/one-year-of-trashed-panda-1/).

articleBody:
arXiv:2611.18642v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

articleBody:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious. Stamp was arrested for suspected breaches of the Financial Services and Markets Act: the FCA believed it had evidence he was offering financial services, such as debt and investment advice, without a licence. The day he was arrested, police also raided an industrial estate in Chessington, south-west London, where Stamp’s company had its offices, and seized dozens of computers and files.

title: Learning the language of machine learning
subtitle: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work.
feedText: Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves. articleBody:
When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice.

Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves.

The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand.

“Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).

Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application.

“We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says.

**A love of language**

Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on.

One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day.

That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming.

Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup.

His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too.

“I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says.

Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text.

“I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls.

**A seismic shift**

He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher.

Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems.

Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein.

Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning.

Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data.

“It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says.

He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them.

“This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls.

He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT.

**Faculty focus**

After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019.

“It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says.

His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information.

The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand.

These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies [“patches of grass near animals” in input images](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11114).

“That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says.

On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior.

“We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says.

**A changing environment**

The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new.

That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments.

It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil.

“I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says.

With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations.

This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet.

“Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says.

In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer.

He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress.

And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.

title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing

articleBody:
### “Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time.”

“‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she [calibrated love and loss](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/05/28/emily-dickinson-grief/). But she did not mean that it is good to ruminate and wallow — Dickinson so deftly played with the surface of meaning, so delighted in startling us into a flinch or furrow before plunging us into the deeper truths she fathomed. She meant, I think, that a love lost is grieved forever, whatever the nature of the loss — this [she knew](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/12/10/emily-dickinson-love-letters-susan-gilbert/), and turned the ongoingness of it into a lifetime of art — but by looking back, we are reminded over and over that the sharp edge of grief does smooth over time, that today’s blunt ache is worlds apart from the first stabs, until grief becomes, as Abraham Lincoln wrote in his [stirring letter of consolation](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/13/letters-of-consolation/) to a bereaved young woman, “a sad sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.”

Art by Sophie Blackall for [“Dirge Without Music”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/25/dirge-without-music-emmy-noether/) from [The Universe in Verse](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/).

And besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway? We never lose people, not really. I don’t mean this in some mystical sense — let there be no confusion about [what actually happens when we die](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/01/10/alan-lightman-death/). I don’t even mean it in [the poetic sense](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/04/07/the-more-loving-one-auden-universe-in-verse/). I am speaking strictly from the point of view of the mind emerging from the dazzling materiality of the brain — that majestic cathedral of cortex and synapse shaping every thought we have and every feeling we tremble with.

I am speaking of the paradox inside the brain:

On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.

On the other hand, no person we have loved is ever fully gone. When they die or vanish, they are physically no longer present, but their personhood permeates our synapses with memories and habits of mind, saturates an all-pervading atmosphere of feeling we don’t just carry with us all the time but live and breathe inside. Or the opposite happens, which is its own devastation — the physical body remains present, but the person we have known and loved, that safehouse of shared memories and trust, is gone — lost to mental illness, to addiction, to neurodegenerative disease.

Art by Sophie Blackall for [“Dirge Without Music”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/25/dirge-without-music-emmy-noether/) from [The Universe in Verse](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/).

In both cases, the brain is tasked with the slow, painful work of reconstituting its map of the world, so that the world makes sense again without the beloved person in it. Mapping, in fact, is not a mere metaphor but what is actually going on in the brain, since our orientation in spacetime and our autonoeic consciousness — the capacity for mental self-representation — [share a cortical region](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/09/24/wayfinding-m-r-oconnor/).

Where the missed and missing person goes on the map, how the remapping actually unfolds, and what it takes to redraw the map in such a way that the world feels whole again are the questions coursing through [The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss](https://www.maryfrancesoconnor.com/book) ([public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/grieving-brain-the-surprising-science-of-how-we-learn-from-love-and-loss/oclc/1314227228&referer=brief_results)) by neuroscientist **Mary-Frances O’Connor** — a pioneer in fMRI research since the technology first became available, who has devoted a quarter century to studying the particular neurophysiology of grief. She writes:

> The brain devotes lots of effort to mapping where our loved ones are while they are alive, so that we can find them when we need them. And the brain often prefers habits and predictions over new information. But it struggles to learn new information that cannot be ignored, like the absence of our loved one.
> […]
> Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve, and grieving necessitates learning to live in the world with the absence of someone you love deeply, who is ingrained in your understanding of the world. This means that for the brain, your loved one is simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time. You are navigating your life despite the fact that they have been stolen from you, a premise that makes no sense, and that is both confusing and upsetting.

Making an important distinction between grief (“the intense emotion that crashes over you like a wave, completely overwhelming, unable to be ignored”) and grieving (an ongoing process punctuated by recurring moments of grief but stringing the moments into a larger trajectory), O’Connor adds:

> Grieving requires the difficult task of throwing out the map we have used to navigate our lives together and transforming our relationship with this person who has died. Grieving, or learning to live a meaningful life without our loved one, is ultimately a type of learning. Because learning is something we do our whole lives, seeing grieving as a type of learning may make it feel more familiar and understandable and give us the patience to allow this remarkable process to unfold.
> […]
> Grief never ends, and it is a natural response to loss. You will experience pangs of grief over this specific person forever. You will have discrete moments that overwhelm you, even years after the death when you have restored your life to a meaningful, fulfilling experience. But… even if the feeling of grief is the same, your relationship to the feeling changes. Feeling grief years after your loss may make you doubt whether you have really adapted. If you think of the emotion and the process of adaptation as two different things, however, then it isn’t a problem that you experience grief even when you have been grieving for a long time.

*Discus chronologicus* — a German depiction of time from the early 1720s, included in [Cartographies of Time](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/02/07/cartographies-of-time/). (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/discus-chronologicus-german-time-model-from-the-1720s_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [a wall clock](https://society6.com/product/discus-chronologicus-german-time-model-from-the-1720s_wall-clock?curator=brainpicker).)

Although volumes have been written about the psychology, philosophy, and poetics of grief — none more piercing than [the Joan Didion classic](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/05/joan-didion-on-grief/), none more practical than [Seneca’s advice to his bereaved mother](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/02/seneca-consolation-to-helvia/) — there is something singularly revealing about exploring grief from the point of view of the brain beneath the mind, which must begin at the developmental beginning. Childhood — the brain’s most fertile growth period, when most of its major infrastructure is laid out — is also our training ground for loss. Every time we are separated from our primary caregivers, we experience scale-models of loss; every time they return, we learn that the loss of their presence is not a loss of their person, of their love. (A pause worth taking: every abandonment is a miniature of grief.)

In those formative attachments, we also learn the role we ourselves play in the relationship. Because, in building its relational world-map, the brain is constantly computing our loved ones’ position in three dimensions — time, space, and closeness, also known as psychological distance — we learn the causal link between our behavior and a caregiver’s position in the closeness dimension, just like we learn the causal link between our bodily movements and our position in space. When there is secure attachment, the child learns that throughout various surface disruptions, situational factors, and passing emotional weather patterns, there is a steadfast underlying closeness. O’Connor writes:

> Closeness is partially under our control, and we learn how to maintain and nurture this closeness, but we also trust those who love us to maintain that closeness as well.

The obvious — and heartbreaking — corollary is that children who grow up without secure attachment experience the pangs of miniature grief much more readily throughout life, with each departure of a loved one, however temporary, because trusting a continuity of closeness does not come naturally to us. But no matter the formative experience of closeness, human beings are universally undone by the death of someone close — the final abandonment, at once the most abstract and the most absolute absence, in which our brains simply cannot compute the total removal of a person so proximate and important from the fabric of psychological spacetime.

*Vanish* by Maria Popova. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/vanish5800978_print?sku=s6-21581797p4a1v46?curator=brainpicker).)

Citing the disoriented devastation of a woman ghosted by a lover, O’Connor notes that “ghosting” is the neurologically appropriate word-choice for such abandonments — studied under fMRI, the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to “ghosting” behaves much the same way as the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to death, the mental map suddenly crumbled and torn to pieces. O’Connor describes the strange yet strangely sensical way in which the brain copes with this incomprehensible disruption of reality:

> If your brain cannot comprehend that something as abstract as death has happened, it cannot understand where the deceased is in space and time, or why they are not here, now, and close. From your brain’s perspective, ghosting is exactly what happens when a loved one dies. As far as the brain is concerned, they have not died. The loved one has, with no explanation, stopped returning our calls — stopped communicating with us altogether. How could someone who loves us do that? They have become distant, or unbelievably mean, and that is infuriating. Your brain doesn’t understand why; it doesn’t understand that dimensions can simply disappear. If they don’t feel close, then they just feel distant, and you want to fix it rather than believe they are permanently gone. This (mis)belief leads to an intense upwelling of emotions.
> […]
> If a person we love is missing, then our brain assumes they are far away and will be found later. The idea that the person is simply no longer in this dimensional world, that there are no here, now, and close dimensions, is not logical.

Drawing on brain imaging studies, she adds:

> The ephemeral sense of closeness with our loved ones exists in the physical, tangible hardware of our brain.

The particular bit of hardware is the brain’s posterior cingulate cortex — our built-in GPS of love. Scanning the environment and processing innumerable bits of sensory information, the PCC is constantly calibrating and recalibrating the psychological distance between us and the people we love, tightening the bond the closer we feel and loosening it when we sense distancing. Death turns the GPS into a crude compass trying to orient to an all-pervading, ever-shifting magnetic field suddenly bereft of its true north. O’Connor writes:

> After the death of a loved one, the incoming messages seem scrambled for a while. At times, closeness with our deceased loved one feels incredibly visceral, as though they are present in the room, here and now. At other times, the string seems to have fallen off the board — not shorter or longer than it was before, but simply stolen from us entirely.

*Liminal Worlds* by Maria Popova. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/liminal-worlds-by-maria-popova_print?curator=brainpicker).)

This confusion is so fundamental and so primal, so beyond the reach of reason, that it befalls minds indiscriminately along the spectrum of intelligence and self-awareness — a reality most clearly and devastatingly evinced in [the extraordinary love letter](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/10/17/richard-feynman-arline-letter/) Richard Feynman wrote to his wife 488 days after her death and 6,994 days before he won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

But O’Connor notes that while Western physicians long believed such continuing bonds across the life-death divide to be a symptom of poor coping with grief that makes for poorer bonds with the living, recent research drawing on various grief rituals and customs from cultures around the world has demonstrated that such ongoing inner dialogue with the dead might actually enrich our relationships with the living and allow us to show up for them in a fuller, more openhearted way. She writes:

> Our understanding of ourselves changes as we gain wisdom through experience. Our relationships with our living loved ones can grow more compassionate and resonant with gratitude as we age. We can also allow our interactions with our beloved ones who are gone to grow and change, even if only in our minds. This transformation of our relationship with them can affect our capacity to live fully in the present, and to create aspirations for a meaningful future. It can also help us to feel more connected to them, to the best parts of them… Their absence from our physical world does not make our relationship to them any less valuable.
> […]
> Instead of imagining an alternate what if reality, we must learn to be connected to them with our feet planted firmly in the present moment. This transformed relationship is dynamic, ever-changing, in the way that any loving relationship is ever-changing across months and years. Our relationship with our deceased loved one must reflect who we are now, with the experience, and perhaps even the wisdom, we have gained through grieving. We must learn to restore a meaningful life.

The greatest challenge, of course, is the perennial challenge of the human mind — how to integrate seemingly contradictory needs or ideas in such a way that they coexist harmoniously, perhaps even magnify each other, rather than cancel each other out. Without such integration, any new relationship can feel like a threat to this ongoing inner bond with the dead, undamming a flood of grief at the notion of emotional erasure: grief for the grief itself, for that outstretched hand holding on to the gone and to ourselves at the same time, to the map as it used to be. This is a fear so understandable as to cusp on the universal. It is also — and this might be the most assuring part of O’Connor’s research — a neurophysiologically misplaced fear. Within the brain, every person we love leaves a tangible, structural imprint, encoded in synapses that can never be vanquished or replaced by new and different love. Because that bond — like every bond, like every idea, like the universe itself — was [“only ever conjured up in the mind,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/04/10/antidotes-to-fear-of-death-rebecca-elson/) it is there too that it always lives, unassailable by other minds and other events.

Art by Sophie Blackall for [“Dirge Without Music”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/25/dirge-without-music-emmy-noether/) from [The Universe in Verse](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/).

O’Connor writes:

> Gaining a new relationship is simply not going to fill the hole that exists. Here is the key — the point of new roles and new relationships is not to fill the hole. Expecting that they will can only lead to disappointment.
> The point is that if we are living in the present, we need to have someone who loves us and cares for us, and we need someone to love and care for as well. The only way to enjoy a fulfilling relationship in the future, however, is to start one in the present. If we can imagine a future in which we are loved, then we must start a relationship that eventually will become important to us in a way that is different from our previous relationship, but rewarding and sustaining.

Understood this way, then, the ongoing relationship with the gone is a lavishment to other loves, for it has made us exactly who we are — the person doing the loving, the person being loved, the mapmaker of present and possible worlds. O’Connor offers neural affirmation for this poetic aspiration:

> After a loved one dies, they are clearly no longer with us in the physical world, which each day proves to us. On the other hand, they are not gone, because they are with us in our brain and in our mind. The physical makeup of our brain — the structure of our neurons — has been changed by them. In this sense, you could say that a piece of them physically lives on. That piece is the neural connections protected within our skull, and these neural connections survive in physical form even after a loved one’s death. So, they are not entirely “out there,” and they are not entirely “in here,” either. You are not one, not two. That is because the love between two people, that unmistakable but usually indescribable property, occurs between two people. Once we have known love, we can bring it into our awareness, we can feel it emerge and emanate from us. This experience reaches beyond the love for the flesh and bones of the person we once knew on this earthly plane. Now loving is an attribute of us, regardless of who we share it with, regardless of what is given to us in return. This is a transcendent experience, a felt sense of being loving without needing anything in return. In the very best moments together, we learned to love and to be loved. Because of our bonded experience, that loved one and that loving are a part of us now, to call up and act on as we see fit in the present and the future.

Complement [The Grieving Brain](https://www.maryfrancesoconnor.com/book) with a mathematician’s [geometric model for living with grief](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/11/10/geometry-of-grief-michael-frame/) and this [soulful animated film](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/25/dirge-without-music-emmy-noether/) of “Dirge Without Music” by Edna St. Vincent Millay — the most beautiful homily on the emotional paradox of loss I know — then revisit Nick Cave’s life-honed wisdom on [grief as a portal to greater aliveness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/07/27/nick-cave-loss-grief/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

articleBody: A massive study of more than 340,000 adults found that moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death, while even light consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was linked to increased risk. Although heavy drinking was harmful regardless of beverage type, the findings suggest that the relationship between alcohol and health may be more complicated than previously thought.

articleBody: This study evaluates the performance of a fully integrated in-ear EEG device by comparing it with simultaneous clinical-grade scalp EEG recordings in 29 healthy adults. The analysis focused on two electrophysiological markers: resting-state alpha activity (8–12 Hz) and auditory steady-state responses (ASSRs). ASSRs were tested using both single-frequency stimulation (40 Hz and 80 Hz) and more complex multi-frequency chirp configurations. A significant alpha peak was detected in the in-ear recordings of 15 of 29 participants (52%), compared with 83–100% for the scalp derivations. In-ear alpha peak power and signal-to-noise ratio were significantly correlated with scalp EEG at all six scalp derivations, indicating that the device preserves inter-individual differences in alpha strength despite reduced signal amplitude. The in-ear device recovered the group-level alpha frequency, but agreement with scalp EEG for individual alpha frequency (IAF) was limited. ASSR performance depended strongly on the stimulation paradigm. In-ear ASSR detection rates were lower than scalp rates at both modulation frequencies; at the two highest intensities, they reached 39–44% of the rate of the ipsilateral temporal scalp derivations at 40 Hz and 74–75% at 80 Hz. More complex multi-frequency stimulation resulted in a marked reduction in detection performance in both recording modalities. Overall, in a short controlled laboratory session, the fully integrated in-ear EEG system captured resting-state alpha activity and detected auditory steady-state responses under simple stimulation conditions in a subset of participants.

subtitle: A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this Canadian house's renovated kitchen, designed by local studio Perron.

articleBody:
A dedicated space for preparing tea has been placed at the heart of this [Canadian](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/canada/) house's renovated [kitchen](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/kitchens/), designed by local studio Perron.

[Perron](https://www.perrondesign.ca/) overhauled the kitchen for a longstanding client, with whom the studio has worked on several professional and personal projects over the years.

### Drawings and photography

Previous

Next

### Drawings and photography

Close

Her residence sits along the south shore of the St Lawrence River, overlooking Quebec City on the opposite bank.

The view across the water, and the client’s love of tea, were the primary guiding elements for the renovation project.

"For this house, we were not simply working from a checklist of requirements," said Perron founder Nathalie Perron.

"We already knew about our client’s lifestyle, energy and the things that are most important to her."

The kitchen space was divided into three zones: a space for tea, a central cooking area and a counter overlooking the river.

At the entrance, a small counter wrapped in glossy oxblood red tiles and a partition of burgundy steel bars form a niche that the client has nicknamed her "teahouse".

Custom lacquered MDF wall shelves store and display cups, saucers, mugs and teapots that she has collected during her travels over the years.

"Each one evokes a specific memory and now has a place in her daily life," said Perron.

An on-demand hot water tap is also installed within this niche, creating a dedicated space for the tea-making ritual.

The main kitchen area revolves around an angular island, which has space for a bar stool and incorporates a built-in electric stove.

Above, a cylindrical burgundy-hued range hood is framed within more steel bars, suspended from the ceiling to support shelves.

Rows of glass blocks are stacked between the upper and lower cabinets, which are both faced in stained white oak.

Ultra-thin steel shelves hang from the upper millwork, adding extra storage without blocking the light through the translucent bricks.

Opposite, a long counter faces the river through a large window, allowing the homeowner to witness passing ships and changing light conditions as she stands working or washing dishes.

[Read: Perron squeezes all its "colourful operations" under one roof in three-storey Québec building](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/12/13/perron-maison-perron-quebec-city/)

Cristallo quartzite from Brazil forms the countertop and a backsplash.

Long, narrow Cotto Manetti terracotta tiles cover the floor, echoing the shapes of the matte and gloss pink Farblok ceramic tiles by Quintessenza that run up the wall in stripes.

A Mousse wall fixture by Quebec lighting brand [JETA](https://www.jeta.studio/en) adds another feminine touch to the kitchen.

"It is a house that reflects a woman who enjoys going on adventures, but who has created a home that she loves returning to," said the studio.

Perron has offices in Montreal and Quebec, the latter in an early 20th-century building renovated to house a [studio, showroom and Nathalie Perron's home](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/12/13/perron-maison-perron-quebec-city/).

See more innovative kitchens in our [Dezeen Lookbooks](https://www.dezeen.com/lookbooks/) series, including examples with [striking islands](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/03/01/ten-striking-kitchen-islands-lookbooks/), [open storage](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/03/kitchens-open-shelving-storage-lookbooks/), [natural wood finishes](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/01/04/kitchens-warm-natural-wood-lookbooks/) and [no wall cabinets](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/03/16/kitchens-without-wall-cabinets-lookbook/).

title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication
subtitle: The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally c…
feedText: We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f4 a…
articleBody: The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

subtitle: Human learning is a dynamic cognitive process in which latent knowledge and competency states evolve through sequential interactions.

articleBody: Human learning is a dynamic cognitive process in which latent knowledge and competency states evolve through sequential interactions. However, existing generative AI learning-support systems often separate learner-state modeling, resource recommendation, knowledge-grounded generation, and pedagogical planning, limiting adaptive performance and interpretability. This study proposes ICG-AGLS, an interdisciplinary competency graph-guided adaptive generative AI learning support framework. It models learner states from historical interactions, projects them into a competency space, and constructs an interdisciplinary competency graph linking courses, concepts, resources, assignments, and competency dimensions. The framework integrates competency-gap-guided recommendation, graph-guided retrieval-augmented generation, adaptive reasoning routing, and multi-agent pedagogical coordination. Experiments on MOOCCubeX, OULAD, and EdNet demonstrate consistent improvements across learner-state modeling, recommendation, knowledge-grounded generation, and multi-agent planning. ICG-AGLS achieves an AUC of 0.871, Recall@10 of 0.812, ROUGE-L of 0.772, and a task completion rate of 0.839, outperforming representative task-specific baselines. These findings suggest that competency-structured latent-state modeling provides an interpretable computational bridge between evolving human learning states and adaptive generative AI at the behavioral and computational-representation levels, rather than establishing direct neural correspondence. The framework offers practical potential for personalized learning support in higher education.

Despite the presence of developing testes and markedly reduced estrogen concentrations in fadrozole-treated ch…
articleBody: Sexual differentiation of the brain of birds is shaped by gonadal steroid hormones and also by cell-autonomous mechanisms resulting from limited sex chromosome dosage compensation. In this study, we compare gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens treated with the aromatase inhibitor fadrozole to their control counterparts. Consistent with a lack of dosage compensation, we find a robust effect of sex chromosomes on hypothalamic gene expression, and a large portion of differentially expressed genes were on the Z and W sex chromosomes. Despite the presence of developing testes and markedly reduced estrogen concentrations in fadrozole-treated chromosomal female (ZW) birds, we find modest effects of gonadal hormones on gene expression in the brain. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis revealed that the most prominent effects were attributable to interactions between chromosomal sex and treatment. Our results highlight that chromosomal sex and steroid hormones together shape the sexual differentiation of the embryonic avian brain, challenging the primacy of the organizational effects of sex steroids on the brain during development.

articleBody: BackgroundVitamin B12, folate and thyroid-function testing are routinely included in dementia workups, but their prognostic significance after a neurocognitive-disorder diagnosis remains uncertain.MethodsWe analyzed a deidentified Taiwanese tertiary-hospital cohort of patients aged ≥65 years with neurocognitive disorders (dementia or mild cognitive impairment; n = 7,969). The prespecified primary analyses were mixed-effects models of annual MMSE and CDR-SB trajectories in which baseline vitamin B12, folate, TSH and free thyroxine were entered jointly, restricted to patients with all four biomarkers and at least two assessments (MMSE n = 818; CDR-SB n = 1,009). CDR progression and all-cause mortality were secondary outcomes, and prescription-record analyses were exploratory. Sensitivity analyses addressed missing data, selection into the analysis sets, competing risks, confounding, laboratory timing and prior treatment.ResultsBiomarker testing and repeated cognitive assessment were clinically driven, so all estimates apply to a selected tested-and-followed subgroup that was younger, less impaired and less likely to die than untested or unfollowed patients. Higher baseline vitamin B12 was associated with slower MMSE decline (β +0.146 points/year per SD, 95% CI +0.038 to +0.255; FDR q = 0.017), an association retained after multiple imputation and selection weighting but attenuated after excluding patients treated before baseline. The full-range association of higher TSH with slower decline on both scales was not robust: it depended on a few patients with TSH > 10 mIU/L and was absent within the euthyroid range. Folate deficiency was associated with faster CDR progression (HR 1.57, 95% CI 1.13–2.19, p = 0.008), including in competing-risk models; the estimate for vitamin B12 deficiency was imprecise (HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.88–1.69, p = 0.23) and does not exclude a clinically relevant increase. Higher vitamin B12 was associated with all-cause mortality (HR 1.035 per 100 pg/mL, 95% CI 1.016–1.055), but this was attenuated after flexible adjustment for renal function. Documented vitamin B12 supplementation showed no detectable association with CDR-SB trajectory in a small exploratory matched analysis.ConclusionIn patients who underwent biomarker testing and repeated cognitive assessment, routine biomarkers from workups for reversible causes provided modest, context-dependent prognostic information. We interpret these associations as possible indicators of clinical state rather than evidence that the biomarkers, or their correction, influence the progression of neurocognitive disorders.

articleBody:
Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the <model> element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update:

- Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal
- transform to move multiple models independently
- position-anchor to snap models together
- @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting,
- Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit,
- Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene.

To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to

**Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**.

You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators)

## The big picture

The 3D <model> element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context. These context cues can include the device display capabilities, window size, and color theme. These requirements will remain**even as we include spatial content** — and ideally, authors should be able to use the same kinds of patterns to build for the spatial web.

And spatial *content* should not just be designed for spatial *devices*. The last few years have seen a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content – on phones, tablets and computers as well as headsets. Spatial web standards should support designing **for browsers wherever they run**.

### New web features, classical CSS

Even better, the numerical parameters can be animated and transitioned in the same way that any other value can be changed on the page.

visionOS 27.3 offers the first components of spatial CSS in a developer preview, and this article demonstrates how to use them through the case study of a simple set of children’s blocks.

## Feature breakdown

### spatial: portal

The feature that kicks this all off is the declaration that an element is acting as a *portal*, through the new spatial:portal syntax. Elements that can contain other elements – think <figure>, <div> – can act as a portal, and will then act as a space that all of the child elements nested inside it share. This preview focuses on model elements, but the specification is written so that this approach should work for all content.

### spatial transform:

Once the models are collected inside a shared space, you can then move, rotate, and scale them using their standard transform attribute. This takes the same DOMMatrix class that creates 2D and pseudo-3D transforms in other contexts, but can now act as a *true* 3D transform to objects inside the portal context.

A simple scene of shaped blocks and a board to slot them in.

< div class = "world" style = "spatial:portal;" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >
< style >
</ stye >

The code for presenting this scene and setting the blocks off to the sides.

The board and the block objects can be moved and rotated independently — an expanded settings panel shows different values. While a model’s animation timeline could manage single sequence of action, this adds the degrees of freedom required for more sophisticated interaction or configuration.

### position-anchor

Fitting 3D objects together can get complicated. We need a way to attach models to specific places on other models — think of putting together pieces of furniture. Model is a [void element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Void_element), which means it means we can’t nest models *inside* other model elements the same way that other DOM is nested. Instead, we’re borrowing from the CSS concept of position-anchor and adding a way to align and orient objects according to their anchors. position-context: anchor is the way to make it work.

#### See it in action

The scene presented earlier with the octagonal block slotted exactly into place.

< div class = "world" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >

< style >
</ style >

The code for using position-anchor to achieve the correct placement for the block.

The board used in the example consists of three separate objects inside the 3D program it was built within: The visible shape of the board itself, and two *reference* positions — often called “null objects” or “empties” in 3D editors. These correspond to the correct position for each of the shape blocks to slot into when they’re on the board. Here’s the scene and its contents inside Blender:

The default view of the block scene presented inside Blender. Note both the block objects and the target objects in-place on the board.

Rather than copy-pasting values from your 3D editor, or having to guess at the right transform, you can nominate specific anchor points — just like in the 2D equivalent of the feature — to place an object in the right location. These anchor points can be animated, too, making it easier to compose elements even when they’re moving around.

### @environment-map

An environment map is the lighting that is reflected off of an object — think of it as the room that an object appears within.

We introduced environment maps as an HTML attribute on the model element, because it was the only element that would be able to use it. Now that there is a broader range of elements that will be able to *share* environment maps. Taking inspiration from @keyframes for animation, we leverage @environment-map to facilitate this. This preview provides support for 360º HDR images and adds the clarifying syntax to indicate what they are and how to work with them.

#### See it in action

The scene showing a spooky-colored underlighting effect.

< div class = "world spooky" >
<!--... -->
</ div >
@ .world The code for setting up the spooky environment lighting.

### portal-action:orbit

One of the main things that users want to do with 3D content is to look around it by rotating the scene in-place. In 3D programs this is often called an ‘orbit’, and spatial CSS enables it with the new portal-action attribute. It may be useful to add more modes in the future like pan-x or pan-y. This mirrors the model element’s stagemode attribute on the HTML element, but by configuring it in CSS it becomes more flexible.

### requestVolumetricScene()

In addition to showing a spatial arrangement inside a portal, visionOS has the ability to show these scenes *outside* of the browser window in what we’re calling a Connected Volumetric Scene. Launch a request from a user action to remove the spatial content from its portal and present it in the user’s space:

launchSpaceButton. addEventListener ( "click", event = > {
const world = document. querySelector ( ".world" );
world. requestVolumetricScene ();
});

The code to launch the volumetric scene.

Users can place the volumetric scene anywhere in their space, and the live link between the web page and the volumetric scene will let you update the scene — add or remove objects, or move them based on your needs.

### Your feedback is essential

There is a long journey ahead, and a lot more to get to in the [proposed spatial CSS specification](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/). While this feature preview is limited to visionOS, we thought it was important to release along with the full specification as an indication of how to approach bringing spatial concepts to the web. Along with the general release of the <model> element on Safari 27, we hope this gives authors enough to think about the opportunities — and requirements — that lie ahead in the spatial web. That’s also why it’s so important for authors to **explore the feature preview** and tell us about their experience of using it. You can download the visionOS simulator with Xcode. If you don’t already have Xcode, you can [download Xcode from the Mac app store.](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/xcode/id497799835?mt=12)

To share your thoughts on the Spatial CSS feature preview, find us on Mastodon at [@jensimmons@front-end.social](https://front-end.social/@jensimmons), [@jondavis@mastodon.social](https://mastodon.social/@jondavis), or on X at [@zachernuk](https://x.com/zachernuk). Or send a reply on X to [@webkit](https://x.com/webkit). You can also follow [WebKit on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/apple-webkit/). If you run into any issues, we welcome your feedback about WebKit at [bugs.webkit.org](https://bugs.webkit.org/). Filing issues really does make a difference. Thanks.

Launch a request from a user action to remove the spatial content from its portal and present it in the user’s space: launchSpaceButton. addEventListener ( "click", event = > { const world = document. querySelector ( ".world" ); world. requestVolumetricScene (); }); The code to launch the volumetric scene. Users can place the volumetric scene anywhere in their space, and the live link between the web page and the volumetric scene will let you update the scene — add or remove objects, or move them based on your needs. ### Your feedback is essential There is a long journey ahead, and a lot more to get to in the [proposed spatial CSS specification](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/). While this feature preview is limited to visionOS, we thought it was important to release along with the full specification as an indication of how to approach bringing spatial concepts to the web. Along with the general release of the element on Safari 27, we hope this gives authors enough to think about the opportunities — and requirements — that lie ahead in the spatial web. That’s also why it’s so important for authors to **explore the feature preview** and tell us about their experience of using it. You can download the visionOS simulator with Xcode. If you don’t already have Xcode, you can [download Xcode from the Mac app store.](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/xcode/id497799835?mt=12) To share your thoughts on the Spatial CSS feature preview, find us on Mastodon at [@jensimmons@front-end.social](https://front-end.social/@jensimmons), [@jondavis@mastodon.social](https://mastodon.social/@jondavis), or on X at [@zachernuk](https://x.com/zachernuk). Or send a reply on X to [@webkit](https://x.com/webkit). You can also follow [WebKit on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/apple-webkit/). If you run into any issues, we welcome your feedback about WebKit at [bugs.webkit.org](https://bugs.webkit.org/). Filing issues really does make a difference. Thanks.

title: ‘He used Pornhub as the gun’
subtitle: Late on a Tuesday night in September 2019, Tina’s phone pinged with a message.
feedText: The subject line read, in part, “fuck you slut!!!!!” The message contained a link to Pornhub, the world’s most popular porn site. articleBody:
Late on a Tuesday night in September 2019, Tina’s phone pinged with a message. The subject line read, in part, “fuck you slut!!!!!” The message contained a link to Pornhub, the world’s most popular porn site.

At the time, Tina — who spoke to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists on the condition that her last name not be used — had recently ended a relationship with an abusive boyfriend. When she had tried to break up with him months earlier, Tina said he coerced her into making sexually explicit videos. It was his way, she told ICIJ, of controlling her.

Tina’s ex-boyfriend had now published those videos on Pornhub. It was the beginning of a months-long campaign of harassment and death threats: He posted videos and photos of her more than 100 times on Pornhub, according to emails reviewed by ICIJ, using accounts created in her name and including her address, phone number and employer.

He also posted photographs of her underage daughters at the beach in bikinis, along with their names and contact information. He emailed one daughter with a link to the videos of Tina and told her to ask her mother “why she put you all in danger from weirdos all over the country.”

“My ex wanted to kill me,” Tina said. “And he used Pornhub as the gun.”

Pornhub’s owner, the Montreal-based company Aylo, runs some of the world’s most popular websites. Its network of over 100 sites — including Pornhub, YouPorn and RedTube — attracts more than 100 million visits every day and has generated hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue, according to the most recent available data.

Aylo’s profits were built in part on some of the most heinous material on the internet. At the time of Tina’s abuse in September 2019, anyone could create a free account on Pornhub and upload videos; Pornhub did not require verification of the uploader’s identity.

Aylo has long employed moderators, whose job includes the identification of instances of sex trafficking, as well as photos and videos of minors. But the company was overwhelmed by the deluge of content: More than 6.8 million videos were uploaded to Pornhub in 2019; the company bragged in its 2019 “year in review” that if a viewer started watching all of them in 1850, they would still be watching.

Tina is just one of the many individuals victimized on the company’s websites. In 2020, Aylo removed more than 347,000 videos for nonconsensual content, according to [a complaint](https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/AyloGroupLtd-et-al-Complaint.pdf) filed by the Federal Trade Commission and the state of Utah. Aylo has made numerous changes since then — such as verifying the identity of uploaders — but its own reports show that potentially abusive and exploitative content continues to be published on Pornhub.

ms because, in the words of one employee in an email to a colleague, they were used frequently in BDSM and staged blackmail videos, and thus “relatively compliant” with the company’s terms of service (Pornhub told ICIJ that “blackmail” and “forced” are currently banned on all Aylo platforms).

This exchange was included in court documents reviewed by ICIJ from a class-action lawsuit against Aylo filed in Alabama in February 2021. The documents, which were supposed to be sealed, inadvertently became publicly accessible on the court’s electronic docket for eight months because of a filing error. A judge recently granted preliminary approval to a settlement agreement in that case and a related California class action. As part of the settlement, Aylo committed to the single largest known payout to victims in the company’s history.

Aylo does not want the world to see what these records reveal about its business practices. After ICIJ approached the company for comment for this article, Aylo asked a federal judge in Alabama to bar ICIJ from publishing “any information learned or derived from” the documents. This extraordinary request threatened to muzzle ICIJ’s reporting on Aylo’s behavior, far beyond the contents of the court filings.

The judge rejected Aylo’s motion to prevent ICIJ from publishing an article based on the records.
