The documents, which largely concern abusive content posted in 2020 and earlier, show a company that often fell short of those standards. Even notification from law enforcement of CSAM on the company’s sites was no guarantee that the illegal content would be promptly removed. In one instance, according to a deposition of an Aylo employee included in the court filings, Pornhub kept a video featuring the abuse of a 12-year-old boy online for more than a month after being informed of it by an Alabama law enforcement special agent.

In an internal email, an Aylo employee wrote that there was a request in this case “NOT to remove the content.” A separate civil complaint filed by the abused boy’s mother alleged that law enforcement officers informed Aylo that the illegal content was on its site three times, over a period of multiple weeks, and requested that it be removed.

Other CSAM videos remained on the site for years. And when discovered, some Aylo employees viewed their presence more with bemusement than horror.

“You guys want to laugh,” one moderator wrote to colleagues in 2020, as the company tested new CSAM detection software. “It caught a cp [child pornography] video from 2009 … a full on cp video on the site for 11 yrs.”

Another employee described a former moderator as “almost blind,” and wrote that he “put through so much stuff loool.”

Pornhub’s victims described a cycle of trauma as they struggled to scrub their name and images from the internet. Tina said Pornhub was too slow to take down the accounts with her name and contact information. And when they were finally removed, she said, her ex-boyfriend would simply create a new account and post the videos again.

The Pornhub email address used by victims to submit takedown requests included an automated response stating that an employee would respond within two days. Perversely, the response also promoted a program enabling users to “make money from your homemade videos.”

Tina would often realize the videos had been reposted because men would deluge her with lewd calls. Pornhub notified Tina that it “fingerprinted” her videos, a technology that generates a unique digital signature of a video to prevent its reupload, seven months after she first notified the company of them, according to emails reviewed by ICIJ.

Even before Tina’s videos first appeared, Pornhub had publicly touted its “state-of-the-art” fingerprinting technology to prevent revenge porn from being reuploaded. As Tina was struggling frantically to get her videos offline, Pornhub’s executives formulated a policy that called for victims of revenge porn to be offered fingerprinting services. But Tina says Pornhub did not tell her that her videos had been fingerprinted until she sent an all-caps email notifying the company that she was a crime victim. “DO BETTER PORNHUB!!!!,” the email read.

But Tina’s nightmare was still not over. Even after Pornhub removed the videos, it would sometimes leave the page on which they resided that included her personal information, emails reviewed by ICIJ showed. To this day, a Google search of her name brings up Pornhub results, though not the videos themselves; other porn sites also include her address at the time.

Tina eventually moved to a new city because she no longer felt safe in her neighborhood. She became anxious if someone looked at her too long or when she was around large groups of men. She wasn’t in a relationship for years.

“I wish I had been raped physically because then it would only have been once,” she said. The reuploading of the videos, the online comments about her body by strangers, the lewd calls, she said, “felt like a rape every single time.”

The documents in the Alabama case also cast doubt on the company’s assurances about its methods to prevent the spread of CSAM. In a 2020 blog post, for example, the company touted its use of fingerprinting technology, which meant that any CSAM videos it found “cannot be re-uploaded,” it wrote.

But a few months before that blog post was published, Aylo executives drafted a policy covering how to respond when law enforcement officers report the existence of CSAM to the company. Aylo would not “communicate fingerprinting action back to complainant unless asked,” the document stated, “because we do not want to be seen as offering a guarantee” that the content would not reappear. This was necessary because the contractor providing fingerprinting services “has its limitations.”

Aylo’s then-CEO also told a Canadian parliamentary committee that requiring uploaders to provide government-issued identification to verify their age and identity meant that “every piece of content on our websites can be traced back to its uploader.” But the court documents show that the contractor tasked to verify the IDs of uploaders warned Aylo that “sophisticated and determined fraudsters” could defeat its technology.

This requirement would also not have thwarted some of the previous abusers mentioned in the Alabama court documents. The person who abused the Jane Doe at the center of the Alabama class-action lawsuit was verified. The abuser who victimized the 12-year-old boy was not only verified but allegedly sold videos of the abuse for $5 to $20 through Pornhub’s revenue-sharing program, according to the civil complaint filed by the boy’s mother. Some of the videos remained for sale for almost seven months and attracted more than 180,000 views and 1,100 subscribers — meaning that Aylo profited directly from the abuse, the complaint alleges.

**The internet is terrestrial. It’s people going into buildings every day and making decisions.** — Justine Li, cyber exploitation victims’ advocate

Tina and other victims described to ICIJ obsessively searching their names on Google, agonizing over the continued presence of their abuse online. For them, one of the most important interventions is the erasure of their names and intimate images from the internet. But it is often relief that remains out of reach.

Justine Li, a sex trafficking survivor herself, launched the National Center for Victims of Internet and Cyber Exploitation last year to offer victims a single portal through which they can manage takedown requests.

Li’s strategy is to target what she calls the “internet iceberg.” At the top are the operators of the sites that host the illegal content. Below the surface are other companies — hosting providers, payment processors and advertising networks — that keep the sites operational and making money.

She works to identify all of the companies that are supporting a site hosting illegal content, along with their contact information — pressure points on an industry that she says is too callous to act.

Li tells victims she will never stop fighting to get their images off the internet. But she is careful not to offer them any guarantees. “We can’t promise that things will come down,” she said. “That’s not the reality.”

Even failure, Li believes, has a purpose. She can use evidence that the options for victims are not working to push for new laws.

“People think the internet is this celestial realm where laws cannot be enforced,” Li said. “No, the internet is terrestrial. It’s people going into buildings every day and making decisions. … There’s a lot we can do that’s still on the table.”

articleBody:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Tons of new vaccines are in the pipeline](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/524-new-vaccines/)

» [Polio is very nearly wiped out](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3037-polio-wiped-out/)

» [The Cost of Renewable Energy is Plunging](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/586-cost-renewables-falling/)

» [The EU Gender Pay Gap is (slowly) Decreasing](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3030-eu-gender-pay-gap/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

articleBody: IntroductionObsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is clinically heterogeneous, and responses to OCD-relevant images remain incompletely understood. We compared oculomotor activity, stimulus-locked event-related potentials (ERPs), and presaccadic measures.MethodsThirty-eight volunteers with OCD and 38 healthy controls (HC) completed an emotional pro−/antisaccade task with neutral and OCD-relevant images (aggression, contamination, checking, symmetry) during simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking. Subjective valence and arousal ratings were collected. Clinical subgroup, image-category, and symptom-severity analyses were exploratory.ResultsVolunteers with OCD rated symmetry images as less pleasant and both symmetry and contamination images as more arousing than HC. Antisaccade correction rates were higher in volunteers with OCD. Mean and peak saccade velocities were higher during prosaccade trials when correct and erroneous saccades were analyzed together. These group differences were no longer statistically significant when only correct saccades were analyzed. Volunteers with OCD showed reduced P2 and N2 amplitudes and prolonged N2 latencies. Significant main effects of the image category were observed for P3 amplitude revealed a significant difference between aggression and symmetry stimuli, with symmetry images eliciting lower amplitudes. Stimulus-locked ERPs showed no statistically significant Group × Image Category interactions. Presaccadic measures showed no statistically significant group differences. Exploratory analyses within the OCD group suggested an association between higher Y-BOCS (Yale–Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale) scores and shorter P2 peak latency for symmetry images. No statistically significant differences were detected among clinical subgroup.DiscussionResponses to individually symptom-matched and unmatched images were not directly compared. Affective symptoms, treatment exposure, and psychiatric comorbidity limit attribution to OCD alone. Exploratory findings require replication in larger samples with adequate subgroup representation. Non-significant results do not establish equivalence between groups or clinical subgroups.

articleBody:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled [“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”](https://calnewport.com/the-deep-life-some-notes/) As I explained:

> “To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote [several](https://calnewport.com/on-productivity-and-the-deep-life/) [more](https://calnewport.com/work-and-the-deep-life/) [essays](https://calnewport.com/more-on-cultivating-a-deep-life-mindset/) on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I [launched my podcast](https://podcasts.apple.com/at/podcast/ep-1-my-new-task-system-deep-work-with-kids-and/id1515786216?i=1000476077409), I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, [ The Deep Life: A Structured Approach ](https://www.thedeeplife.com/), is now [available for pre-order](https://www.thedeeplife.com/).

*The Deep Life* brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend [Oliver Burkeman](https://www.amazon.com/Four-Thousand-Weeks-Management-Mortals/dp/1250849357/), to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

> “It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is *the* *key* that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

- [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach/dp/0593544870/)
- [Barnes & Noble](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/w/the-deep-life-cal-newport/1150475131)
- [Bookshop.org](https://bookshop.org/p/books/the-deep-life-tk-cal-newport/e0548b9282c19397)
- [Amazon UK](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Deep-Life-Structured-Approach-Meaning/dp/024184777X?maas=maas_adg_5415FAC779DFD0467C9715278D881B94_afap_abs&ref_=aa_maas&tag=maas&th=1)
- [Waterstones ](https://www.waterstones.com/book/9780241847770?sv1=affiliate&sv_campaign_id=117976&awc=3787_1794332947_70780920f00186c80dbe28e794089d47&utm_source=117976&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_campaign=Penguin+Books)

You can also pre-order [ a signed copy ](https://peoplesbooktakoma.com/product/the-deep-life/) from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, **I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it**, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. *Why not make it deep?*

articleBody: MEKK3/MAP3K3 links experimentally defined receptor, scaffold and endothelial mechanisms that could influence spinal cord injury (SCI), but their relevance depends on the initiating lesion and the intervention tested. This critical narrative Review separates mechanical traumatic SCI from spinal cord ischemia–reperfusion (SCIR) and compares MEKK3 with related MAP3Ks. We audit the experimental attributes of 19 selected published primary studies and retain author-reported quantitative observations with their assay conditions and sampling units. The only spinal injury intervention study in this collection concerns SCIR; it combines direct MEKK3 knockdown in cultured cells with an upstream miRNA intervention in animals. Published comparisons identify preferential p62 binding by MEKK3 relative to MEKK2, stimulus-dependent inflammatory requirements, and distinct roles for mitochondrial clearance and mitochondrial signaling. Vascular experiments distinguish loss of a physiological MEKK3 function from release of cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM)-complex restraint. Drug studies further separate changes in lesion size from lesion number and prevention from treatment of established disease. These comparisons explain why a shared downstream marker or beneficial drug response cannot independently identify MEKK3 as the causal target. The synthesis supplies a traceable account of what the published experiments resolve and derives focused questions for myeloid, mitochondrial and endothelial responses after spinal trauma. MEKK3-specific therapeutic efficacy in mechanical SCI remains unestablished.

articleBody:
*“Hey, I’ll get a job…when I hear the true call.” — Slacker (1990)*

About 10 years ago, I met a woman who worked as a mid-level software engineer at Facebook. She didn’t work on machine learning, but just for fun, she read a bunch of papers and got into the subject as a hobby. Later, in the pandemic, she quit her boring corporate job and spent a few years unemployed, contemplating the meaning of life. She made her own clothes, learned ballet, made cute Instagram videos, dyed her hair, and went to a bunch of hackathons (almost all of which she won).

Also in the late 2010s, I knew a man who had been a promising software engineer and data scientist, and before that a top performer on the International Math Olympiad. But when I met him, he was spending a few years unemployed — crashing at his girlfriend’s place, playing Hearthstone (and becoming one of the top-ranked players in the world), learning to skateboard, going on hippie retreats, and contemplating the meaning of life.

Both of those people are billionaires now. They are Sasha Sheng and Diogo Almeida, two of the three founders of [TypeSafe AI](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/09/the-maker-of-non-text-ai-model-jev-valued-at-7-5b-just-weeks-after-launch/), a startup that was recently valued at $7.5 billion (and in which I invested a small amount of money). TypeSafe invented Jev, an all-new kind of AI model that bypasses human language, and so is able to make decisions much faster and more cheaply than Claude or GPT. It was an incredibly creative idea — one that the big labs are [racing to copy](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/30/openais-jev-clone-could-help-the-frontier-lab-stop-its-swarming-agents/) — and it took an incredible amount of hard work to realize.1

Sasha’s and Diogo’s roundabout, seemingly improbable route to stunning success is actually more common in the tech world than you might think. Steve Jobs is the most famous example — he famously dropped out of college, not to start Apple, but to do psychedelic drugs, crash on friends’ floors, immerse himself in hippie spirituality, live on a commune, and travel around India looking for enlightenment before eventually inventing the personal computer and becoming the most beloved tech icon in American history. Jack Dorsey, Larry Ellison, and Mitch Kapor all had their own periods of aimlessness.

Nor is this sort of life path confined to the tech world. History is full of examples of people who looked lackadaisical until they suddenly rose to greatness:

- [Ulysses S. Grant](https://www.ericfoner.com/reviews/110212washpost.html) drank copiously, worked as a clerk in a leather store, engaged in various failed business ventures and was said to lack ambition — until one day he rejoined the military and became the most successful and important military commander in the entire Civil War, as well as President of the United States.
- [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin#Early_life_and_education) neglected his medical studies and turned in a mediocre performance on his exams at Cambridge, routinely going hunting and riding instead of studying, before becoming a naturalist, signing up for an ocean voyage, and inventing the theory of evolution.
- [James Cameron](https://achievement.org/achiever/james-cameron/) was a college dropout and a truck driver, before seeing Star Wars prompted him to quit his job and teach himself how to make movies, ultimately becoming one of the most commercially successful movie directors of all time. ([Kevin Smith](https://blogs.iu.edu/establishingshot/2017/08/10/no-one-is-supposed-to-be-anywhere-at-anytime-the-irreverence-and-freedoms-of-clerks/) had a similar path to success, except his inspiration was the movie Slacker.)
- [Haruki Murakami](https://stephenphelan.co.uk/articles/murakami/) ran a jazz bar and had little ambition, before suddenly deciding to become a novelist, and eventually becoming one of the most celebrated writers in the world.

I like to tell these stories because they demonstrate an approach to success in life that I believe is overlooked and deserves more recognition. I call it “bumbition”.

“Bumbition” is an obvious portmanteau of “bum” and “ambition”. In general, we think of ambitious people and slackers as polar opposites — ambitious people work hard, set goals for themselves, and are constantly motivated, while slackers drift aimlessly, laze around, or fail to apply their talents. A lot of our culture is oriented around pushing young people to be ambitious instead of turning into bums.

Bumbition, however, defies placement on the ambitious/bum spectrum. It exhibits elements of both. For a significant portion of their life, a bumbitious person doesn’t strive hard, or apply themselves to definite goals…until a clear and compelling opportunity presents itself. When that opportunity to do something really interesting or impactful *does* come up, the bumbitious person is quick to recognize it, and works very hard to exploit it.

The key here is that bumbition is not simply *intermittent ambition*. It’s a fundamentally different approach to life — it has different goals and motivations, and when it succeeds, it succeeds for different reasons.

An ambitious person is always working toward a set of goals — either those they define for themselves, or those defined by the people around them. Those goals could include:

- “Make partner by age 30”
- “Start a unicorn startup”
- “Get a tenured job at a top 10 research university”
- “Make a hundred million dollars”
- “Conquer Central Asia”

…And so on. The purpose of achieving those goals — the motivation that drives ambitious people — is to feel a sense of personal success.

A bumbitious person does *not* automatically have a goal at all times,2 because they tend to be motivated less by the need to feel successful than by the desire to do something intrinsically *interesting or worthwhile*. Such projects are inherently in short supply, in part because what constitutes an inherently “interesting” or “worthwhile” project is highly subjective. An ambitious person can always identify some brass ring that would make them feel like a success; a bumbitious person will often wait years or even decades before finding that one magical opportunity or life calling.

In fact, this is bumbition’s inherent limitation. Sitting around waiting for the right opportunity to present itself is a highly uncertain, risky endeavor. There’s always the possibility that it won’t come until you’re old, or that it’ll come but you’ll fail to see it in time.

The other problem with bumbition is that waiting around for the right opportunity comes with a bunch of costs and risks. Your technical skills and work ethic can decay over time. You can get caught up in life’s various stumbling blocks — bad relationships, drug addictions, depression, etc.

But bumbition also has some big advantages over the ambitious life. One is that *ambition can keep people overly busy*. If you’re the kind of person that always has to be working toward a goal, and you can’t find a truly great project to work on, you’ll end up working on a modest or mediocre one. If Steve Jobs had become distracted by getting a perfect GPA at Reed College, he might never have had time to start Apple. If Ulysses S. Grant had focused on owning his own leather goods store, he might not have leapt at the chance to join the U.S. Army. If Sasha Sheng had focused on climbing the corporate ladder at Meta, she wouldn’t have founded TypeSafe.

Paul Graham talks about this in his essay “[How to Do Great Work](https://www.paulgraham.com/greatwork.html)”:

> Ambition comes in two forms, one that precedes interest in the subject and one that grows out of it. Most people who do great work have a mix, and the more you have of the former, the harder it will be to decide what to do…The trouble with planning is that it only works for achievements you can describe in advance. You can win a gold medal or get rich by deciding to as a child and then tenaciously pursuing that goal, but you can't discover natural selection that way.

In his book *Zero to One*, Peter Thiel — who I’d classify as an ambitious rather than a bumbitious person — recounts a vivid example of how his ambition almost prevented him from becoming a tech titan:

> [A]fter a conventionally successful undergraduate career, I enrolled at Stanford Law School, where I competed even harder for the standard badges of success. The highest prize in a law student’s world is…a Supreme Court clerkship…I was invited to interview for clerkships with Justices Kennedy and Scalia. My meetings with the Justices went well. I was so close to winning this last competition. If only I got the clerkship, I thought, I would be set for life. But I didn’t.
> At the time, I was devastated…With the benefit of hindsight…winning that ultimate competition would have changed my life for the worse…Had I actually clerked on the Supreme Court, I probably would have spent my entire career taking depositions or drafting other people’s business deals instead of creating anything new.

Nor is this bumbition’s only advantage. The “bum” phase — the time spent traveling in India, or working at a convenience store, or playing Hearthstone on a couch — isn’t just a holding pattern. The seeming aimlessness of this period of life can serve several important functions that facilitate rapid success once a good opportunity gets spotted.

First, and most importantly, time away from the grind of constant striving allows people to *broaden their perspective*. A lot of unique and original ideas come from *recombinant innovation* — from combining insights and perspectives from vastly different fields.3 Even something as simple as changing the context of your surroundings can [improve creativity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19210055/). For an intelligent person with a restless mind, the “bum” phase of life leads to a lot of play and exploration that can end up sparking novel ideas. Here’s [a fun example](https://www.asc.ohio-state.edu/kilcup.1/262/feynman.html) from Richard Feynman:

> I used to enjoy doing physics. Why did I enjoy it? I used to play with it. I used to do whatever I felt like doing - it didn't have to do with whether it was important for the development of nuclear physics, but whether it was interesting and amusing for me to play with…Now that I am burned out…I'm going to play with physics, whenever I want to…
> Within a week I was in the cafeteria and some guy, fooling around, throws a plate in the air. As the plate went up in the air I saw it wobble…I had nothing to do, so I start to figure out the motion of the rotating plate…I went on to work out equations of wobbles. Then I thought about how electron orbits start to move in relativity. Then there's the Dirac Equation in electrodynamics. And then quantum electrodynamics.

Steve Jobs’ study of calligraphy, during his hippie period, [famously helped him](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2005/06/youve-got-find-love-jobs-says) to think about what would make the letters on a personal computer look beautiful to the eye.

A related advantage is that the “bum” phase also allows people to develop their *interests*. [Paul Graham talks about](https://www.paulgraham.com/greatwork.html) how “excited curiosity” will often lead people to their most important life’s work. Bumbitious people aren’t just waiting around; they’re *playing* around, actively searching for something that sparks their interest. In contrast, if you’re constantly grinding away, it can be hard to develop that curiosity.

A “bum” phase also gives people a chance to broaden their *human networks*. When you’re working hard towards a goal, you usually don’t have much time to meet a lot of people outside work — i.e., outside your narrow current field of endeavor. Ambitious people are *always* working toward a goal, and thus get relatively little time to go meet interesting people from other walks of life. But the “bum” phase gives bumbitious people time to meet all kinds of folks. This can lead to hearing about radical new opportunities, getting insights from other fields, or even meeting useful partners for a new venture.

Broadly speaking, the “bum” phase of bumbition serves two purposes. It represents *waiting and exploration time*, as people patiently wait for the big opportunity that will define their career. But it also represents *personal development time*, either deliberate or unconscious, that helps bumbitious people to better see the big opportunities when they come along.

Now, I don’t mean to claim that bumbition is better than ambition, or vice versa — either in terms of personal success, or in terms of changing the world. Among the greats of any field — politics, business, academia, literature — you can find plenty of examples of both ambitious and bumbitious people.

But I think our society *underemphasizes bumming*. We have a tendency to frown on people who spend years unemployed, neglecting work in order to play video games or make Instagram videos. We assume that these people are being lazy or squandering their potential, and we tell them to get back to the grind and make something of themselves. Other societies, of course, tend to be even worse on this score — China treats its slacker generation as [a national security threat](https://thediplomat.com/2026/05/why-china-treats-lying-flat-as-a-national-security-threat/).

In the AI age, this could be even more consequential. AI algorithms are consummate hill-climbers — set them to a task, give them some data, and they’ll be more ambitious than the hardest-working Stanford law student. In a world of abundant AI, *setting AI on the right goals* will be an increasingly central human task. Figuring out the right goals requires exploration, unique perspectives, and curiosity — all things that bumbition facilitates. We should be teaching our young people to be more bumbitious.

At the same time, we should remember that being bumbitious isn’t just a matter of sitting around on the couch. Just because you tell yourself you’re waiting to hear the true call doesn’t mean you’ll actually hear it when it comes. You have to actually want to do something great — whatever that means to you — and you have to be ready to work incredibly hard for years when that something presents itself. Bumbition isn’t the same as ambition, but it also isn’t the same as being a lifelong bum.
